concepts.metaphor: Two dancers may move together, oppositely, or without a consistent linear rhythm.
concepts.question: For equally likely pairs (0,6) and (4,2), what is the covariance?
concepts.feedback: The means are 2 and 4. The deviation products are (−2)×2 and 2×(−2), so covariance is (−4−4)/2 = −4.

sources.title: Deep Learning: Probability and Information Theory
sources.label: Textbook

questions.question: For equally likely pairs (0,6) and (4,2), what is the covariance?
questions.feedback: The means are 2 and 4. The deviation products are (−2)×2 and 2×(−2), so covariance is (−4−4)/2 = −4.
questions.retryFeedback: Center each coordinate using its own mean. Multiply the paired deviations, preserving their signs, and average those products.

questions.question: What does negative covariance indicate?
options: Opposite deviations from the means tend to occur together
questions.feedback: When one variable is above its mean, the other tends to be below its mean.
questions.retryFeedback: Examine the sign of a product when one deviation is positive and the other negative. Covariance averages those paired products.

questions.question: What is the possible range of Pearson correlation when defined?
questions.feedback: Correlation normalizes covariance by both positive standard deviations.
questions.retryFeedback: Pearson correlation normalizes covariance by both standard deviations. The resulting measure of linear association has bounded magnitude.

questions.question: If covariance is 6 and standard deviations are 2 and 3, what is correlation?
questions.feedback: Divide 6 by 2×3.
questions.retryFeedback: Normalize covariance by the product of the two standard deviations, rather than their sum.

questions.question: What happens to covariance with Y if X is multiplied by positive 10?
questions.feedback: Covariance scales with the units of its inputs; correlation does not change under positive rescaling.
questions.retryFeedback: Only one factor in each paired-deviation product is scaled. The centering step scales that deviation by the same amount.

questions.question: If X is replaced by X+100, what happens to its covariance with Y?
questions.feedback: Subtracting the new mean removes the added constant from every deviation.
questions.retryFeedback: Adding a constant to a variable also adds it to that variable's mean. Compare the centered values.

questions.question: Let X be equally likely to be −1, 0, or 1, and let Y = X². Their correlation is 0. Are X and Y independent?
options: Only because all Y values are nonnegative
Only because X has three possible values
questions.feedback: Knowing X determines Y: X = 0 forces Y = 0, while X = ±1 forces Y = 1. Zero linear correlation can coexist with this nonlinear dependence.
questions.retryFeedback: Independence would mean learning X does not change probabilities for Y. Compare the possible Y values when X is zero and when it is not.

questions.question: Why is Pearson correlation undefined when one variable is constant?
options: There are always too many observations
questions.feedback: The normalization would divide by zero.
questions.retryFeedback: Write the correlation denominator as the product of standard deviations. A constant has no variation around its mean.

questions.question: What changes if one variable is multiplied by −1?
options: The sign of a defined correlation flips
questions.feedback: A negative rescaling reverses deviations but leaves standard deviation positive.
questions.retryFeedback: Negating one variable reverses its centered deviations but leaves its standard deviation's magnitude unchanged.

questions.question: Does strong correlation between two measurements establish causation?
questions.feedback: Shared causes, selection, and other mechanisms can produce association without one variable causing the other.
questions.retryFeedback: An association can arise from a common cause, selection, or other mechanisms. Correlation alone does not distinguish them.

concepts.title: Monte Carlo estimation
concepts.definition: Monte Carlo estimation uses random samples to approximate an expected value. Average the results of independent draws from the target distribution. More samples usually make the estimate more stable, but cannot correct a wrong simulation model.
concepts.formulaNote: Average f over n samples from the target distribution. A random seed lets the same implementation reproduce the sampled draws.
concepts.example: Four simulated rewards are 0, 2, 4, and 6. Their sample average is 12/4 = 3, an estimate of expected reward rather than its exact value.
concepts.metaphor: Taste many randomly chosen spoonfuls to estimate the average flavor of a large pot.
concepts.question: Six simulated rewards are 2, 3, 7, 8, 9, and 13. What is their Monte Carlo estimate of expected reward?
concepts.feedback: Their sum is 42. Dividing by the six draws gives the sample-average estimate 7, not a guarantee of the true expectation.

questions.question: Six simulated rewards are 2, 3, 7, 8, 9, and 13. What is their Monte Carlo estimate of expected reward?
questions.feedback: Their sum is 42. Dividing by the six draws gives the sample-average estimate 7, not a guarantee of the true expectation.
questions.retryFeedback: Use every simulated reward, including repeated values if present, and divide their total by the number of draws.

questions.question: Why should ordinary Monte Carlo samples represent the target distribution?
options: Every sample must equal the mean
The average otherwise estimates the wrong expectation
questions.feedback: The sampling scheme determines which population the average represents.
questions.retryFeedback: An unweighted sample mean reflects the distribution that generated its samples. More draws do not change which distribution that is.

questions.question: Standard error describes how much an estimate varies across repeated samples. If it scales as 1/√n for n independent draws, what happens when n is quadrupled?
questions.feedback: The square root of the sample count doubles.
questions.retryFeedback: Apply the square root to the sample-size factor before considering the inverse relation for standard error.

questions.question: If 30 of 100 independent simulated trials succeed, what is the Monte Carlo probability estimate?
questions.feedback: Average the success indicators: 30/100.
questions.retryFeedback: Represent a success as one and a failure as zero. Their sample mean estimates the success probability.

questions.question: Does running more samples automatically fix a biased simulation model?
questions.feedback: More sampling can reduce sampling error while leaving model error intact.
questions.retryFeedback: Sampling error and model error are different. Additional draws can estimate a flawed simulator's predictions more precisely.

questions.question: What does setting a random seed help with?
options: Reproducing sampled draws under the same implementation
questions.feedback: A seed controls the pseudo-random sequence, not the validity of the model or estimator.
questions.retryFeedback: A seed controls the pseudorandom sequence under a particular implementation. It does not establish that the model is correct.

questions.question: Why can highly correlated samples provide less information than the same number of independent samples?
options: They repeat more of the same random variation
questions.feedback: Dependence changes the variance of the average and its effective information content.
questions.retryFeedback: Repeatedly seeing similar fluctuations supplies less independent information. Raw sample count can overstate the effective sample size.

questions.question: For independent samples, estimate the mean’s standard error (variation across repeated estimates) as s/√n. With sample standard deviation s=6 and n=100, what is it?
questions.retryFeedback: Divide the sample standard deviation by the square root of the independent sample count, not by the count itself.

questions.question: Can a Monte Carlo estimate differ on another run?
options: Only if its code is incorrect
questions.feedback: Different random samples usually produce different finite-sample estimates.
questions.retryFeedback: The estimate depends on sampled outcomes. Another set of draws can produce a different average even under the same model.

questions.question: Why might plain Monte Carlo struggle to estimate a very rare event?
options: Too few simulated trials may contain the event
Rare events have probability zero by definition
questions.feedback: Special sampling methods may help, but their weighting and assumptions need to be handled correctly.
questions.retryFeedback: Estimating an event rate requires observing that event. Consider how many occurrences a finite simulation is likely to contain.

concepts.title: Exponential and logarithm
concepts.definition: An exponential raises a fixed base to a variable power. A logarithm gives the power needed to obtain a number. Natural logarithms use the base e ≈ 2.718.
concepts.formula:
log_b(bˣ) = x;   ln(x) = log_e(x)
ln(ab) = ln(a) + ln(b)
concepts.formulaNote: The base b must be positive and different from 1. A real logarithm requires a positive input; the product rule assumes a,b > 0.
concepts.example: 2³ = 8, so log₂(8) = 3. Likewise, e² ≈ 7.389, so ln(7.389) ≈ 2.
concepts.metaphor: An exponential climbs a multiplicative ladder; a logarithm tells you how many rungs you climbed.
concepts.question: What is ln(e³)?
concepts.feedback: The logarithm reverses exponentiation. In later probability losses, logarithms also turn products of probabilities into sums.

questions.question: What is ln(e³)?
questions.feedback: The logarithm reverses exponentiation. In later probability losses, logarithms also turn products of probabilities into sums.
questions.retryFeedback: A natural logarithm asks which power of e produced its input. Apply the inverse relationship before calculating any decimal approximation.

questions.question: What is log₂(16)?
questions.feedback: Two to the fourth power is sixteen.
questions.retryFeedback: Ask which exponent applied to the stated base produces the argument. Multiplying the base by an exponent is a different operation.

questions.question: What is b⁰ for b > 0?
questions.feedback: The zero exponent gives the multiplicative identity.
questions.retryFeedback: Use the exponent rule for bᵃ divided by itself, with a permitted nonzero base, to understand the zero exponent.

questions.question: What is ln(1)?
questions.feedback: e raised to zero equals one.
questions.retryFeedback: Ask what power of e yields the logarithm's argument. A logarithm returns an exponent, not its input.

questions.question: For positive a and b, what is ln(ab)?
questions.feedback: Logarithms turn products into sums.
questions.retryFeedback: Logarithms convert multiplication of positive arguments into an operation on their exponents. Check the product rule rather than the power rule.

questions.question: What is 2⁻³?
questions.feedback: A negative exponent takes the reciprocal of the positive power.
questions.retryFeedback: A negative exponent takes a reciprocal. First evaluate the corresponding positive power, then invert it.

questions.question: Which real input is outside the domain of ln(x)?
questions.feedback: The real logarithm requires strictly positive input.
questions.retryFeedback: The real natural logarithm inverts the positive-valued exponential function. Check which proposed input falls outside that range.

questions.question: If a quantity doubles five times, by what factor has it been multiplied overall?
questions.feedback: Five successive doublings multiply by 2⁵ = 32. The factors multiply rather than add.
questions.retryFeedback: Treat each doubling as another multiplication by two. Count how many such factors appear in the repeated product.

questions.question: What is ln(e⁵)?
questions.feedback: Natural logarithm inverts the exponential with base e.
questions.retryFeedback: The exponential and natural logarithm are inverse operations. Track the exponent through that pair of operations.

questions.question: A computer rounds extremely small positive products to zero. Why might adding log probabilities help when combining many probabilities?
options: It forces events to be independent
It avoids repeatedly multiplying tiny positive values
questions.feedback: The product rule turns a product into a sum of logarithms. Keeping the result as a log value avoids repeatedly multiplying already tiny numbers; converting back can still underflow.
questions.retryFeedback: Use the logarithm product rule to express the combined value differently. Consider what happens when positive numbers below one are multiplied repeatedly.

concepts.title: Derivative
concepts.definition: The derivative is a function's instantaneous rate of change, defined by the limit of slopes over shrinking intervals. A local minimum is lowest among nearby inputs; a global minimum is lowest over the whole domain. A zero derivative alone guarantees neither.
concepts.formula:
f′(x) = limₕ→₀ [f(x + h) − f(x)] / h
d(xⁿ)/dx = n xⁿ⁻¹
concepts.formulaNote: The second equation is the power rule, shown here for a positive integer n.
concepts.example: For f(x) = x²: f(3.01) − f(3) = 0.0601. The slope over this interval is 0.0601/0.01 = 6.01, close to f′(3) = 6.
concepts.metaphor: A speedometer measures the slope of your distance-versus-time journey at this instant.
concepts.question: For f(x) = x², what is the derivative at x = 4?
concepts.feedback: The derivative is 2x, so its value is 8. The function's value is 16. Local slope and height are different quantities.

questions.question: For f(x) = x², what is the derivative at x = 4?
questions.feedback: The derivative is 2x, so its value is 8. The function's value is 16. Local slope and height are different quantities.
questions.retryFeedback: Differentiate the expression before substituting the location. For a power, reduce the exponent and bring down its original value.

questions.question: What is the derivative of a constant function?
questions.feedback: A constant has no change as the input varies.
questions.retryFeedback: A derivative measures output change per input change. Check how much a constant output moves as its input changes.

questions.question: For f(x) = 3x, what is f′(x)?
questions.feedback: A straight line through the origin has its coefficient as slope.
questions.retryFeedback: The slope of this straight line is fixed. Distinguish the coefficient of x from the function's value at x.

questions.question: If f′(a) < 0, what does that indicate locally?
options: The function decreases as input increases near a
questions.feedback: Derivative sign describes local change, not the sign of the output.
questions.retryFeedback: Use the local approximation Δf ≈ f′(a)Δx with a small positive input change. Track the sign of the product.

questions.question: For f(x) = x², what is f′(0)?
questions.feedback: The derivative 2x equals zero at the origin.
questions.retryFeedback: First derive the slope function for the square. Then evaluate that slope at the requested input.

questions.question: Does a zero derivative guarantee a global minimum?
questions.feedback: A stationary point can be a maximum or neither; global behavior needs more information.
questions.retryFeedback: A stationary point can be a maximum, minimum, or neither. Its slope alone does not compare it with every other point.

questions.question: A rate of change is computed between two distinct input values. How does this differ from an instantaneous derivative?
options: It averages change over a finite interval
questions.feedback: The derivative is the limit of such slopes as the interval shrinks.
questions.retryFeedback: A derivative is obtained from slopes as the interval shrinks toward the point. A secant uses separated endpoints.

questions.question: If position is measured in metres and time in seconds, what units does its time derivative have?
questions.feedback: A rate of change divides output units by input units.
questions.retryFeedback: Keep units in the ratio of output change to input change. Here the input variable is time.

questions.question: At x = 2, f′(x) = 5. Approximately how much does f change for a small input increase of 0.01?
questions.feedback: The local linear approximation is slope times input change.
questions.retryFeedback: Use the local linear approximation: output change is approximately slope times the small input change.

questions.question: For f(x) = x³, what is f′(2)?
questions.feedback: Differentiate to 3x², then substitute 2.
questions.retryFeedback: Apply the power rule before substituting the input. The requested quantity is slope, not the original cubic value.

concepts.title: Integral
concepts.definition: A definite integral is the limit of sums of a function's values times small interval widths. It measures signed accumulation.
concepts.formula:
∫ₐᵇ f(t) dt = limₙ→∞ Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ f(a + iΔt)Δt
Δt = (b − a)/n
concepts.example: A flow of 2 litres/second for 3 seconds delivers ∫₀³ 2 dt = 6 litres.
concepts.metaphor: A derivative reads the tap's flow rate; an integral counts the water collected in the bucket.
concepts.question: A constant speed of 4 metres/second lasts 5 seconds. Integral of speed?
concepts.feedback: For the constant speed, 4 × 5 = 20 metres. Integrating nonnegative speed gives distance; integrating signed velocity gives displacement. The displayed equal-width limit defines the integral for continuous functions, and more generally for Riemann-integrable functions.

questions.question: A constant speed of 4 metres/second lasts 5 seconds. Integral of speed?
questions.feedback: For the constant speed, 4 × 5 = 20 metres. Integrating nonnegative speed gives distance; integrating signed velocity gives displacement. The displayed equal-width limit defines the integral for continuous functions, and more generally for Riemann-integrable functions.
questions.retryFeedback: For a constant rate, accumulation is the rate multiplied by the duration. Keep the units through the multiplication.

questions.question: What is ∫₂⁶ 3 dt?
questions.feedback: The constant height is 3 and the interval width is 6−2 = 4. The integral is 3×4 = 12.
questions.retryFeedback: For a constant integrand, multiply its value by the interval width. Find that width from both bounds, not just the upper bound.

questions.question: What does integrating signed velocity over time give?
questions.feedback: Negative velocity contributes negative signed movement.
questions.retryFeedback: Signed velocity distinguishes opposite directions. Its contributions accumulate with their signs, unlike total distance traveled.

questions.question: What happens when the bounds of a definite integral are reversed?
questions.feedback: Orientation determines the sign of signed accumulation.
questions.retryFeedback: Integration bounds specify the direction of accumulation. Reversing that direction changes the orientation of the signed total.

questions.question: What is ∫₂² f(t) dt for a continuous function?
questions.feedback: An interval of zero width contributes no accumulation.
questions.retryFeedback: Identical bounds leave no interval over which to accumulate. A nonzero integrand alone does not create interval width.

questions.question: A material arrives at a rate measured in grams per minute. What unit results from integrating that rate over minutes?
questions.feedback: The time unit cancels: (grams/minute) × minutes = grams. The integral measures accumulated mass.
questions.retryFeedback: Track the units through a rate multiplied by a small time interval, then summed. Cancel matching numerator and denominator time units.

questions.question: The area under t from 0 to 2 is a triangle. Using triangle area = base × height / 2, what is ∫₀² t dt?
questions.feedback: The base is 2 and the height is 2, so the integral is the triangle area 2×2/2 = 2.
questions.retryFeedback: The graph rises linearly from the origin. Compute its triangular area or evaluate an antiderivative at both bounds.

questions.question: Why multiply each sampled function value by interval width in a Riemann sum?
options: To estimate each small area's contribution
questions.feedback: Height times width approximates accumulation over that piece.
questions.retryFeedback: A function value supplies a height. An accumulated contribution also needs the width of the piece it represents.

questions.question: Can a definite integral of a nonzero function be zero?
options: Yes, positive and negative contributions can cancel
questions.feedback: Signed areas can cancel, as for t over [−1, 1].
questions.retryFeedback: A definite integral is signed accumulation. Regions on different sides of the axis can contribute opposite amounts.

questions.question: A tank receives water at 3 litres/second for 2 seconds, then 1 litre/second for 4 seconds. What total does the integral of this flow give?
questions.feedback: Add each interval’s accumulation: 3×2 + 1×4 = 10 litres.
questions.retryFeedback: Find the amount delivered during each constant-flow interval by multiplying rate by duration, then combine the amounts.

concepts.title: Gradient
concepts.definition: For a scalar function of several variables, the gradient collects its partial derivatives. Each partial varies one coordinate while holding the others fixed. When nonzero, the gradient points in the direction of fastest local increase among directions of equal Euclidean length.
concepts.example: If L = x² + 3y², then ∇L = (2x, 6y). At (1, 2), it is (2, 12).
concepts.metaphor: A hill's gradient is a local uphill compass, with one component for each direction.
concepts.question: For L = x² + y² at (2, 3), what is ∇L?
concepts.feedback: Differentiate with respect to each coordinate. The negative gradient points locally downhill; the gradient itself points toward fastest local increase under Euclidean geometry.

questions.question: For L = x² + y² at (2, 3), what is ∇L?
questions.feedback: Differentiate with respect to each coordinate. The negative gradient points locally downhill; the gradient itself points toward fastest local increase under Euclidean geometry.
questions.retryFeedback: Differentiate the loss with respect to each coordinate separately, then evaluate both derivatives at the given point.

questions.question: For L(x, y) = x² + y², what is ∇L(1, −2)?
questions.feedback: The partial derivatives are 2x and 2y.
questions.retryFeedback: Apply the power rule coordinate by coordinate. Substitute the negative coordinate with its sign intact.

questions.question: What is held fixed when taking ∂L/∂x?
questions.feedback: A partial derivative varies one coordinate at a time.
questions.retryFeedback: A partial derivative isolates one coordinate's effect. Do not let other independent input coordinates change during that calculation.

questions.question: For a scalar loss with five parameters, how many gradient coordinates are there?
questions.feedback: Each parameter has its own partial derivative.
questions.retryFeedback: Each parameter has its own partial derivative. The scalar output's size does not determine the number of gradient entries.

questions.question: Under Euclidean geometry, what direction gives fastest local increase when the gradient is nonzero?
questions.feedback: The gradient points toward steepest local ascent.
questions.retryFeedback: The directional derivative is a dot product with the gradient. Compare directions of equal Euclidean length.

questions.question: For L(x, y) = 3x + 2y, what is ∇L?
questions.feedback: Differentiate each linear term with respect to its coordinate.
questions.retryFeedback: Each partial derivative treats the other variable's term as constant. Differentiate the two linear terms separately.

questions.question: Does a zero gradient always mean a minimum?
questions.feedback: Maxima and saddle points can also have zero gradients.
questions.retryFeedback: Stationarity alone does not classify a point. Consider a surface that curves upward in one direction and downward in another.

questions.question: If ∂L/∂w is negative, what does a small positive change in w tend to do?
questions.feedback: A negative local slope gives a negative first-order loss change.
questions.retryFeedback: Approximate the loss change by the partial derivative times the small parameter change. The product's sign determines the local trend.

questions.question: What does a large gradient coordinate suggest locally?
options: Sensitivity to that coordinate in its current scale
questions.feedback: Derivative magnitudes depend on units and local behavior.
questions.retryFeedback: A derivative measures change per unit of its coordinate. Coordinate units and scaling affect the numerical magnitude.

questions.question: For L(x, y) = xy, what is ∇L(2, 3)?
questions.feedback: The partial derivatives are y and x.
questions.retryFeedback: When differentiating a product of independent inputs with respect to one input, hold the other input fixed, then substitute the point.

concepts.title: Hessian and curvature
concepts.definition:
The Hessian is the matrix of second partial derivatives of a scalar function. It describes local curvature.

For smooth functions, its eigenvalues help classify a stationary point where the gradient is zero. All-positive eigenvalues (positive definite) imply a strict local minimum; mixed positive and negative eigenvalues imply a saddle, rising in some directions and falling in others. Zero Hessian eigenvalues can leave the classification inconclusive.
concepts.example: For f(x,y)=x²+3y², H=[[2,0],[0,6]]. At (0,0), the gradient is zero and both curvature directions are positive, so this is a strict local minimum.
concepts.metaphor: A slope tells you which way a road tilts; curvature tells you how that slope changes.
concepts.question: For f(x,y) = 4x² + 2y², what is the Hessian in (x,y) order?
concepts.feedback: The first partials are 8x and 4y. Differentiating again gives diagonal entries 8 and 4, with zero mixed partials.

questions.question: For f(x,y) = 4x² + 2y², what is the Hessian in (x,y) order?
questions.feedback: The first partials are 8x and 4y. Differentiating again gives diagonal entries 8 and 4, with zero mixed partials.
questions.retryFeedback: Differentiate twice for each Hessian entry. A term depending only on one coordinate contributes nothing to a mixed partial.

questions.question: What is the Hessian of f(x,y)=x²−y²?
questions.feedback: Differentiate twice: the two coordinate curvatures have opposite signs.
questions.retryFeedback: Differentiate twice and preserve the sign of the negative squared term. The two coordinate directions have different curvature signs.

questions.question: At a smooth stationary point, what do positive and negative Hessian eigenvalues indicate?
questions.feedback: The function curves upward in some directions and downward in others.
questions.retryFeedback: At a stationary point, inspect whether small moves can increase the function in one direction and decrease it in another.

questions.question: What does a positive-definite Hessian establish at a smooth stationary point?
options: A global minimum for every function
That every first derivative is positive
questions.feedback: The second-derivative test is local; a global conclusion needs more information such as global convexity.
questions.retryFeedback: Positive definiteness gives upward second-order curvature in every nonzero direction. The conclusion is local to the stationary point.

questions.question: Does a zero Hessian at a stationary point always classify it?
options: Yes, it is always a minimum
Yes, the function is constant everywhere
Yes, it is always a maximum
questions.feedback: For example, x⁴ and −x⁴ both have zero second derivative at zero but opposite behavior.
questions.retryFeedback: When second-order terms vanish, higher-order terms may still determine the behavior. Compare x⁴ with −x⁴ at the origin.

questions.question: For f(x)=x⁴, use the power rule d(xⁿ)/dx = n xⁿ⁻¹ twice. What is the second derivative at x=2?
questions.feedback: The second derivative is 12x², giving 48.
questions.retryFeedback: Differentiate the fourth power twice before substituting the input. Evaluating the first derivative answers a different question.

questions.question: How many entries does the Hessian have for a scalar function of three variables?
questions.feedback: There are three first-derivative components, each differentiated with respect to three variables.
questions.retryFeedback: A Hessian contains one derivative for each ordered pair of input coordinates. Count the positions in that square array.

questions.question: For variables ordered (x, y), a Hessian is [[2,5],[5,8]]. Which entry records ∂²f/∂x²?
questions.feedback: The x,x derivative is in the first row and first column, so its value is 2.
questions.retryFeedback: Match both derivative variables to the row and column order. A repeated variable selects a diagonal entry.

questions.question: What is the Hessian of an affine function f(x,y)=2x+3y+1?
questions.feedback: Its first derivatives are constants, so all second derivatives vanish.
questions.retryFeedback: An affine function has constant first derivatives. Check what happens when those constants are differentiated again.

questions.question: For f(x,y) = x² + 9y² at (0,0), which coordinate direction has greater upward curvature?
questions.feedback: The second derivatives are 2 in x and 18 in y. The y direction has the greater upward curvature.
questions.retryFeedback: Hold one coordinate fixed and differentiate twice with respect to the other. Compare the resulting second derivatives.

concepts.title: Chain rule
concepts.definition: When one function feeds another, a change passes through both. The chain rule multiplies their local derivatives to find the derivative of the combined function.
concepts.formulaNote: Here y = f(g(x)): the output of g becomes the input of f.
concepts.example: Let u = 2x and y = u². At x = 3, u = 6. The two slopes are du/dx = 2 and dy/du = 12, so dy/dx = 12×2 = 24. If y is a sum of two paths from x, compute each path’s derivative and add them: for y = (2x)² + (3x)², dy/dx = 8x + 18x.
concepts.metaphor: Linked gears multiply their speed ratios. A change travels through every gear.
concepts.question: For y = (3x)², what is dy/dx at x = 2?
concepts.feedback: Let u = 3x. Then dy/dx = 2u × 3 = 18x = 36. Forgetting the inner derivative loses a factor of 3.

questions.question: For y = (3x)², what is dy/dx at x = 2?
questions.feedback: Let u = 3x. Then dy/dx = 2u × 3 = 18x = 36. Forgetting the inner derivative loses a factor of 3.
questions.retryFeedback: Differentiate the outer square and multiply by the inner linear derivative. Evaluate the composed factors at the given input.

questions.question: For y = (x + 1)², what is dy/dx at x = 2?
questions.feedback: The outer derivative is 2(x+1); the inner derivative is 1.
questions.retryFeedback: The outer function sees the whole parenthesized expression as its input. Differentiate it and then include the inner derivative.

questions.question: For y = (5x)², which factor is missed if the inner derivative is omitted?
questions.feedback: With u = 5x, dy/dx = (2u)×5. The inner derivative du/dx supplies the factor 5.
questions.retryFeedback: Separate the expression into an inner function and an outer function. The chain rule includes one derivative from each stage.

questions.question: If dy/du = 4 and du/dx = 3, what is dy/dx?
questions.feedback: Local derivative factors multiply through a composition.
questions.retryFeedback: Along a composition, changes pass through successive stages. Combine the rates multiplicatively rather than adding them.

questions.question: For y = u² and u = 4x, which expression gives dy/dx?
questions.feedback: The chain rule gives (2u)×4. Substituting u = 4x yields 32x, also obtained by differentiating 16x².
questions.retryFeedback: Differentiate y with respect to u and u with respect to x, multiply, and only then express the result entirely in x.

questions.question: What is the derivative of a composition if its inner derivative is zero and the outer derivative is finite?
questions.feedback: The chain-rule product includes a zero factor.
questions.retryFeedback: The composition's derivative multiplies its inner and outer factors. Track the effect of a vanishing factor with the stated finite assumption.

questions.question: A calculation uses u = −3x, then y = u². Why is dy/du alone insufficient to find dy/dx?
options: Squaring removes every dependence on x
A negative inner coefficient prevents differentiation
It already includes the inner derivative twice
It omits how u changes when x changes
questions.feedback: The required derivative is (dy/du)(du/dx), and du/dx = −3. Using dy/du alone leaves out this signed factor.
questions.retryFeedback: Follow a small change from x to u and then from u to y. Each stage contributes its own rate, including its sign.

questions.question: Let y = f(2x), where f′(u) = eᵘ is given. What is dy/dx?
questions.feedback: Evaluate the supplied outer derivative at u = 2x, then multiply by du/dx = 2 to obtain 2e^(2x).
questions.retryFeedback: You are given the derivative of the outer function. Substitute its full input, then account for the derivative of that input.

questions.question: With derivatives 2, 3, and 4 along one three-stage path, what is the path derivative?
questions.feedback: The local effects multiply along the path.
questions.retryFeedback: Each stage scales the change received from the previous stage. Follow the complete path before combining its factors.

questions.question: If a variable influences a loss along two computational paths, what happens to their derivative contributions?
questions.feedback: The multivariable chain rule sums contributions from all paths.
questions.retryFeedback: A variable may contribute through more than one route. Compute each path's effect before combining the contributions to the total change.

concepts.title: Optimization
concepts.definition: An objective assigns a score to each choice. Optimization finds an allowed choice with the smallest or largest score. The allowed choices form the constraint set C.
concepts.example: For L(x) = (x − 3)² and C = [0, 2], x* = 2 and L(x*) = 1.
concepts.metaphor: Find the lowest campsite inside the fence. A lower valley outside it is unavailable.
concepts.question: Minimize (x − 5)² subject to 0 ≤ x ≤ 3. Which x wins?
concepts.feedback: The unconstrained minimum is 5, but it is not allowed. Among allowed inputs, 3 is closest to 5. The optimum input differs from its objective value.

questions.question: Minimize (x − 5)² subject to 0 ≤ x ≤ 3. Which x wins?
questions.feedback: The unconstrained minimum is 5, but it is not allowed. Among allowed inputs, 3 is closest to 5. The optimum input differs from its objective value.
questions.retryFeedback: The unconstrained best point may be forbidden. Compare feasible points by how close they can get to the square's center.

questions.question: How does arg min differ from min?
options: They always return the same number
arg min identifies an input; min is the objective value
questions.feedback: The best choice and its score are different objects.
questions.retryFeedback: Distinguish the location where the best value is reached from the value of the objective at that location.

questions.question: For L(x) = (x − 2)² over real x, where is the minimum?
questions.feedback: A square is smallest when its inside is zero.
questions.retryFeedback: A square cannot be negative. Identify the input that makes the quantity inside the square vanish.

questions.question: What makes an optimization choice feasible?
questions.feedback: Feasibility is determined by the allowed set.
questions.retryFeedback: A good objective value is not sufficient if the choice violates the allowed conditions. Check the permitted set first.

questions.question: Can a constrained optimum lie on a boundary?
options: Only if the objective is constant
questions.feedback: The best unconstrained point may lie outside the allowed region.
questions.retryFeedback: Constraints can exclude the unconstrained optimum. The best allowed point can occur where further improvement would leave the permitted region.

questions.question: Which is a maximization objective?
questions.feedback: Maximization seeks the greatest objective value among allowed choices.
questions.retryFeedback: Check whether the goal prefers larger or smaller objective values. Maximizing reward reverses the preference used when minimizing loss.

questions.question: Does a local minimum have to be the best point everywhere?
questions.feedback: Local optimality compares nearby points, not all feasible points.
questions.retryFeedback: Local optimality compares nearby choices. It does not evaluate distant regions of the feasible set.

questions.question: For x in {1, 2, 3}, which maximizes 5 − x?
questions.feedback: The objective values are 4, 3, and 2.
questions.retryFeedback: Evaluate the objective for the allowed inputs, or examine whether it rises or falls as x increases.

questions.question: Can an optimization problem have several equally good solutions?
questions.feedback: Distinct feasible inputs can share the optimal objective value.
questions.retryFeedback: Different inputs can produce the same objective value. Uniqueness requires additional properties beyond the existence of an optimum.

questions.question: Why specify an objective before optimizing a system?
options: Different goals can prefer different choices
questions.feedback: A scoring rule defines what the optimization is trying to improve.
questions.retryFeedback: Performance can mean accuracy, speed, cost, or something else. An optimizer needs a stated criterion for comparing choices.

concepts.title: Lagrange multipliers
concepts.definition: Lagrange multipliers help minimize or maximize a score while obeying an equality rule. With two inputs x and y, f(x,y) is the score and g(x,y)=0 is the rule. Each function takes the pair (x,y) and returns one number; y is an input, not the value of f.
concepts.formulaNote: The extra number λ (lambda) links the score and the rule. For a smooth rule whose gradient is nonzero, set the x and y derivatives of ℒ to zero and also solve g(x,y)=0. These equations give candidates to check; they do not guarantee a minimum. λ may be positive, zero, or negative.
concepts.example:
Goal: choose x and y to minimize f(x,y)=x²+y². For example, f(0,2)=0²+2²=4. Both x and y are inputs to this score.

Rule: the chosen numbers must total 2. Write g(x,y)=x+y−2, so an allowed pair has g(x,y)=0.

Combine them: ℒ=x²+y²+λ(x+y−2). Its x derivative gives 2x+λ=0; its y derivative gives 2y+λ=0. Both 2x and 2y equal −λ, so x=y.

Use the rule: x+y=2 gives (x,y)=(1,1). The objective is f(1,1)=1²+1²=2. The multiplier is λ=−2. Moving away from this equal split raises the score.
concepts.metaphor: The rule is a path you must stay on; the score is the height along that path. Find the lowest allowed point.
concepts.question: The score is f(x,y)=x²+3y² and the rule is x+y=8. The Lagrange equations give x=3y. Which pair satisfies both x=3y and x+y=8?
concepts.feedback: Substitute x = 3y into x+y = 8 to obtain 4y = 8. Thus y = 2 and x = 6.

questions.question: The score is f(x,y)=x²+3y² and the rule is x+y=8. The Lagrange equations give x=3y. Which pair satisfies both x=3y and x+y=8?
questions.feedback: Substitute x = 3y into x+y = 8 to obtain 4y = 8. Thus y = 2 and x = 6.
questions.retryFeedback: A candidate must satisfy both gradient balance and the constraint. Substitute the stated relation between coordinates into the equality constraint.

questions.question: In a Lagrange problem, what does the rule g(x,y)=0 describe?
options: The feasible points for the optimization
questions.feedback: It describes which input pairs are allowed. The separate function f(x,y) assigns a score to each pair.
questions.retryFeedback: Keep the two roles separate: one function scores an input pair, while the other checks whether that pair obeys the required rule.

questions.question: Let f(x,y)=x²+y² be the score, and let the rule be 2x+y=7, written g(x,y)=2x+y−7. Which expression is ℒ=f+λg?
questions.feedback: Move 7 to the left to write g = 2x+y−7 = 0, then add λg to the objective.
questions.retryFeedback: Start with the score function. Then add the multiplier times the entire rule function, including the constant that makes the rule equal zero.

questions.question: Why must a candidate also satisfy g(x,y)=0 after solving the derivative equations?
options: Feasibility is automatic for every gradient
Gradient balance alone does not ensure feasibility
questions.feedback: Balancing derivatives does not by itself establish that an input pair obeys the rule. Both requirements must hold.
questions.retryFeedback: The derivative equations compare changes in the score and rule. Separately check whether the candidate pair is actually allowed by the original rule.

questions.question: Minimize f(x,y)=x²+y² while x+y=6. The derivative equations give x=y. Which equal values also obey the rule?
questions.feedback: With x=y, the rule becomes 2x=6. Thus x=y=3.
questions.retryFeedback: Use the supplied equality between the two inputs in the total rule. The score and the total are different functions of the same pair.

questions.question: Do the Lagrange equations alone guarantee that every candidate is a minimum?
questions.feedback: No. They identify candidates; compare their scores and check the allowed choices to determine whether a candidate is a minimum.
questions.retryFeedback: Finding a candidate and proving it has the lowest allowed score are separate steps. Think about what the derivative equations establish.

questions.question: Using ℒ=f+λg, the x derivative at an allowed pair gives −3+λ=0. Which statement about λ follows?
options: It cannot be positive for an equality rule
questions.feedback: Adding 3 to both sides gives λ=3, a positive multiplier. Equality-rule multipliers can be positive, zero, or negative depending on the problem.
questions.retryFeedback: Treat the derivative condition as an equation for one unknown. Choose the value that makes the two terms add to zero; keep track of the existing minus sign.

questions.question: For score f(x,y)=x²+y² and rule x+y=8, a minimizing pair is x=y=4. The x derivative gives 2x+λ=0. What is λ?
questions.feedback: Substitute x=4 into 2x+λ=0: 8+λ=0, so λ=−8.
questions.retryFeedback: Use the supplied input value in the derivative equation. Then isolate the multiplier, keeping the sign needed to make the sum zero.

questions.question: For f(x,y) = x² + 4y² subject to x+y=5, gradient balance gives 2x+λ=0 and 8y+λ=0. What relation follows?
questions.feedback: Both 2x and 8y equal −λ, so 2x = 8y and x = 4y.
questions.retryFeedback: Eliminate the shared multiplier by equating the remaining terms. Keep the different coefficients of the two coordinates when simplifying.

questions.question: The rule is x+y=10. Which function g(x,y) equals zero exactly when that rule holds?
questions.feedback: Move the required total to the left: x+y−10=0 is equivalent to x+y=10.
questions.retryFeedback: Write the equality with zero on one side by subtracting the required total from both sides. Check the result using any allowed pair.

concepts.title: Gradient descent
concepts.definition: Gradient descent updates a variable or parameter vector in the direction opposite its gradient. The learning rate η sets the step size. A sufficiently small step can lower the loss.
concepts.example: For L(θ) = θ², θ = 3 and η = 0.1: θ⁺ = 3 − 0.1×6 = 2.4. The loss falls from 9 to 2.4² = 5.76.
concepts.metaphor: Feel the ground's slope, take a short downhill step, then measure again.
concepts.question: For θ = 4, gradient 6, and learning rate 0.1, what is the next θ?
concepts.feedback: Subtract 0.1 × 6 from 4. Large steps can increase the loss, and nonconvex objectives need not lead to a global minimum.

questions.question: For θ = 4, gradient 6, and learning rate 0.1, what is the next θ?
questions.feedback: Subtract 0.1 × 6 from 4. Large steps can increase the loss, and nonconvex objectives need not lead to a global minimum.
questions.retryFeedback: Compute the learning-rate-scaled gradient, then subtract that step from the current parameter. Do not return the step alone.

questions.question: With θ = 2, gradient = −3, and η = 0.1, what is the next θ?
questions.feedback: Subtracting a negative gradient increases the parameter.
questions.retryFeedback: Write the subtraction explicitly before replacing the gradient with its signed value. Subtracting a negative step changes direction.

questions.question: What happens when the learning rate is zero?
questions.feedback: The update subtracts zero times the gradient.
questions.retryFeedback: The learning rate multiplies the gradient in the update. Track what happens when that multiplier vanishes.

questions.question: Why can a large learning rate increase loss?
options: The step can overshoot the useful local region
questions.feedback: A downhill direction is a local statement; an excessive step can cross the valley.
questions.retryFeedback: The gradient describes local behavior. A large move can leave the region where that direction gives improvement.

questions.question: Which update performs gradient ascent instead of descent?
questions.feedback: Adding the gradient follows local increase for positive η.
questions.retryFeedback: The gradient points toward local increase. Inspect the sign used before the gradient term in each update.

questions.question: For L(θ) = θ², θ = 1 and η = 0.25, what is the new θ?
questions.feedback: The gradient is 2, so the update is 1 − 0.25×2.
questions.retryFeedback: Differentiate the squared loss at the current parameter, multiply by the learning rate, and subtract from the current value.

questions.question: What does a zero gradient do in plain gradient descent?
questions.feedback: The basic update has no movement when the gradient is zero.
questions.retryFeedback: Plain gradient descent uses the current gradient directly. It has no momentum or random perturbation to supply another step.

questions.question: If a loss surface has several valleys with different lowest values, does gradient descent always reach the globally lowest one?
options: Only with a small positive rate
questions.feedback: Gradient descent follows local slopes. Its starting point and updates can lead into a valley whose minimum is not the lowest overall.
questions.retryFeedback: Following a slope uses nearby information. Consider whether that information compares the bottom of the current valley with every other valley.

questions.question: What changes when η is halved while the gradient stays fixed?
questions.feedback: The learning rate scales the step, not the objective directly.
questions.retryFeedback: Hold the gradient fixed and change only its multiplier. Compare the resulting step lengths, not the resulting parameter values.

questions.question: Which quantity must be computed for plain gradient descent?
options: The objective's gradient at the current parameters
questions.feedback: The current gradient supplies the local update direction.
questions.retryFeedback: The update needs local information about how the objective changes with its parameters. The loss value alone does not supply a direction.

concepts.title: Dataset and features
concepts.definition: A dataset collects examples. Features describe each example numerically. In supervised learning, each input x is paired with a target answer y.
concepts.example: Two rooms have features (length, width): (2, 3) and (4, 3) metres. X = [[2, 3], [4, 3]] has two rows and two features per row.
concepts.metaphor: Features are the clues on a detective's case card; the target is the answer being learned.
concepts.question: There are 20 samples and 4 features per sample. Shape of X?
concepts.feedback: By the row-per-sample convention, X has 20 rows and 4 columns. A measured target must not accidentally be included as an input feature.

questions.question: There are 20 samples and 4 features per sample. Shape of X?
questions.feedback: By the row-per-sample convention, X has 20 rows and 4 columns. A measured target must not accidentally be included as an input feature.
questions.retryFeedback: Use one row for each sample and one column for each feature. Matrix shape records these counts in that order.

questions.question: With rows as samples, what does a column represent?
questions.feedback: A column tracks the same input attribute for each example.
questions.retryFeedback: Follow one column downward through the rows. The sample changes while the feature associated with that position stays fixed.

questions.question: In predicting tomorrow's temperature, what is the target?
questions.feedback: The target is the outcome the model is trained to predict.
questions.retryFeedback: The target is the quantity the model is meant to predict. Distinguish it from measurements available before making that prediction.

questions.question: How many scalar feature values are in 12 samples with 3 features each?
questions.feedback: The feature matrix has 12×3 entries.
questions.retryFeedback: Each sample supplies the same stated number of entries. Count entries across all samples using multiplication.

questions.question: Why keep feature names and units with numerical data?
options: To preserve what each value means
questions.feedback: Numerical arrays alone do not describe their semantics.
questions.retryFeedback: The same number can represent different measurements or scales. Names and units establish the meaning expected by the model.

questions.question: Which input would leak a target when predicting a final exam score before the exam?
questions.feedback: The answer is unavailable at prediction time and must not be an input.
questions.retryFeedback: Ask whether the input would actually be available at the prediction time. Including the outcome being predicted defeats that boundary.

questions.question: Can a supervised target be a category?
options: Only if there are ten categories
questions.feedback: Classification uses categorical targets.
questions.retryFeedback: Supervised learning requires paired inputs and desired outputs. Those outputs need not be continuous measurements.

questions.question: What is one example in a row-per-sample table?
options: One row of inputs and its associated target
questions.feedback: A sample groups the information belonging to one prediction case.
questions.retryFeedback: Use the table's stated organization. One example pairs the inputs of a particular observation with its corresponding outcome.

questions.question: A dataset records each room as (length, width). A prediction rule expects that order, but new rooms arrive as (width, length). What should happen?
questions.feedback: Restore the expected order so each coordinate retains its meaning. Sorting by magnitude would not preserve length and width.
questions.retryFeedback: A feature column names what is measured, not how large its value is. Match the incoming positions to the positions the rule expects.

questions.question: Does a larger dataset automatically remove measurement bias?
questions.feedback: More biased observations can preserve the same systematic error.
questions.retryFeedback: More observations can reduce sampling noise while preserving the same systematic measurement error. Size alone does not repair bias.

concepts.title: Linear regression
concepts.definition: Linear regression predicts a numerical target using a weighted sum of features plus an intercept. A residual is target minus prediction. Patterns in residuals can show relationships the fitted line has missed.
concepts.example: A toy taxi fare model is ŷ = 2x + 3 dollars for x kilometres. At 5 km: ŷ = 2×5 + 3 = $13. The intercept is the starting fare.
concepts.metaphor: A recipe assigns each ingredient a fixed contribution, then adds a fixed starting amount.
concepts.question: A regression model predicts ŷ = 4x + 2. What does it predict at x = 3?
concepts.feedback: Substituting x = 3 gives 4×3 + 2 = 14. The intercept is added after the weighted input.

questions.question: A regression model predicts ŷ = 4x + 2. What does it predict at x = 3?
questions.feedback: Substituting x = 3 gives 4×3 + 2 = 14. The intercept is added after the weighted input.
questions.retryFeedback: Evaluate the fitted rule at the stated input. Multiply by the coefficient first, then include the intercept once.

questions.question: For ŷ = 3x − 2, what is ŷ at x = 4?
questions.feedback: Multiply by three, then subtract two.
questions.retryFeedback: The negative intercept is added after the slope-times-input term. Keep the subtraction sign when evaluating the rule.

questions.question: What does the intercept b represent in ŷ = wx + b?
questions.feedback: When x is zero, the weighted input term vanishes.
questions.retryFeedback: Set the input to zero in the prediction equation. Observe which part of the expression remains.

questions.question: If w = −2, how does a one-unit rise in x change ŷ?
questions.feedback: The coefficient specifies prediction change per input unit.
questions.retryFeedback: The slope measures output change per unit input change. Its sign determines the direction of that change.

questions.question: For w = (2, 1), x = (3, 4), and b = 0, what is ŷ?
questions.feedback: The weighted sum is 2×3 + 1×4.
questions.retryFeedback: Pair each feature with its own weight, sum those products, and then include the bias.

questions.question: Which task is naturally a regression task?
questions.feedback: Regression predicts numerical quantities.
questions.retryFeedback: Regression predicts a numerical magnitude. Distinguish that from choosing a label or discovering unlabeled groups.

questions.question: A fitted line predicts higher sales on hotter days. The data did not control other influences. Does the fitted slope alone prove that heating a shop will increase sales?
options: Only if the fit is accurate
questions.feedback: No. The line describes a predictive association. Other differences between hot and cool days may explain it; a fitted slope alone does not establish an intervention’s effect.
questions.retryFeedback: Distinguish describing the observed data from predicting the effect of deliberately changing one condition while other influences remain.

questions.question: What does w = 0 imply in one-feature regression?
options: The prediction is constant at b
questions.feedback: The input contributes nothing to the prediction.
questions.retryFeedback: If the feature's multiplier vanishes, varying the feature no longer contributes to the prediction.

questions.question: Why inspect residuals after fitting a line?
options: They can reveal patterns the model missed
questions.feedback: Structured errors can indicate an inadequate model or data issue.
questions.retryFeedback: Residuals show what is left after the prediction. Systematic remaining structure suggests the fitted rule has not captured everything useful.

questions.question: A line fits the observed range well. Is extrapolation far outside that range assured?
questions.feedback: The relationship may change beyond the data used to fit it.
questions.retryFeedback: Observed fit tests only the supported input region. The relationship outside that region may behave differently.

concepts.title: Mean squared error
concepts.definition: Mean squared error is the average squared difference between predictions and targets. It penalizes larger errors more strongly.
concepts.example: Predictions (2, 5), targets (3, 3): MSE = (1 + 4)/2 = 2.5.
concepts.metaphor: Large misses get disproportionately heavier penalty weights than small misses.
concepts.question: Errors are 1 and 3. What is their MSE?
concepts.feedback: Square first: 1 and 9. Then average: 5. The loss has squared target units, so it is not directly an average absolute error.

questions.question: Errors are 1 and 3. What is their MSE?
questions.feedback: Square first: 1 and 9. Then average: 5. The loss has squared target units, so it is not directly an average absolute error.
questions.retryFeedback: Square each error separately, then average those squares. Squaring the mean error is a different operation.

questions.question: For errors 0 and 4, what is MSE?
questions.feedback: Average the squared errors: (0 + 16)/2.
questions.retryFeedback: The zero error still contributes an example to the denominator. Average over both observations after squaring.

questions.question: Why do errors −3 and 3 contribute equally to MSE?
questions.feedback: Squaring removes the sign of each error.
questions.retryFeedback: Squaring removes the sign of an error. Compare the magnitudes before considering which direction the prediction missed.

questions.question: When is MSE zero?
options: When every prediction equals its target
questions.feedback: An average of nonnegative squares is zero only if every square is zero.
questions.retryFeedback: MSE averages nonnegative terms. Consider what must be true of every term for their average to vanish.

questions.question: If every error doubles, what happens to MSE?
questions.feedback: Each squared error is multiplied by four.
questions.retryFeedback: The scale factor acts on each error before squaring. Track that factor through the square and the average.

questions.question: Which error contributes more to MSE: 1 or 5?
questions.feedback: Squaring makes large deviations count disproportionately.
questions.retryFeedback: The contribution is the square of the error, not the error itself. Larger mistakes grow disproportionately under this loss.

questions.question: MSE averages squared errors. If the targets are measured in metres, what are the units of MSE?
questions.feedback: Each error is measured in metres, so each squared error has units of square metres. Averaging preserves those units.
questions.retryFeedback: Track the units through subtraction, squaring, and averaging. Dividing by a count does not undo the squaring.

questions.question: For predictions (1,7) and targets (3,3), what is the mean squared error?
questions.feedback: The errors are −2 and 4. Square and average: (4 + 16)/2 = 10.
questions.retryFeedback: Match each prediction with its own target, then square both errors. Average the squares rather than squaring the average error.

questions.question: A line has low MSE on the examples used to fit it. No new examples have been checked. Is this enough to establish low error on new inputs?
questions.feedback: No. This MSE measures errors on the examples already used. To assess new-input accuracy, predictions must be compared with answers from relevant new examples.
questions.retryFeedback: An average describes the cases included in it. Ask what evidence the stated calculation contains about cases it never included.

questions.question: If targets are rescaled from metres to centimetres, how does the same physical error's MSE change numerically?
questions.feedback: Errors multiply by 100, so their squares multiply by 100².
questions.retryFeedback: Converting a length changes each numerical error by the conversion factor. MSE then squares that factor.

concepts.title: Supervised learning
concepts.definition: Supervised learning uses examples with known answers to learn a rule for new inputs. A loss measures prediction error; training adjusts the rule to reduce that loss. Using the learned rule to make predictions is called inference. Classification predicts a category; regression predicts a number. Generalization means performing well on new examples.
concepts.formulaNote: The model f uses parameters θ. The loss ℓ scores one prediction against its target; training minimizes the average loss.
concepts.example: Inputs 1, 2, 3 paired with targets 2, 4, 6 suggest f(x) = 2x; it predicts 8 for input 4.
concepts.metaphor: A coach gives both a problem and a worked answer so a learner can improve its rule.
concepts.question: Which task is supervised learning?
options: Learn rock type from logs paired with rock labels
concepts.feedback: Supervision supplies target answers for inputs. Those targets may be numeric or categorical. The learned rule still needs evaluation on unseen examples.

questions.question: Which task is supervised learning?
options: Learn rock type from logs paired with rock labels
questions.feedback: Supervision supplies target answers for inputs. Those targets may be numeric or categorical. The learned rule still needs evaluation on unseen examples.
questions.retryFeedback: Look for training inputs paired with the desired outputs. Merely grouping similar inputs does not supply that pairing.

questions.question: What supplies the learning signal in supervised learning?
questions.feedback: Predictions are compared with known target answers.
questions.retryFeedback: The learning procedure needs a reference outcome against which to compare each prediction, not just a collection of inputs.

questions.question: Which example is supervised classification?
options: Learning from emails labelled spam or not spam
questions.feedback: The supplied category labels define the prediction task.
questions.retryFeedback: Classification learns to predict categories from labeled examples. Look for a task with both examples and class labels.

questions.question: What does training usually adjust?
options: The meaning of the target after every prediction
questions.feedback: Optimization changes parameters to reduce prediction loss.
questions.retryFeedback: Separate values fitted from examples from fixed data and settings that govern the training procedure.

questions.question: Why evaluate on unseen examples?
options: To increase training accuracy by definition
questions.feedback: Remembering training answers is not enough for future predictions.
questions.retryFeedback: Good fit to already-seen examples can include memorization. Evaluation needs evidence about performance beyond those examples.

questions.question: Can incorrect labels harm supervised learning?
questions.feedback: The model is trained toward the supplied targets, including their errors.
questions.retryFeedback: Training treats labels as the reference signal. Systematic mistakes in that signal can teach an undesirable association.

questions.question: What is inference?
options: Using a trained model to make predictions
Labelling the test set with predictions as truth
questions.feedback: Inference evaluates the learned rule on inputs.
questions.retryFeedback: Distinguish the stage that adjusts a model from the stage that applies its learned rule to an input.

questions.question: Does supervised learning require a human to hand-label every target?
questions.feedback: Targets can come from measurements or other reliable processes.
questions.retryFeedback: Targets may come from measurements, recorded outcomes, or other processes. The learning setup depends on pairing, not who created each label.

questions.question: Why match training inputs to information available at deployment?
options: Otherwise evaluation may overstate usable performance
questions.feedback: Unavailable inputs cannot support real predictions.
questions.retryFeedback: A model evaluated with unavailable future information is solving an easier problem than the one it will face in use.

questions.question: Which pairing is essential for a supervised example?
options: A parameter and a learning rate
An input and its corresponding target
questions.feedback: A mismatched target teaches the wrong relationship.
questions.retryFeedback: The association between the example and its desired output matters. A separate unpaired list of outcomes does not define those training pairs.

concepts.title: Parameter and hyperparameter
concepts.definition: A parameter is fitted during learning. A hyperparameter configures the model or training procedure rather than being fitted by that procedure.
concepts.formula: ŷ = wx + b;   w⁺ = w − η ∂L/∂w
concepts.example: In this update, w = 2 is a parameter; the chosen learning rate η = 0.01 is a hyperparameter.
concepts.metaphor: The learner adjusts recipe quantities; the teacher chooses how large each adjustment may be.
concepts.question: A training procedure fits weights and biases but stops after a user-chosen limit of 500 updates. Which quantity is a hyperparameter?
options: A weight fitted by the procedure
A bias fitted by the procedure
concepts.feedback: The update limit configures the training procedure and is chosen outside its parameter-fitting steps. The fitted coefficients are parameters.

questions.question: A training procedure fits weights and biases but stops after a user-chosen limit of 500 updates. Which quantity is a hyperparameter?
options: A weight fitted by the procedure
A bias fitted by the procedure
questions.feedback: The update limit configures the training procedure and is chosen outside its parameter-fitting steps. The fitted coefficients are parameters.
questions.retryFeedback: Distinguish a setting used to configure the fitting procedure from values that the procedure itself learns from data.

questions.question: Which quantity is usually learned by gradient descent?
options: Number of epochs chosen in advance
questions.feedback: Weights are fitted parameters; the other choices configure training.
questions.retryFeedback: Gradient descent updates quantities inside the parameterized model. Compare those with choices made about the training procedure.

questions.question: During training, a fitted weight changes from 2 to 1.8 while the chosen learning rate stays at 0.1. Which change is a parameter update?
options: Deciding how many examples to collect
questions.feedback: The weight is fitted by training. Its change is a parameter update; the chosen learning rate configures that update.
questions.retryFeedback: Identify the quantity being fitted by the learning procedure. A setting that controls the procedure has a different role.

questions.question: Is a fitted bias term a parameter?
options: No, it is always a label
questions.feedback: Training can learn biases along with weights.
questions.retryFeedback: A bias can be adjusted to reduce loss just as a weight can. Its name does not place it outside the fitted model.

questions.question: A user chooses a quadratic model ax²+bx+c instead of a linear model wx+b. The fitting procedure learns coefficients but cannot change that choice. What was changed?
questions.feedback: Choosing the model family configures what can be fitted. The coefficients learned within the chosen family are its parameters.
questions.retryFeedback: Ask whether the quantity is selected to define the fitting problem or adjusted by the stated fitting procedure.

questions.question: Batch size means the chosen number of examples grouped into one training update. If batch size changes, what has changed?
questions.feedback: Batch size configures how examples are grouped into updates.
questions.retryFeedback: Changing how many examples contribute to one update changes the training procedure, not an individual learned coefficient.

questions.question: Can a separate search procedure tune hyperparameters?
options: Only by backpropagating the test score
questions.feedback: Hyperparameters can be selected by search, even though the inner training run does not fit them as weights.
questions.retryFeedback: Hyperparameters can be searched over by another procedure. They need not remain fixed by a human's first guess.

questions.question: In ŷ = wx + b, which are fitted parameters in ordinary regression?
questions.feedback: The model fits its coefficient and intercept.
questions.retryFeedback: Identify the coefficients that fitting adjusts in this prediction equation. The input and observed target play different roles.

questions.question: A model is built from a chosen number of intermediate processing layers. The layer count stays fixed while weights are fitted. What is that count?
questions.feedback: The chosen count specifies the model’s structure rather than a value fitted as a weight. It is an architecture hyperparameter.
questions.retryFeedback: Focus on how the quantity is obtained: chosen as part of the design, or adjusted as one of the fitted weights.

questions.question: Why record both parameters and training settings for reproducibility?
options: They describe the learned model and how it was obtained
questions.feedback: Reproducing training requires more than saved weights alone.
questions.retryFeedback: The final coefficients do not describe every choice made during training. Conversely, training settings do not specify the learned coefficients.

concepts.title: Training, validation and test
concepts.definition: Training data fit parameters; validation data guide model choices; a held-out test estimates performance after those choices are fixed.
concepts.formulaNote: These sets are disjoint: an example belongs to only one split.
concepts.example: A 100-well study might use 70 wells to train, 15 to choose settings, and 15 for final testing.
concepts.metaphor: Practice exercises, a mock exam, and a sealed final exam have different jobs.
concepts.question: Which set should choose the learning rate?
options: All data including the final test
concepts.feedback: Use validation performance to choose settings. Reusing the final test to tune the model makes it part of the development process.

sources.title: Training, validation, and test data sets, Wikipedia
sources.label: Wikipedia

questions.question: Which set should choose the learning rate?
options: All data including the final test
questions.feedback: Use validation performance to choose settings. Reusing the final test to tune the model makes it part of the development process.
questions.retryFeedback: Choosing an update setting is model selection. It needs a comparison set while preserving a separate final evaluation.

questions.question: Which split is used to fit model weights?
questions.feedback: Training examples drive the parameter updates.
questions.retryFeedback: Fitting weights directly uses examples to reduce the training objective. Distinguish fitting from model selection and final assessment.

questions.question: Which split helps choose between two model architectures?
options: A mix of all test labels
questions.feedback: Validation is reserved for development choices.
questions.retryFeedback: Comparing architectures is a model-selection step. Reserve a separate split whose results do not guide that choice.

questions.question: When should the final test be evaluated for a final estimate?
options: After every choice to select the best
questions.feedback: Repeated test-driven tuning turns the test into development data.
questions.retryFeedback: If evaluation results change the model choice, that evaluation has joined the selection process. An independent final estimate comes afterward.

questions.question: What does disjoint mean for dataset splits?
options: An example belongs to only one split
questions.feedback: Disjoint sets do not share examples.
questions.retryFeedback: Check membership at the example level. Different filenames or shuffled ordering alone do not establish separation.

questions.question: Each well provides many related measurements. To evaluate predictions on entirely new wells, why keep all measurements from a well in one split?
options: Related samples can otherwise cross the boundary
questions.feedback: Otherwise a model could train on measurements from the same wells used for evaluation. Grouping wells better matches the intended new-well task.
questions.retryFeedback: Samples from one well can share geology and measurement conditions. Splitting their rows can make held-out data less independent than intended.

questions.question: A preprocessing step subtracts a mean estimated from data before the model is fitted. Which split should supply that fitted mean?
questions.feedback: Estimate the mean from training data and reuse it for the other splits. Held-out examples should not fit either the model or its preprocessing.
questions.retryFeedback: Preprocessing values estimated from data are part of fitting the pipeline. Keep the held-out evaluation separate from that fitting.

questions.question: Is a validation set still an untouched final test after many model choices use it?
questions.feedback: Development choices adapt to validation results over time.
questions.retryFeedback: Repeated selection adapts decisions to the observed scores. A dataset used that way no longer provides an untouched assessment.

questions.question: For future-time prediction, which split can reflect deployment?
options: Randomly mix future labels into training
Duplicate every row into all splits
questions.feedback: A chronological holdout tests prediction beyond the training period.
questions.retryFeedback: Match the information boundary of deployment. Future observations should not influence a model intended to predict them from the past.

questions.question: What does strong test performance establish most directly?
options: Performance on that test under its evaluation setup
questions.feedback: The test must represent the intended use to support broader conclusions.
questions.retryFeedback: A test score is conditional on the sampled data, metric, and procedure. Extending it to other settings requires additional evidence.

concepts.title: Data leakage
concepts.definition: Data leakage occurs when model development uses information that would be unavailable in the intended prediction setting. A window is a short consecutive segment of a sequence, so nearby windows can include the same measurements.
concepts.formulaNote: For testing on new wells, keep every well entirely within one split.
concepts.example:
Leakage: train on depths 100, 101, 102 m from Well A, then test on 101, 102, 103 m from that same well. The two shared measurements make the test partly familiar, so its score can look too good.

Fix for testing on new wells: assign all of Well A to training and all of a different Well B to testing before making windows. Fit preprocessing using training wells only, then apply it to the test well. No measurements from Well B influence training.
concepts.metaphor: An exam is misleading when the practice sheet contains copies of its questions.
concepts.question: A model trained on Wells A and B will be used on new wells. Which test set best checks that goal?
options: Measurements from previously unused Wells C and D
Copies of the training rows with different row IDs
Shuffled training measurements from A and B
concepts.feedback: Previously unused wells test performance beyond the wells used to fit the model. New windows or row IDs from training wells do not create that separation.

questions.question: A model trained on Wells A and B will be used on new wells. Which test set best checks that goal?
options: Measurements from previously unused Wells C and D
Copies of the training rows with different row IDs
Shuffled training measurements from A and B
questions.feedback: Previously unused wells test performance beyond the wells used to fit the model. New windows or row IDs from training wells do not create that separation.
questions.retryFeedback: The intended use is a well the model has never learned from. Identify which choice keeps the underlying source measurements separate, not just their row names.

questions.question: A preprocessing mean is fitted using all the data before splitting into training and test sets. Why is this risky?
questions.feedback: Preprocessing must be fitted using only the permitted training information.
questions.retryFeedback: Preprocessing can learn from data even without labels. A held-out distribution should not influence the fitted transformation during evaluation.

questions.question: Which feature leaks information when predicting tomorrow's failure today?
questions.feedback: The future repair outcome is not available at prediction time.
questions.retryFeedback: Ask whether the feature exists at the moment the prediction is made. Later outcomes cannot be available to a real-time predictor.

questions.question: Why can overlapping windows in train and test inflate performance?
questions.feedback: Shared measurements make the held-out examples less independent.
questions.retryFeedback: Different windows can contain many of the same raw observations. Distinct row IDs do not make them independent examples.

questions.question: What is a useful first step before windowing new-well evaluation data?
questions.feedback: Split deployment-relevant groups before deriving related examples.
questions.retryFeedback: Decide the held-out groups before constructing examples that could share their measurements across the split.

questions.question: Is repeatedly tuning against test results a leakage risk?
options: Only if the model is linear
questions.feedback: Test information is being used to shape model development.
questions.retryFeedback: Using a test score to revise choices makes those choices depend on the test. That weakens its independence as a final evaluation.

questions.question: Which is a suspicious target proxy for predicting approval before review?
options: A field filled only after approval
questions.feedback: A post-decision field can indirectly reveal the answer.
questions.retryFeedback: Feature presence can reveal an outcome even without storing the outcome's name. Inspect when and why the field is populated.

questions.question: Does removing the explicit target column eliminate every leak?
questions.feedback: Proxies, duplicates, preprocessing, and split design can still leak information.
questions.retryFeedback: Information about a target can remain in proxies, duplicated records, preprocessing statistics, or future measurements.

questions.question: What should feature availability be checked against?
options: The end of the whole project
questions.feedback: A feature is legitimate only if the deployment process can supply it then.
questions.retryFeedback: Availability is a time-dependent property. A feature in an eventual record may be absent when the model must act.

questions.question: What result would most warrant investigating leakage?
options: Near-perfect held-out scores from overlapping train/test records
questions.feedback: Shared records can make apparent generalization misleading.
questions.retryFeedback: Unusually strong results deserve extra scrutiny when training and test examples share underlying information. A score alone does not identify the cause.

concepts.title: Normalization
concepts.definition: Normalization rescales data to a chosen reference scale. Standardization, one common method, subtracts the mean μ and divides by the standard deviation σ.
concepts.formulaNote: This is standardization: subtract the mean, then divide by the standard deviation.
concepts.example: Training data give μ = 100 and σ = 20. A new value x = 140 becomes z = 2.
concepts.metaphor: Convert different measuring rulers into a common “distance from typical” scale.
concepts.question: With training mean 15 and standard deviation 4, what standardized value does x = 27 become?
concepts.feedback: Standardization gives (27−15)/4 = 12/4 = 3.

questions.question: With training mean 15 and standard deviation 4, what standardized value does x = 27 become?
questions.feedback: Standardization gives (27−15)/4 = 12/4 = 3.
questions.retryFeedback: Subtract the fitted mean before dividing by the fitted standard deviation. The numerator is a deviation, not the original reading.

questions.question: For x = 8, μ = 10, and σ = 2, what is z?
