questions.retryFeedback: The contract's expected units determine how a value is interpreted. Supplying a number in another scale changes its physical meaning.

questions.question: Why define error responses?
options: Callers need to handle failed operations
Errors prove every result is correct
questions.feedback: Failures are part of an interface's behavior.
questions.retryFeedback: Failure is a possible outcome of a call. A caller needs a defined way to recognize it and decide what to do next.

questions.question: Does an API name alone tell you its complete semantics?
questions.feedback: Documentation and implementation define what the operation actually does.
questions.retryFeedback: Names can be suggestive but leave assumptions unstated. Units, defaults, constraints, and failure behavior need explicit documentation.

questions.question: An API named mean requires a list of numbers. Which argument satisfies that requirement?
options: An object containing only a field named mean
questions.feedback: The first argument is a list whose entries are all numbers. A text string, a single number, or a differently structured object does not meet this stated contract.
questions.retryFeedback: Check both the outer structure and the types of its entries. Looking like numerical text is not the same as supplying a list of numbers.

questions.question: Can two implementations expose the same API?
questions.feedback: An interface can stay stable while its implementation changes.
questions.retryFeedback: An interface describes observable behavior. Different internal programs can satisfy the same external agreement.

questions.question: An API returns an explicit failure because its input is invalid. What should an SDK calling it report?
options: A new numeric answer invented by the SDK
The last successful value as if it were current
The failure, so the caller can handle it
questions.feedback: A failed computation is different from a valid zero or a previous result. The SDK should preserve that distinction for the caller.
questions.retryFeedback: Consider what evidence exists for a new result after the service rejects the input. Failure information is part of the interaction.

questions.question: Why record an API or model version used for a result?
questions.feedback: Version context helps reproduce and interpret computations.
questions.retryFeedback: The same request can behave differently after an implementation or model update. Reproducing a result needs its relevant version context.

concepts.title: Tool calling
concepts.definition: Tool calling lets a model request a structured operation from external software, then use the returned result. The software defines the operation's semantics.
concepts.example: A model requests mean([10, 20, 30]); the calculator returns 20, which the answer reports.
concepts.metaphor: A coordinator asks a calculator to calculate instead of guessing the result from memory.
concepts.question: Who should compute an exact average in a grounded answer?
options: A defined numerical tool on the cited data
concepts.feedback: A tool can execute exact arithmetic or a computational model. Its inputs, units, implementation, and result still need to be checked and linked to the answer.

sources.title: Large language model: Tool use, Wikipedia
sources.label: Wikipedia

questions.question: Who should compute an exact average in a grounded answer?
options: A defined numerical tool on the cited data
questions.feedback: A tool can execute exact arithmetic or a computational model. Its inputs, units, implementation, and result still need to be checked and linked to the answer.
questions.retryFeedback: Exact arithmetic should follow a specified operation on identified inputs. Fluent text generation alone does not execute that calculation reliably.

questions.question: What should a model send to invoke a defined tool?
options: A training label for every user
A structured operation name and arguments
questions.feedback: The runtime needs an identified operation and valid arguments.
questions.retryFeedback: The execution system must identify the operation and parse its inputs. A vague natural-language claim that a tool was used is insufficient.

questions.question: Who defines what a tool operation actually computes?
options: The tool's software contract and implementation
questions.feedback: Language cannot redefine a computation simply by describing it differently.
questions.retryFeedback: A model can request a tool, but that request does not define arbitrary new semantics for the tool's existing operation.

questions.question: Why validate tool arguments before execution?
options: Every generated argument is guaranteed valid
Malformed or misinterpreted inputs can produce bad results
questions.feedback: Check structure, units, ranges, and relevant assumptions.
questions.retryFeedback: Execution can be technically successful yet use wrong units, missing values, or invalid inputs. Check the operation's contract first.

questions.question: Does a tool result automatically justify any statement attached to it?
questions.feedback: The explanation must follow from the returned result and its context.
questions.retryFeedback: A computed result supports only conclusions justified by its inputs, method, and scope. Surrounding prose can still overstate it.

questions.question: If a tool returns an error, what should the answer do?
options: Report or handle the failure honestly
Claim success from the request alone
Treat the error as a measurement
questions.feedback: A requested computation is not a successful computation.
questions.retryFeedback: A failed operation supplies no successful result to report. The response must reflect what actually happened.

questions.question: Why use a calculator tool for exact arithmetic?
questions.feedback: Exact computation still depends on appropriate inputs.
questions.retryFeedback: The tool applies an explicit arithmetic procedure to the provided values. Input validity and interpretation still need to be checked.

questions.question: A tool averages sensor readings taken from 10 m to 12 m depth. Which information should accompany the reported average?
options: Source, depth interval, units, and method
questions.feedback: State which readings were used, their depth interval and units, and how the average was computed so the result can be checked.
questions.retryFeedback: A number alone does not identify what was measured or combined. Look for enough context to reproduce and interpret this particular calculation.

questions.question: Does choosing a tool itself train the language model?
questions.feedback: Tool use is generally an inference-time interaction with external software.
questions.retryFeedback: Choosing an inference-time operation changes the workflow. It does not ordinarily run a parameter-fitting procedure.

questions.question: Why distinguish requesting an action from reporting its outcome?
options: Requests and results are always identical
Execution may fail or return an unexpected result
questions.feedback: The answer should reflect observed tool output, not merely the intended call.
questions.retryFeedback: Issuing a request does not establish successful completion. Inspect the returned status and output before describing the result.

concepts.title: State, observation and action
concepts.definition: A state contains enough information to predict the system’s next-state distribution given an action. An observation is a measurement of the system. An action is an input we choose.
concepts.formula: sₜ₊₁ = F(sₜ, aₜ);   oₜ = H(sₜ) + noise
concepts.example: In a simple tank model, state s = 10 litres. A noisy sensor reports observation o = 9.8 litres. Choosing to add 3 litres is action a = 3.
concepts.metaphor: The whole room is the state; a keyhole view is the observation; turning the handle is an action.
concepts.question: A thermometer reads 29.8 °C. What is that reading?
concepts.feedback: Measurements can be noisy and incomplete. A hidden-state problem may require a history or belief over states, rather than treating one reading as a complete Markov state.

sources.title: Partially observable Markov decision process, Wikipedia
sources.label: Wikipedia

sources.title: Sensor Selection for Crowdsensing Dynamical Systems, Schnitzler, Yu and Mannor, 2015
sources.label: Paper

questions.question: A thermometer reads 29.8 °C. What is that reading?
questions.feedback: Measurements can be noisy and incomplete. A hidden-state problem may require a history or belief over states, rather than treating one reading as a complete Markov state.
questions.retryFeedback: A sensor reading is obtained through a measurement process. Distinguish the reported value from the full underlying physical condition.

questions.question: A robot has a true position, a camera reading of that position, a desired destination, and a chosen motor command. Which is an observation?
questions.feedback: The camera reading measures the system and may contain error. It is distinct from the desired outcome, chosen action, and full physical state.
questions.retryFeedback: Identify what is measured from the system, rather than what the controller wants or commands. A measurement need not fully reveal reality.

questions.question: A temperature controller receives a sensor reading and chooses a heater power. Which quantity is its action?
questions.feedback: The heater setting is an input selected by the controller. The reading is an observation, while actual temperature and outside changes are not this chosen command.
questions.retryFeedback: Look for the input the controller actively selects. Separate it from measured conditions and changes arriving from outside the controller.

questions.question: Must one observation reveal the full state?
questions.feedback: Measurements can be partial or noisy.
questions.retryFeedback: Noise and partial sensing can leave relevant physical quantities unknown. One reading may be compatible with several underlying conditions.

questions.question: What makes a state sufficient for prediction in this setting?
options: It summarizes the information needed for next-state probabilities given an action
It contains only the latest displayed number
questions.feedback: A state supports prediction without needing omitted relevant history.
questions.retryFeedback: The state representation should retain information needed for the transition distribution. A convenient measurement list may omit some of it.

questions.question: Why might a controller use observation history?
options: To infer hidden aspects of state
questions.feedback: Several measurements can provide information missing from a single reading.
questions.retryFeedback: Past readings can constrain hidden quantities that a single noisy reading cannot reveal. Their usefulness depends on the dynamics and observation model.

questions.question: A noisy sensor leaves two possible tank volumes: 9 litres with probability 0.3 and 10 litres with probability 0.7. What does this probability distribution describe?
options: A list of allowed actions only
A distribution representing uncertainty about the hidden state
A certainty that the sensor is exact
questions.feedback: It represents uncertainty about the hidden state. Such a distribution is often called a belief over states; it is not a chosen action or an exact sensor reading.
questions.retryFeedback: The alternatives are possible actual tank volumes. Distinguish uncertainty about those volumes from uncertainty about which action to choose.

questions.question: In o = H(s) + noise, what does H represent?
questions.feedback: H maps the underlying state to an ideal observation before noise.
questions.retryFeedback: Separate the mapping from physical condition to reported signal from the additional random measurement perturbation.

questions.question: Can two different states produce the same observation?
options: Only if the sensor is broken
Only if both states are zero
questions.feedback: A partial measurement may not distinguish all underlying conditions.
questions.retryFeedback: A measurement mapping may discard information or include noise. It need not assign distinct readings to every distinct state.

questions.question: Why is confusing observation with full state risky?
options: It always makes the system deterministic
The controller may omit information needed to predict consequences
questions.feedback: Incomplete state information can invalidate the assumed prediction model.
questions.retryFeedback: Different hidden conditions can lead to different action consequences despite a similar reading. Prediction needs an adequate information representation.

concepts.title: Dynamical system
concepts.definition: A dynamical system has a state that changes over time. Its transition rule describes how the next state depends on the current state, any chosen action, and disturbances.
concepts.formulaNote: s is state, a is action, ξ is a disturbance, and t is the time step.
concepts.example: A tank holds 10 litres. Add 3 and drain 2 during one step: next volume = 10 + 3 − 2 = 11.
concepts.metaphor: The present is a frame in a movie; dynamics specify how the next frame can unfold.
concepts.question: A tank has 8 litres, receives 4, and drains 3. Next volume?
concepts.feedback: Use conservation: 8 + 4 − 3 = 9. A model may use physical equations, learned relationships, or both to describe its dynamics.

sources.title: Sensor Selection for Crowdsensing Dynamical Systems, Schnitzler, Yu and Mannor, 2015
sources.label: Paper

questions.question: A tank has 8 litres, receives 4, and drains 3. Next volume?
questions.feedback: Use conservation: 8 + 4 − 3 = 9. A model may use physical equations, learned relationships, or both to describe its dynamics.
questions.retryFeedback: Start with the current quantity, add inflow, and subtract outflow. Keep chosen signs consistent with the physical balance.

questions.question: What does a transition rule predict?
options: The next state from current conditions and inputs
questions.feedback: Dynamics describe how the system evolves.
questions.retryFeedback: A transition relates a system before and after one time step. It uses current conditions and any specified driving inputs.

questions.question: For sₜ₊₁ = sₜ + aₜ and sₜ = 4, aₜ = −1, what is next state?
questions.feedback: Substitute into the stated transition equation.
questions.retryFeedback: Substitute both signed terms into the recurrence. A negative action reduces the state under this additive model.

questions.question: What is a disturbance in a dynamics model?
questions.feedback: Disturbances represent effects the controller does not directly choose.
questions.retryFeedback: Separate influences selected by the controller from influences outside its choice, such as unmodeled inflow or external noise.

questions.question: Can a dynamical system have random transitions?
questions.feedback: A transition can assign probabilities to different next states.
questions.retryFeedback: A transition can specify a distribution of possible outcomes rather than one fixed next value. Randomness does not exclude dynamics.

questions.question: Why include an action in F(s, a, ξ)?
questions.feedback: Control inputs can change what the system does next.
questions.retryFeedback: The same current state may evolve differently under different commands. The transition rule needs to represent that dependence.

questions.question: For sₜ₊₁ = 0.5sₜ with initial state 8, what is the state after two steps?
questions.feedback: The sequence is 8, 4, 2.
questions.retryFeedback: Apply the recurrence twice in sequence. The second update uses the result of the first, not the original state.

questions.question: For the deterministic transition sₜ₊₁ = 0.5sₜ + 2, which state remains unchanged after one step?
questions.feedback: At s = 4, the next state is 0.5×4 + 2 = 4. A state mapped back to itself is called an equilibrium.
questions.retryFeedback: Substitute each proposed current state into the transition rule. Look for an output equal to that same input state.

questions.question: Can a dynamics model combine physical equations with learned corrections?
questions.feedback: Hybrid models can combine known structure with estimated residual behavior.
questions.retryFeedback: Known physical structure can supply a baseline while data estimate remaining discrepancies. Those sources of information need not be mutually exclusive.

questions.question: Why validate a model over the intended operating range?
options: Prediction errors can vary across conditions
Range has no role in control
A model is exact outside training by definition
questions.feedback: Useful accuracy in one region need not transfer to another.
questions.retryFeedback: A model's fit can depend on the conditions covered by its data. Intended operating conditions need relevant validation evidence.

concepts.title: Markov decision process
concepts.definition: An MDP describes states, actions, rewards and transition probabilities. Given the current state and action, the next-state distribution does not depend on earlier history.
concepts.formula: P(sₜ₊₁ ∣ history, aₜ) = P(sₜ₊₁ ∣ sₜ, aₜ)
concepts.example: In state “low,” choosing “fill” reaches “safe” with probability 0.9 and stays “low” with probability 0.1. Suppose reaching “safe” earns reward 1, otherwise 0.
concepts.metaphor: A board-game position contains everything needed to determine the next move's possibilities.
concepts.question: What is the Markov assumption?
options: Observations always reveal every state variable
The current state and action suffice for the next-state distribution
concepts.feedback: An MDP can be stochastic. The key condition is conditional dependence on the current state, not the whole history. Observations may require a partially observable extension.

sources.title: Reinforcement Learning: Foundations, Mannor, Mansour and Tamar
sources.label: Textbook

questions.question: What is the Markov assumption?
options: Observations always reveal every state variable
The current state and action suffice for the next-state distribution
questions.feedback: An MDP can be stochastic. The key condition is conditional dependence on the current state, not the whole history. Observations may require a partially observable extension.
questions.retryFeedback: The assumption concerns whether additional past history changes the next-state distribution after the current state and action are known.

questions.question: Two histories lead to the same current state. The same action is chosen in both. In an MDP, how do their next-state probability distributions compare?
options: The longer history always has a larger next state
The realized next states must always be identical
questions.feedback: Given the same state and action, the earlier histories do not change the next-state distribution. Separate random draws can still produce different realized states.
questions.retryFeedback: The Markov condition concerns a probability distribution given the present information. Equal distributions do not require identical outcomes on separate trials.

questions.question: Which collection describes an MDP's core ingredients?
options: Only a loss and learning rate
Only observations and a file format
questions.feedback: An MDP specifies sequential decision-making structure.
questions.retryFeedback: Sequential decision making needs to describe situations, available choices, their consequences, and how those consequences are scored.

questions.question: Can an MDP have random transitions?
questions.feedback: Markov does not mean deterministic.
questions.retryFeedback: The transition component is generally a probability distribution. A Markov assumption is about history dependence, not absence of randomness.

questions.question: If the recorded state omits relevant history, what may fail?
options: The Markov property for that representation
questions.feedback: The future can then depend on omitted information.
questions.retryFeedback: If omitted information changes future probabilities, the recorded representation is not sufficient for the claimed transition rule.

questions.question: One rule chooses an action from the current state; another gives probabilities of next states after an action. How do their roles differ?
options: The first selects what to do; the second describes possible consequences
The first measures sensor noise; the second chooses a target
Both must predict the same single next state
questions.feedback: Choosing an action is the decision rule’s job. The transition model describes what may happen once that action is chosen.
questions.retryFeedback: Separate a choice under the agent’s control from the system’s response to that choice. One precedes the other.

questions.question: A tank sensor reports only "low" for many different volumes. If those volumes lead to different next-state probabilities under the same action, is "low" alone a sufficient Markov state?
options: Yes; using a word removes randomness
Yes; every sensor reading is a complete state
No; states are never allowed to contain observations
No; it hides information needed for those probabilities
questions.feedback: The same recorded value combines situations with different transition behavior. More information may be needed to represent a sufficient state.
questions.retryFeedback: Ask whether the recorded state and chosen action identify the required transition distribution. A measurement may omit information the system’s dynamics depend on.

questions.question: What must transition probabilities over possible next states sum to?
questions.feedback: For a given state and action, they form a probability distribution.
questions.retryFeedback: For each fixed state and action, possible next states form the outcome distribution. Their complete probability mass must normalize.

questions.question: Can the chosen state include a history summary?
options: Only a single scalar is allowed
Only the current observation is allowed
questions.feedback: A suitable summary can capture predictive information from history.
questions.retryFeedback: A state is a modeling representation. Relevant past information can be summarized within it when that helps make transitions well defined.

questions.question: Does modeling a problem as an MDP ensure its assumptions are correct?
options: Only if written as an equation
questions.feedback: The representation and transition assumptions need to fit the real task.
questions.retryFeedback: Writing down a formal model states assumptions. Evidence about the real system is needed to determine whether those assumptions are adequate.

concepts.title: Reward and return
concepts.definition: A reward scores one outcome. Return adds rewards over several steps. A discount factor γ gives less weight to later rewards when 0 ≤ γ < 1.
concepts.formulaNote: H is the number of remaining steps. The reward rₜ follows action aₜ; γ discounts later rewards.
concepts.example: For three rewards (2, 0, 10) and γ = 0.5, return = 2 + 0 + 0.25 × 10 = 4.5.
concepts.metaphor: Immediate reward is one coin; return is the discounted value of the entire trail of coins.
concepts.question: Rewards are (1, 4), γ = 0.5. What is the two-step return?
concepts.feedback: The return is 1 + 0.5 × 4 = 3. Finite horizons permit γ = 1; infinite-horizon convergence needs appropriate assumptions, often γ < 1.

sources.title: Reinforcement Learning: Foundations, Mannor, Mansour and Tamar
sources.label: Textbook

questions.question: Rewards are (1, 4), γ = 0.5. What is the two-step return?
questions.feedback: The return is 1 + 0.5 × 4 = 3. Finite horizons permit γ = 1; infinite-horizon convergence needs appropriate assumptions, often γ < 1.
questions.retryFeedback: The first reward is undiscounted; the next receives one factor of γ. Apply the factors before combining the rewards.

questions.question: What distinguishes reward from return?
options: Reward scores one outcome; return accumulates rewards
questions.feedback: Return aggregates consequences over multiple steps.
questions.retryFeedback: Distinguish a score received at one step from the objective that combines scores over several steps.

questions.question: For rewards 2, 4, and 8 with γ = 0.5, what is return?
questions.retryFeedback: Apply successive powers of the discount factor to rewards at successive positions. Later terms do not all use the same multiplier.

questions.question: What does γ = 0 emphasize?
options: Equal weight on all future rewards
questions.feedback: Every later reward is multiplied by a positive power of zero.
questions.retryFeedback: Every later reward contains a positive power of γ. Examine those terms when the discount factor vanishes.

questions.question: What does γ = 1 do over a finite horizon?
questions.feedback: A finite number of terms can be summed without discounting.
questions.retryFeedback: Over the stated finite horizon, evaluate the multiplier on each reward when every power of γ has the same value.

questions.question: Can rewards be negative?
questions.feedback: Negative rewards can represent costs or penalties.
questions.retryFeedback: Rewards are numerical scores defined by the task. Penalties can be represented with signed values.

questions.question: For rewards −1 and 4 with γ = 0.5, what is return?
questions.feedback: The discounted sum is −1 + 0.5×4.
questions.retryFeedback: Keep the immediate reward's negative sign, and discount only the later reward before adding.

questions.question: Why might maximizing immediate reward give a poor long-term result?
questions.feedback: A short-term gain can create worse later conditions.
questions.retryFeedback: A locally attractive action can change the states and opportunities encountered afterward. The full objective includes those later consequences.

questions.question: Does a high return under a specified reward prove the real objective was achieved?
questions.feedback: The reward may be an imperfect proxy for the intended goal.
questions.retryFeedback: The reward is a chosen proxy for the desired behavior. Maximizing it can exploit omissions or mismatches in that proxy.

questions.question: Two rewards of 10 occur now and one step later. Which discount factor, 0.5 or 0.9, gives the later reward more weight?
questions.feedback: The later reward contributes γ×10: 9 with γ = 0.9 versus 5 with γ = 0.5. The immediate reward has weight 1 in both cases.
questions.retryFeedback: Compare the factor multiplying the second reward in the return formula. The immediate reward does not receive that one-step discount.

concepts.title: Policy
concepts.definition: A policy specifies how an agent chooses actions. A stochastic policy gives an action probability for each state or available information.
concepts.example: In a low tank, π(fill) = 0.8 and π(wait) = 0.2. A deterministic policy might always fill.
concepts.metaphor: A playbook says what to do when a particular situation appears.
concepts.question: What does a policy map a state to?
options: An action or distribution over actions
concepts.feedback: The policy chooses behavior. The environment transition rule determines what happens next, and the reward rule assigns the resulting feedback.

sources.title: Reinforcement Learning: Foundations, Mannor, Mansour and Tamar
sources.label: Textbook

questions.question: What does a policy map a state to?
options: An action or distribution over actions
questions.feedback: The policy chooses behavior. The environment transition rule determines what happens next, and the reward rule assigns the resulting feedback.
questions.retryFeedback: A policy specifies the agent's choice behavior. Distinguish that from an environment model or a score of future outcomes.

questions.question: What does π(a given s) describe?
options: The probability of choosing action a in state s
questions.feedback: A stochastic policy specifies action selection.
questions.retryFeedback: Read the condition as the available state information. The probability describes the agent's selection among permitted choices.

questions.question: For two actions with probabilities 0.7 and p, what must p be?
questions.feedback: Action probabilities sum to one.
questions.retryFeedback: The two available choices exhaust the policy's probability mass. Subtract the known allocation from the total.

questions.question: What is a deterministic policy?
options: A guarantee the environment is deterministic
A rule selecting one action for each state
questions.feedback: Deterministic action choice does not remove environmental randomness.
questions.retryFeedback: Compare a rule that always chooses one specified action in a state with a rule that randomizes among several actions.

questions.question: Can two policies produce different returns in the same environment?
questions.feedback: Different actions lead to different distributions of outcomes.
questions.retryFeedback: Choices affect state trajectories and their rewards. Holding the environment fixed does not make all decision rules equivalent.

questions.question: What should a policy respect in a constrained task?
questions.feedback: Action choices must remain compatible with the task's constraints.
questions.retryFeedback: The decision rule must choose among actions the task allows. A high predicted reward does not make a forbidden action permissible.

questions.question: Does the policy itself determine exactly what the environment does next?
questions.feedback: The transition model describes how the environment responds.
questions.retryFeedback: The policy chooses what to do; the transition dynamics describe what follows, possibly with randomness or disturbances.

questions.question: What is policy evaluation?
options: Estimating the return from following a policy
questions.feedback: Evaluation measures the performance of the decision rule.
questions.retryFeedback: Evaluation asks how well a fixed decision rule performs. It is different from directly changing that rule to seek improvement.

questions.question: What is policy improvement trying to do?
options: Find action choices with better expected return
Increase the number of sensor names
questions.feedback: The goal is improved behavior under the specified objective.
questions.retryFeedback: Improvement changes decision behavior according to expected future outcomes. It is not merely estimating an unchanged rule's performance.

questions.question: Can a policy condition on available history rather than a single raw observation?
questions.feedback: History or a belief can provide the needed information under partial observability.
questions.retryFeedback: When one observation is incomplete, available history can inform the choice. The policy's input representation must be specified accordingly.

concepts.title: Value function
concepts.definition: A state-value function is the expected return starting in a state and following a specified policy. An action-value also fixes the first action.
concepts.formula: Vπ(s) = Eπ[Gₜ ∣ sₜ = s];   Qπ(s, a) = Eπ[Gₜ ∣ s, a]
concepts.example: A policy yields return 10 with probability 0.6 and 0 otherwise, so Vπ(s) = 6.
concepts.metaphor: Value is a forecast of the whole journey's worth, not the reward on the next step.
concepts.question: A state's possible returns are 4 and 8, equally likely. Its value?
concepts.feedback: Value is the expected return: (4 + 8)/2 = 6. It depends on the policy, reward definition, discounting, and environment.

sources.title: Reinforcement Learning: Foundations, Mannor, Mansour and Tamar
sources.label: Textbook

questions.question: A state's possible returns are 4 and 8, equally likely. Its value?
questions.feedback: Value is the expected return: (4 + 8)/2 = 6. It depends on the policy, reward definition, discounting, and environment.
questions.retryFeedback: A value averages possible returns using their probabilities. Equal probabilities require equal weighting of the listed returns.

questions.question: What does Vπ(s) estimate?
options: The probability of the state name
Expected return from state s under policy π
questions.feedback: Value combines future consequences under a specified policy.
questions.retryFeedback: The superscript specifies which decision rule is followed. Value combines future rewards under that rule from the given starting point.

questions.question: How does Qπ(s, a) differ from Vπ(s)?
options: It never depends on a policy
It fixes the first action as well as the state
questions.feedback: Action-value evaluates a particular initial action followed by the policy.
questions.retryFeedback: An action-value function conditions on an additional initial choice. Subsequent behavior still follows the specified policy.

questions.question: For equally likely returns 2 and 8, what is expected value?
questions.feedback: Average the two returns.
questions.retryFeedback: Weight both possible returns equally, add, and normalize. Returning either outcome alone ignores the other possibility.

questions.question: Can a state's value change when the policy changes?
options: Only when the state is renamed
questions.feedback: Future behavior affects expected return.
questions.retryFeedback: Value depends on the future decisions made from a state. Changing those decisions can change its expected accumulated reward.

questions.question: Can a value be negative?
questions.feedback: Negative rewards can produce negative expected return.
questions.retryFeedback: Value averages the task's reward totals. If penalties dominate, the expected total can lie below zero.

questions.question: Does a high value imply a guaranteed high realized return?
questions.feedback: Expectation averages possible outcomes, which can vary.
questions.retryFeedback: Expectation summarizes possible trajectories rather than eliminating their uncertainty. One realized trajectory may perform differently.

questions.question: Which change can alter a value function without changing the physical states?
questions.feedback: Value depends on the chosen reward and discounting, not state labels alone.
questions.retryFeedback: Physical dynamics are only one part of value. The scoring rule determines which outcomes count as beneficial or costly.

questions.question: How are Vπ and Qπ related for discrete actions?
options: Vπ(s) = Σₐ π(a given s)Qπ(s, a)
Vπ is always the largest Qπ
questions.feedback: State value averages action-values under the policy's action probabilities.
questions.retryFeedback: State value averages the action-conditioned values according to how often the policy selects each action in that state.

questions.question: If a policy chooses returns valued at 4 and 10 with probabilities 0.75 and 0.25, what is V?
questions.feedback: The weighted average is 0.75×4 + 0.25×10.
questions.retryFeedback: Multiply each action-conditioned value by its selection probability, then add. The two choices are not equally weighted.

concepts.title: Bellman equation
concepts.definition: The Bellman equation decomposes a policy's value into expected immediate reward plus discounted value of the next state.
concepts.example: Reward now is 2. Next-state value is 10 or 0, equally likely, under the policy. At γ = 0.9: V = 2 + 0.9×(0.5×10 + 0.5×0) = 6.5.
concepts.metaphor: A journey's worth is this leg's reward plus what remains beyond the next stop.
concepts.question: Reward 3, deterministic next value 4, γ = 0.5. Current value?
concepts.feedback: Compute 3 + 0.5 × 4 = 5. In stochastic settings, average over next states and actions under the specified policy.

sources.title: Reinforcement Learning: Foundations, Mannor, Mansour and Tamar
sources.label: Textbook

questions.question: Reward 3, deterministic next value 4, γ = 0.5. Current value?
questions.feedback: Compute 3 + 0.5 × 4 = 5. In stochastic settings, average over next states and actions under the specified policy.
questions.retryFeedback: The current backup combines the immediate reward with a discounted continuation value. Discount the continuation, not both terms.

questions.question: What two parts appear in a Bellman value decomposition?
options: Immediate reward and discounted next-state value
questions.feedback: It separates one step from the remaining expected return.
questions.retryFeedback: Separate what is received now from the estimate of what follows. The recursive expression connects those two time scales.

questions.question: With immediate reward 2, γ = 0.5, and next value 6, what is the Bellman value estimate?
questions.feedback: Compute 2 + 0.5×6.
questions.retryFeedback: Multiply the next-state value by the discount factor before adding the current reward.

questions.question: Why is an expectation needed for stochastic transitions?
options: The value must be an integer
questions.feedback: Average the possible continuation outcomes with their probabilities.
questions.retryFeedback: A stochastic transition can reach different outcomes. Weight their contributions by the transition probabilities rather than selecting one arbitrarily.

questions.question: Under zero continuation value at termination, what is the last-step Bellman value estimate?
questions.feedback: There is no later value to add.
questions.retryFeedback: At termination, the assumed continuation contributes nothing. Substitute that boundary condition into the backup expression.

questions.question: For next values 2 and 6, equally likely, reward 1 and γ = 0.5, what is the Bellman value estimate?
questions.feedback: Expected next value is 4, giving 1 + 0.5×4.
questions.retryFeedback: Average the possible next-state values first, then discount that expectation and add the immediate reward.

questions.question: Under a fixed policy, the next state has value 10 with probability 0.2 and value 0 with probability 0.8. What continuation value enters the Bellman expectation before discounting?
questions.feedback: The expected continuation value is 0.2×10 + 0.8×0 = 2. A policy expectation averages outcomes; it does not select the best outcome.
questions.retryFeedback: Weight each possible next-state value by its probability. Do not replace a probabilistic outcome with the most favorable possibility.

questions.question: What happens to the Bellman equation when γ = 0?
options: Value depends only on expected immediate reward
questions.feedback: The continuation term is multiplied by zero.
questions.retryFeedback: The discount factor multiplies continuation. Check which part of the equation survives when that multiplier vanishes.

questions.question: Does a Bellman equation itself prove a learned value estimate is accurate?
questions.feedback: The estimate must satisfy the relevant model and data constraints.
questions.retryFeedback: The equation states a relationship for the modeled problem. A numerical estimate still needs to satisfy it accurately under appropriate assumptions.

questions.question: Why is the decomposition useful computationally?
options: It links local updates to future return estimates
questions.feedback: Dynamic programming and temporal-difference methods exploit this recursive structure.
questions.retryFeedback: A long-horizon quantity can be expressed using one step and a continuation estimate. That structure supports repeated local calculations.

concepts.title: Exploration and exploitation
concepts.definition: Exploitation chooses what currently appears best. Exploration gathers information by trying alternatives that may improve future decisions.
concepts.formulaNote: In ε-greedy action selection, exploration chooses uniformly from all actions. Exploitation chooses an action with the largest estimated Q value.
concepts.example: With ε = 0.1 over 100 decisions, expect about 10 exploration-branch choices, not exactly 10.
concepts.metaphor: Return to your favorite food stall, but sometimes try another to discover a better one.
concepts.question: Why try an action with a lower current value estimate?
options: Its uncertain true value might be better
Lower estimates always mean higher true rewards
concepts.feedback: Learning needs information about alternatives. Exploration should respect constraints. In ε-greedy, the random branch can sometimes select the currently best action too.

sources.title: Reinforcement Learning: Foundations, Mannor, Mansour and Tamar
sources.label: Textbook

questions.question: Why try an action with a lower current value estimate?
options: Its uncertain true value might be better
Lower estimates always mean higher true rewards
questions.feedback: Learning needs information about alternatives. Exploration should respect constraints. In ε-greedy, the random branch can sometimes select the currently best action too.
questions.retryFeedback: Current estimates are uncertain and may be wrong. An action with a modest estimate can supply information about a potentially better option.

questions.question: Which behavior is exploitation?
options: Choosing the action currently estimated best
Trying an uncertain alternative to learn
questions.feedback: Exploitation uses current knowledge to seek a good outcome.
questions.retryFeedback: Exploitation uses what the agent currently believes about action quality. It does not necessarily seek the most informative alternative.

questions.question: Which behavior is exploration?
options: Trying an alternative to gather information
questions.feedback: Exploration can improve knowledge about future choices.
questions.retryFeedback: Exploration accepts a possible short-term cost to learn about uncertain choices. Compare that motivation with using the current best estimate.

questions.question: In ε-greedy selection, what does ε control?
options: The probability of taking the exploration branch
questions.feedback: The random branch is selected with probability ε.
questions.retryFeedback: The ε-greedy procedure first chooses a branch. Distinguish the probability of that branch from the final probability of a particular action.

questions.question: With ε = 0, what does ε-greedy do?
questions.feedback: No random exploration branch is taken.
questions.retryFeedback: Evaluate the branch-selection probabilities at the stated endpoint. The exploration branch then has no probability mass.

questions.question: Can the random exploration branch choose the currently best action?
questions.feedback: Uniform random selection can include the greedy action too.
questions.retryFeedback: Uniform random selection usually includes every allowed action. It need not exclude the action that the greedy branch would choose.

questions.question: With two actions, one uniquely greedy, and ε = 0.2 with uniform exploration, what is the probability of the greedy action?
questions.feedback: It is selected by the 0.8 greedy branch plus half of the 0.2 random branch.
questions.retryFeedback: The greedy action can be selected through either branch. Add its guaranteed greedy-branch probability and its share of random exploration.

questions.question: Why can pure exploitation miss a better action?
options: An untried action may be underestimated
questions.feedback: Without new information, mistaken estimates can persist.
questions.retryFeedback: Without new information, an initially pessimistic estimate may never be corrected. A decision rule can remain committed to an inferior choice.

questions.question: Should exploration ignore safety constraints?
options: Only during training on real equipment
questions.feedback: Information gathering still needs appropriate operating limits.
questions.retryFeedback: Gathering information does not remove the task's permitted-action boundary. Exploration must still operate within applicable constraints.

questions.question: Does trying every action once guarantee the best long-term policy is known?
questions.feedback: Uncertainty and sequential consequences may require much more evidence.
questions.retryFeedback: One observation does not reveal a noisy reward distribution or long-term consequences. The required evidence depends on the problem.

concepts.title: Q-learning
concepts.definition: Q-learning updates an action-value estimate toward a target using observed reward and the largest estimated next-state action value.
concepts.formula: Q(s, a) ← Q(s, a) + α[r + γ max_b Q(s′, b) − Q(s, a)]
concepts.metaphor: Revise a travel guide whenever a journey reveals a better estimate of the route's payoff.
concepts.question: A Q-learning transition has reward −2, discount γ = 0.9, and best next-state Q value 10. What is the target r + γ max Q before averaging?
concepts.feedback: The target is −2 + 0.9×10 = 7. The learning-rate interpolation with the old Q value would be a separate step.

sources.title: Reinforcement Learning: Foundations, Mannor, Mansour and Tamar
sources.label: Textbook

questions.question: A Q-learning transition has reward −2, discount γ = 0.9, and best next-state Q value 10. What is the target r + γ max Q before averaging?
questions.feedback: The target is −2 + 0.9×10 = 7. The learning-rate interpolation with the old Q value would be a separate step.
questions.retryFeedback: Discount the best estimated continuation value, then add the immediate signed reward. Do not average with an old estimate yet.

questions.question: Which next-state quantity appears in the Q-learning target?
options: Only the previously chosen action name
questions.feedback: The target uses a greedy next-action value.
questions.retryFeedback: The target uses a greedy comparison over next-state actions. It need not use the action selected by the behavior policy.

questions.question: For r = 2, γ = 0.5, and max Q(next) = 8, what is the target?
questions.feedback: Compute 2 + 0.5×8.
questions.retryFeedback: Scale the best next-state estimate by γ and add the observed reward. Do not average those two terms.

questions.question: If old Q = 4, target = 10, and α = 0.5, what is updated Q?
questions.feedback: Move halfway from 4 toward 10: 4 + 0.5×6.
questions.retryFeedback: Move the old estimate a fraction α of the way toward the target. Equivalently, form the corresponding weighted average.

questions.question: What does α = 0 do to a Q estimate?
questions.feedback: The correction is multiplied by zero.
questions.retryFeedback: The learning rate scales the correction from the old estimate toward the target. Evaluate that correction at the stated endpoint.

questions.question: When Q values are stored directly in a table, what does α = 1 do to the entry being updated?
questions.feedback: The full difference between target and current estimate is added.
questions.retryFeedback: Use Qnew = Qold + α(target − Qold). Substitute the endpoint learning rate before simplifying.

questions.question: The update moves current Q toward a target. Which difference in the Q-learning formula determines the direction of that adjustment?
options: Next state minus current state always
questions.feedback: Target minus current Q determines whether the update raises or lowers Q. This difference is called the temporal-difference error.
questions.retryFeedback: Inspect the correction inside the brackets. It should be positive when the target is above the current estimate and negative when it is below.

questions.question: Experience was collected by sometimes choosing exploratory actions. The update target still uses max_b Q(s′, b). What next-state action value does that target use?
options: The largest estimated value, even if exploration would choose another action
Always the value of the least tried action
Only the action with the smallest estimated value
The sum of every action value
questions.feedback: The max operation selects the best estimated next-state action value. It need not match the exploratory action the agent would actually sample.
questions.retryFeedback: Distinguish the rule for collecting experience from the max operation written in the learning target. Read that operation literally.

questions.question: At a terminal transition with zero continuation, what is the target?
questions.feedback: There is no future return after termination.
questions.retryFeedback: The terminal boundary removes the next-state value term. Evaluate the target using that continuation convention.

questions.question: At a next state, action A has estimated Q = 2 and action B has Q = 5. Which value enters the max Q term of the Q-learning target?
questions.feedback: Q-learning uses the largest estimated next-state action value. Of 2 and 5, that maximum is 5.
questions.retryFeedback: Identify the operation requested by the target formula. Compare the action values rather than averaging or adding them.

concepts.title: Policy gradient
concepts.definition: Policy-gradient methods adjust a policy’s parameters to increase expected return. They add a step along the gradient, which points toward local improvement.
concepts.example: Choose A with probability p. Rewards: A gives 4, B gives 1. J(p) = 4p + (1−p) = 1+3p, so J′(p) = 3. With η = 0.1: p⁺ = 0.5 + 0.1×3 = 0.8.
concepts.metaphor: Strengthen decisions that led to better outcomes, using measured credit rather than copying every action.
concepts.question: A policy chooses A with probability 0.7 and B otherwise. A gives reward 6 and B gives reward −2. What is expected reward?
concepts.feedback: The other probability is 0.3. Expected reward is 0.7×6 + 0.3×(−2) = 3.6.

sources.title: Reinforcement Learning: Foundations, Mannor, Mansour and Tamar
sources.label: Textbook

questions.question: A policy chooses A with probability 0.7 and B otherwise. A gives reward 6 and B gives reward −2. What is expected reward?
questions.feedback: The other probability is 0.3. Expected reward is 0.7×6 + 0.3×(−2) = 3.6.
questions.retryFeedback: Use both action probabilities, which must sum to one, and keep the sign of each reward in the weighted average.

questions.question: Does policy-gradient ascent add or subtract the expected-return gradient?
questions.feedback: To increase J, the update moves along its gradient.
questions.retryFeedback: The objective is expected return, which this update maximizes. Check the direction indicated by its gradient.

questions.question: For θ = 1, η = 0.2, and ∇J = 3, what is the updated θ?
questions.feedback: Compute 1 + 0.2×3.
questions.retryFeedback: Scale the expected-return gradient by the learning rate and move in the increasing-objective direction.

questions.question: If action A pays 4 and B pays 1, what is expected reward when P(A) = 0.6?
questions.retryFeedback: The two action probabilities must add to one. Compute both probability-weighted rewards before combining them.

questions.question: For expected return J(p) = 2p + 5(1−p), what is dJ/dp?
questions.feedback: Expanding gives J(p) = 5−3p, so its derivative is −3. Increasing p favors the lower-reward action here.
questions.retryFeedback: Expand the contribution of the alternative action before differentiating. Changing p also changes the other action's probability.

questions.question: Why must direct probability updates respect constraints?
options: Probabilities must stay between zero and one and sum to one
Every action must be equally likely
questions.feedback: An invalid probability vector is not a valid stochastic policy.
questions.retryFeedback: A direct numerical update can leave the valid probability set. The representation or update rule must enforce its constraints.

questions.question: Why are policy gradients often estimated from sampled experience?
options: The gradient must always be zero
The expected return is not known exactly
questions.feedback: Sampled outcomes provide information about the policy's effect on return.
questions.retryFeedback: Expected return averages possible trajectories, which are often too numerous or unknown to calculate exactly. Experience supplies an estimate.

questions.question: Does one favorable sampled return prove a policy update will improve expected performance?
options: Only with a small learning rate
questions.feedback: Sampling noise can make a single outcome misleading.
questions.retryFeedback: A sampled trajectory is one random outcome. Its favorable score does not establish the expectation over all trajectories.

questions.question: For a valid policy parameter θ, the expected-return gradient is −2 and the step size is 0.1. What increment does gradient ascent add to θ?
questions.feedback: Gradient ascent adds η∇J = 0.1×(−2) = −0.2. Increasing expected return can require decreasing a parameter.
questions.retryFeedback: Use the ascent update as written, including the sign of the gradient. Increasing the objective does not mean every parameter must increase.

questions.question: In a one-step decision task, what does increasing an action’s selection probability mean?
options: The policy is more likely to choose it
Its reward is guaranteed to increase
questions.feedback: Policy updates change behavior probabilities, not the reward values themselves.
questions.retryFeedback: Changing a policy probability changes the frequency of the corresponding choice. It does not change the action's physical reward by itself.

concepts.title: Model-based RL
concepts.definition: Model-based RL uses a model of environment changes or rewards to help choose actions. It can plan with this model or learn from simulated experience.
concepts.formulaNote: Use a model F̂ to predict the next state, then compare actions using predicted returns.
concepts.example: A learned tank model predicts that “fill” yields return 7 and “wait” yields 5. Choose “fill,” observe the real outcome, and use it to check or improve the model.
concepts.metaphor: Practice routes in a flight simulator before flying the aircraft.
concepts.question: What is a central risk of planning with a learned model?
options: Model errors can compound across predicted steps
More imagined steps always improve accuracy
Planning removes the need for rewards
concepts.feedback: Plans can exploit model mistakes. Test the model in the relevant operating range and measure real outcomes. A mechanistic model and learned residual can complement each other.

sources.title: Reinforcement Learning: Foundations, Mannor, Mansour and Tamar
sources.label: Textbook

questions.question: What is a central risk of planning with a learned model?
options: Model errors can compound across predicted steps
More imagined steps always improve accuracy
Planning removes the need for rewards
questions.feedback: Plans can exploit model mistakes. Test the model in the relevant operating range and measure real outcomes. A mechanistic model and learned residual can complement each other.
questions.retryFeedback: Each imagined next state can become input to another prediction. An early error can therefore influence several later steps.

questions.question: What distinguishes model-based RL?
options: Using an environment model to help choose or learn actions
questions.feedback: The model predicts transitions or rewards for planning or simulated learning.
questions.retryFeedback: Look for an explicit representation of environmental consequences used in decision making or learning. A value estimate alone has a different role.

questions.question: Can a learned dynamics model be imperfect?
options: Only if it has one parameter
questions.feedback: Prediction error must be considered when using model-based plans.
questions.retryFeedback: A model is an approximation supported by limited data or assumptions. Learning it does not make every transition prediction exact.

questions.question: What does planning do with a model?
options: Compares predicted consequences of possible actions
questions.feedback: The model supports evaluating candidate behavior.
questions.retryFeedback: Planning considers candidate actions and uses predicted outcomes to compare them before executing a choice.

questions.question: Why can model errors compound over a long sequence of predicted steps?
options: Every reward is independent of state
The first error is always canceled
questions.feedback: An early state error can change subsequent predicted outcomes.
questions.retryFeedback: Rollouts repeatedly reuse the model's own outputs as inputs. Those inputs may drift away from states represented accurately during fitting.

questions.question: What is a risk of optimizing too aggressively against an inaccurate model?
options: The policy may exploit model mistakes
questions.feedback: A high modeled return may reflect unrealistic predicted behavior.
questions.retryFeedback: An optimizer searches for favorable predictions. If those predictions contain errors, it may prefer actions that exploit the errors rather than reality.

questions.question: Must the model be entirely learned from data?
questions.feedback: Physical knowledge and learned components can be combined.
questions.retryFeedback: Models can come from physical knowledge, system identification, learned functions, or combinations. Data-only fitting is not a requirement.

questions.question: Why compare predicted and observed outcomes after acting?
options: To prove all future plans safe
To remove the need for measurements
To assess model accuracy in use
questions.feedback: Real feedback reveals where the model's assumptions or estimates fail.
questions.retryFeedback: The real transition supplies feedback about the model's prediction. Comparing them helps detect drift and missing dynamics.

questions.question: How can simulated experience be useful?
options: It can support learning without executing every candidate action in reality
questions.feedback: Simulation can save real interactions but inherits model limitations.
questions.retryFeedback: A simulator lets the learner examine hypothetical consequences. Those benefits depend on how well the simulated experience reflects the real task.

questions.question: Does using a model automatically make reinforcement learning necessary?
questions.feedback: Planning and control can use models without an RL training procedure.
questions.retryFeedback: Planning with a model can be done with other control or optimization methods. Reinforcement learning is one possible surrounding framework.

concepts.title: Safety constraint
concepts.definition: A safety constraint restricts allowed states or actions. A constrained controller optimizes only among choices satisfying its stated limits.
concepts.example: If a valve setting must satisfy a ≤ 5, a proposed setting of 7 is rejected even if its predicted reward is high.
concepts.metaphor: A game's boundary line is a rule, not a small negative score you may pay to ignore.
concepts.question: A hard limit requires 0 ≤ a ≤ 4. Actions a=2, a=4, and a=6 have predicted rewards 8, 7, and 12 respectively. Which action should maximize reward subject to the limit?
concepts.feedback: Action 6 violates the limit. Among feasible actions 2 and 4, action 2 has the higher reward, 8.

questions.question: A hard limit requires 0 ≤ a ≤ 4. Actions a=2, a=4, and a=6 have predicted rewards 8, 7, and 12 respectively. Which action should maximize reward subject to the limit?
questions.feedback: Action 6 violates the limit. Among feasible actions 2 and 4, action 2 has the higher reward, 8.
questions.retryFeedback: First exclude choices violating the hard limit. Compare predicted rewards only among the actions still permitted by the constraint.

questions.question: How does a hard constraint differ from a reward penalty?
options: It is only a source citation
It guarantees the model is exact
It excludes choices rather than merely lowering their score
questions.feedback: A penalty can be traded against reward; a constraint defines feasibility.
questions.retryFeedback: A penalty changes an objective value, potentially allowing a tradeoff. A hard boundary changes which choices are allowed at all.

questions.question: If allowed pressure is at most 10, which predicted pressure satisfies the stated limit?
questions.feedback: The inequality permits values no greater than ten.
questions.retryFeedback: Translate “at most” into an inclusive upper-bound comparison. Check each proposed value against that bound.

questions.question: Why may predicted constraint satisfaction be insufficient for real safety?
options: Rewards become irrelevant to every choice
Model and measurement errors can change actual outcomes
questions.feedback: A real implementation must account for uncertainty and execution.
questions.retryFeedback: The constraint is being checked on an estimate. Uncertainty in the model or measurement can make the actual outcome differ.

questions.question: Which action should a constrained optimizer select?
options: The highest-scoring action even if prohibited
The action with the largest magnitude always
questions.feedback: Optimization occurs inside the permitted set.
questions.retryFeedback: First filter the candidate set by its constraints, then compare objective values among the remaining candidates.

questions.question: If g(a) ≤ 0 is required, which value is a violation?
questions.feedback: Positive g(a) fails the stated inequality.
questions.retryFeedback: The allowed side of the inequality includes zero and values below it. Check which candidate lies on the excluded side.

questions.question: Why use an independent limit check in a controller?
options: To catch unsafe commands before execution
questions.feedback: Separate enforcement can provide protection beyond an optimizer's proposal.
questions.retryFeedback: An optimizer or learned policy can make mistakes. A separate check can enforce a permitted-command boundary before acting.

questions.question: Does a large reward justify violating a hard safety constraint?
options: Only for a short time automatically
questions.feedback: A hard constraint is not a reward tradeoff in the stated formulation.
questions.retryFeedback: A hard constraint is not simply another weighted objective term. Reward ranking applies only after admissibility is established.

questions.question: What is the role of a safety margin under uncertain predictions?
options: Increase the allowed risk without analysis
questions.feedback: Margins can help account for uncertainty when appropriately justified.
questions.retryFeedback: A prediction near the boundary can become a violation under error. A margin accounts for some of that possible discrepancy.

questions.question: If no feasible action exists in the planned set, what should a controller have defined?
options: A safe fallback or failure-handling policy
questions.feedback: Infeasibility requires explicit handling rather than silently violating constraints.
questions.retryFeedback: Optimization may return no permitted candidate. The system needs a defined response rather than silently executing an infeasible plan.

concepts.title: Model predictive control
concepts.definition: MPC plans several actions using a model, executes the first, then replans using new measurements. It minimizes a cost over a fixed number of future steps.
concepts.formula:
minimize Σₖ₌₀ᴴ⁻¹ c(sₖ₊₁, aₖ)
sₖ₊₁ = F(sₖ, aₖ)
concepts.formulaNote: H is the planning horizon and c is a step’s cost. Planned states and actions must satisfy the stated limits.
concepts.example: A tank has 10 L, target 14 L, drain 2 L/step. Plan inflows (6, 2) L. Apply 6 now. If the tank actually reaches 13 L, replan the next inflow as 3 L.
concepts.metaphor: A navigator redraws the route at every junction as traffic changes.
concepts.question: How many actions from a newly solved MPC plan are typically applied before replanning?
concepts.feedback: Receding-horizon control uses fresh feedback. MPC is a control method and does not inherently require reinforcement learning; the model can be physical or learned.

questions.question: How many actions from a newly solved MPC plan are typically applied before replanning?
questions.feedback: Receding-horizon control uses fresh feedback. MPC is a control method and does not inherently require reinforcement learning; the model can be physical or learned.
questions.retryFeedback: MPC plans several steps but then incorporates a new observation. Distinguish the sequence optimized from the portion executed before replanning.

questions.question: An MPC controller should bring a tank to 25 litres next step. The new measurement is 20 litres and the expected drain is 3 litres during that step. What inflow should it plan?
questions.feedback: Solve 20 + inflow − 3 = 25, giving inflow = 8 litres. The new measurement supplies the starting state.
questions.retryFeedback: Write the next-volume balance using the new measurement. The inflow must cover both the desired increase and the expected loss during the step.

questions.question: Why replan after receiving new measurements?
options: To guarantee the model is perfect
To update the plan using current information
questions.feedback: Feedback corrects the plan as actual conditions unfold.
questions.retryFeedback: Measured outcomes can differ from predicted outcomes. Replanning starts from the updated estimate rather than an obsolete planned state.

questions.question: What does the planning horizon H specify?
options: How many future steps the optimization considers
questions.feedback: The horizon controls how far ahead the plan looks.
questions.retryFeedback: The horizon limits how far ahead candidate consequences are evaluated. It does not directly count repeated replanning cycles.

questions.question: Does MPC inherently require reinforcement learning?
questions.feedback: MPC can use physical or learned models without RL.
questions.retryFeedback: MPC requires a model and a repeated planning optimization. Those can be supplied without a reinforcement-learning training procedure.

questions.question: What can a longer planning horizon increase?
options: The number of real observations already available
Computation and exposure to model error
questions.feedback: Longer lookahead can help but adds cost and uncertainty.
questions.retryFeedback: Looking farther ahead increases the search and relies on more predicted transitions. Both computational cost and uncertainty can grow.

questions.question: Where should state and action limits enter MPC?
options: Only in the final prose explanation
questions.feedback: Candidate trajectories should respect the stated limits.
questions.retryFeedback: The optimization must know which predicted trajectories are allowed. Checking reward alone does not enforce those limits.

questions.question: If predicted costs for feasible plans A and B are 7 and 4, which does a cost-minimizing MPC choose?
questions.feedback: The smaller feasible predicted cost is preferred.
questions.retryFeedback: Compare only feasible candidates, then follow the objective's stated preference for smaller costs rather than larger rewards.

questions.question: What makes the horizon receding?
options: The model loses one parameter per step
The system always stops after one step
Planning repeats from the updated current state
questions.feedback: Each new plan moves the lookahead window forward.
questions.retryFeedback: After each action and new observation, the planning window is anchored to the new current situation.

questions.question: Does solving the planning problem ensure the real system exactly follows its predicted trajectory?
options: Only with a low predicted cost
questions.feedback: Disturbances, modeling error, and execution differences can affect reality.
questions.retryFeedback: The optimizer solves its mathematical model. Disturbances and modeling errors can make the realized path differ from that solution.

concepts.title: RLHF
concepts.definition: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) often learns a reward model from human preferences, then trains a policy to earn higher scores.
concepts.formulaNote: For a fixed question, πθ(y) is the probability of answer y and r(y) is its learned reward.
concepts.example: People prefer answer A to B. Suppose learned rewards are 2 and 0. Raising P(A) from 0.5 to 0.75 raises expected reward from 1 to 1.5.
concepts.metaphor: A judge compares performances; the learner improves toward the judge's scoring pattern.
concepts.question: Does optimizing a human-preference reward guarantee factual truth?
options: Only if the answer is longer
Yes, a reward model verifies physics
No, preference and truth can diverge
Yes, every preferred answer is true
concepts.feedback: Human preference and factual truth can diverge. The displayed objective illustrates reward maximization only. Common RLHF systems also constrain departure from a reference policy and often begin with supervised fine-tuning. The reward model estimates human preferences; it does not establish scientific truth.

sources.title: Reinforcement learning from human feedback, Wikipedia
sources.label: Wikipedia

sources.title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback, Ouyang et al., 2022
sources.label: Paper

questions.question: Does optimizing a human-preference reward guarantee factual truth?
options: Only if the answer is longer
Yes, a reward model verifies physics
No, preference and truth can diverge
Yes, every preferred answer is true
questions.feedback: Human preference and factual truth can diverge. The displayed objective illustrates reward maximization only. Common RLHF systems also constrain departure from a reference policy and often begin with supervised fine-tuning. The reward model estimates human preferences; it does not establish scientific truth.
questions.retryFeedback: The learned reward summarizes preference judgments under a procedure. Preference can favor an appealing response even when its claims are wrong.

questions.question: What signal often trains an RLHF reward model?
options: A guaranteed truth label for every statement
questions.feedback: Preference data teach a model to score outputs in line with those judgments.
questions.retryFeedback: The reward model needs examples of which outputs people favor. Distinguish those judgments from a universal ground-truth score.

questions.question: What does the policy optimization stage try to increase?
options: The number of human annotators necessarily
questions.feedback: The learned reward provides an optimization signal.
questions.retryFeedback: The optimization follows its defined reward proxy, often with other constraints. The proxy does not automatically equal every desirable quality.

questions.question: Does human preference always agree with factual truth?
questions.feedback: People can prefer plausible or appealing answers that are mistaken.
questions.retryFeedback: Preferences may reflect style, helpfulness, or confidence as well as correctness. Those criteria can disagree.

questions.question: Why might RLHF constrain departure from a reference policy?
questions.feedback: Reference constraints can stabilize adaptation, but do not certify correctness.
questions.retryFeedback: A reference supplies a baseline behavior distribution. Limiting divergence can help avoid extreme changes driven by an imperfect reward proxy.

questions.question: An RLHF reward-model score rises, but the answers become less useful to people. What does this show?
options: The learned score can improve without the intended improvement
questions.feedback: Optimizing a learned proxy can exploit its weaknesses.
questions.retryFeedback: Compare what the scoring system rewards with what its designers intended. An improvement in one need not establish an improvement in the other.

questions.question: Can different annotators have different preferences?
questions.feedback: Human judgments vary with priorities, context, and interpretation.
questions.retryFeedback: Judgments depend on people's goals, context, knowledge, and values. Aggregating them does not imply universal agreement.

questions.question: Why evaluate factuality separately from preference scores?
options: The two quantities are always equal
A preferred answer may still be wrong
questions.feedback: The evaluation needs to measure the actual property of interest.
questions.retryFeedback: An answer can be persuasive or useful-looking while containing false claims. A preference score does not test those claims independently.

questions.question: Does the toy reward-maximization equation show every part of a full RLHF pipeline?
questions.feedback: Practical pipelines may include supervised tuning and reference-policy constraints.
questions.retryFeedback: A compact equation describes a particular optimization idea. Data collection, supervised stages, reward modeling, and constraints add further structure.

questions.question: For answer rewards 3 and 1 with policy probabilities 0.25 and 0.75, what is expected reward?
questions.retryFeedback: Weight each possible response's reward by the policy's probability of selecting it, then combine the contributions.

concepts.title: CPU
concepts.definition: A central processing unit (CPU) executes program instructions: arithmetic, comparisons, and decisions about what to run next. A computer can use several CPU cores at once. A core is an execution unit that can run its own stream of instructions.
concepts.formulaNote: An example program accumulates values and computes their average.
concepts.example: To average (2, 4, 6), a program starts total = 0. Add each value: 2, then 6, then 12. Divide by 3 to return 4.
concepts.metaphor: A versatile workshop supervisor handles varied jobs and directs specialist machines.
concepts.question: Which statement best describes a CPU?
options: A device that cannot do matrix multiplication
A general-purpose processor that also coordinates work
A disk for permanent storage only
concepts.feedback: CPUs can perform matrix operations and parallel work. Their strengths include flexible control flow and low-latency general tasks. Actual speed also depends on memory and instructions.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a CPU?
options: A device that cannot do matrix multiplication
A general-purpose processor that also coordinates work
A disk for permanent storage only
questions.feedback: CPUs can perform matrix operations and parallel work. Their strengths include flexible control flow and low-latency general tasks. Actual speed also depends on memory and instructions.
questions.retryFeedback: Consider both general instruction execution and control of other system components. A processor's role is not limited to one mathematical operation.

questions.question: What does a CPU execute?
questions.feedback: CPUs perform general computation, including arithmetic and control flow.
questions.retryFeedback: Software describes operations through instructions. The processor carries out those operations on data.

questions.question: Can a CPU perform matrix multiplication?
questions.feedback: Matrix arithmetic is not exclusive to specialized accelerators.
questions.retryFeedback: General-purpose instruction execution can implement numerical algorithms. Specialized hardware changes efficiency, not whether the operation is conceptually possible.

questions.question: What is a CPU core?
options: An execution unit capable of running instruction streams
questions.feedback: Multiple cores can support concurrent work.
questions.retryFeedback: Distinguish an individual processing resource from the complete chip, a memory unit, or a stored program.

questions.question: Which workload often suits a CPU well?
questions.feedback: CPUs support flexible branching and general-purpose execution.
questions.retryFeedback: Some workloads make frequent data-dependent decisions with irregular dependencies. General-purpose control is valuable for those patterns.

questions.question: Does doubling core count guarantee halving program time?
questions.feedback: Serial work, memory, and coordination can limit scaling.
questions.retryFeedback: Parallel speedup depends on how much work can run independently, along with coordination and memory costs. Core count alone does not fix it.

questions.question: For a sequential running sum of (2, 3, 5), what is the final total?
questions.feedback: The program adds each input to the accumulator.
questions.retryFeedback: Accumulate every input value in sequence. Intermediate partial sums are not the requested final total.

questions.question: Why can memory access limit CPU performance?
options: More memory always lowers clock speed
Programs run only from the network
questions.feedback: Compute speed alone does not determine how quickly data arrive.
questions.retryFeedback: An arithmetic instruction needs its operands. If memory cannot deliver them quickly enough, execution resources may spend time waiting.

questions.question: A program adds each input to a running total and then divides by the number of inputs. Which CPU capability is being used?
options: Executing arithmetic instructions in the specified order
Changing the meaning of the input measurements
Replacing the program with a probability distribution
Guaranteeing that every input is accurate
questions.feedback: The CPU executes the program’s additions and division. The numerical result still depends on the supplied inputs and instructions.
questions.retryFeedback: Separate executing a sequence of operations from verifying the real-world truth of the data. Follow what this particular program asks the processor to do.

questions.question: Does clock frequency, measured in cycles per second, alone determine which CPU runs an application faster?
questions.feedback: Architecture, instructions, memory, and the workload also matter.
questions.retryFeedback: Instructions per cycle, memory, architecture, and workload all affect time. Frequency measures only one part of that system.

concepts.title: GPU
concepts.definition: A graphics processing unit (GPU) performs many similar calculations in parallel. Large matrix operations supply repeated arithmetic to keep its execution units busy.
concepts.formulaNote: Each output can be calculated independently, illustrating work that can run in parallel.
concepts.example: For x = (1, 2, 3, 4), compute y = (2, 4, 6, 8). Each output can be calculated independently. The same pattern scales to millions of entries.
concepts.metaphor: A large team folds many identical paper cranes at once.
concepts.question: Which workload is especially suitable for a GPU?
options: One tiny operation with heavy transfer overhead
A task with no parallel work at all
concepts.feedback: GPUs excel when enough regular work amortizes coordination and transfer costs. More parallel workers do not automatically accelerate a small or sequential problem.

questions.question: Which workload is especially suitable for a GPU?
options: One tiny operation with heavy transfer overhead
A task with no parallel work at all
questions.feedback: GPUs excel when enough regular work amortizes coordination and transfer costs. More parallel workers do not automatically accelerate a small or sequential problem.
questions.retryFeedback: Parallel hardware benefits from many operations that can proceed together with regular structure. Long serial dependencies limit that opportunity.

questions.question: Which workload is a good candidate for GPU parallelism?
options: Strictly sequential decisions with no parallel work
A tiny task dominated by startup cost
questions.feedback: Many similar operations can keep parallel execution resources busy.
questions.retryFeedback: Look for a workload with many similarly organized numerical tasks. Irregular or tiny tasks may not use the hardware efficiently.

questions.question: Sending a small task to a GPU and starting it takes time, in addition to the arithmetic itself. Why can the whole task be slower than running it on a CPU?
options: Transfer and launch overhead can dominate
