questions.feedback: The transfer and startup time can outweigh the arithmetic speedup for a small task. Compare total elapsed time, not just time inside the calculation.
questions.retryFeedback: Add the stated preparation costs to the device’s computation time. Accelerating one part does not guarantee that the whole job finishes sooner.

questions.question: For a fixed input array, each output is yᵢ = xᵢ + xᵢ₊₁ and is written to its own location. Can these outputs be calculated independently in parallel?
options: No; outputs must all have equal values
No; sharing any input forbids parallel computation
Yes; shared input reads do not create dependence on other outputs
Yes, but only if every input is identical
questions.feedback: Each output reads already available input values and writes a separate result. Sharing a read-only input does not require another output to finish first.
questions.retryFeedback: Check whether a calculation needs another calculation's new result, rather than merely reading an input that another worker also reads.

questions.question: Does more parallel hardware guarantee speedup for a sequential algorithm?
questions.feedback: Dependencies can limit how much work runs concurrently.
questions.retryFeedback: Hardware cannot remove a required chain of dependencies simply by offering more execution units. The algorithm's structure matters.

questions.question: For which task can all four outputs be calculated directly and independently from the supplied inputs?
options: Overwrite one shared running total four times in a specified order
Set y₁=x₁, then calculate each later yᵢ=2yᵢ₋₁
yᵢ = xᵢ² + 1 for four supplied x values
Compute y₁ first, then use that computed result in every other output
questions.feedback: Each squared-input output uses only its own supplied input. The other descriptions require earlier results or an ordered update to shared state.
questions.retryFeedback: Trace what each output needs before it can be computed. Distinguish available inputs from results that another step must produce first.

questions.question: Several operations can use the same data already on a GPU. Moving the data between devices takes time. Why keep them on the GPU between those operations?
questions.feedback: Reusing data in place avoids unnecessary transfers between devices. It can reduce total runtime without changing the calculation.
questions.retryFeedback: Count the data movements required by each approach. Reusing an available input can avoid repeating a cost unrelated to the arithmetic.

questions.question: Memory bandwidth is the amount of data delivered per second. Can a GPU be limited by this rate even when its arithmetic units could calculate faster?
questions.feedback: Yes. Arithmetic units can wait for inputs when memory cannot supply data fast enough. This is a bandwidth limit.
questions.retryFeedback: A calculation requires both data and processing. Compare how quickly the input can arrive with how quickly it could be consumed.

questions.question: What should be measured when assessing a GPU speedup?
options: End-to-end runtime for the actual workload
questions.feedback: Transfers, preprocessing, and coordination contribute to real performance.
questions.retryFeedback: Include transfer, setup, synchronization, and useful computation. A fast isolated kernel may not produce the same application-level improvement.

questions.question: Are a GPU and a graphics application the same thing?
questions.feedback: A GPU is hardware that can run many kinds of computation.
questions.retryFeedback: One term describes a computing device; the other describes software using it. The device can support workloads beyond graphics.

concepts.title: Tensor core
concepts.definition: A Tensor Core is a specialized circuit inside an NVIDIA GPU that multiplies small matrix blocks and adds another matrix. Supported number formats depend on the GPU generation.
concepts.metaphor: A factory station stamps whole groups of arithmetic steps using a specialized mold.
concepts.question: For scalar A = 2, B = 3, C = 4, what does AB + C produce?
concepts.feedback: Multiply then add: 2 × 3 + 4 = 10. The toy scalar example illustrates the operation; real Tensor Cores process supported matrix tiles and precisions.

questions.question: For scalar A = 2, B = 3, C = 4, what does AB + C produce?
questions.feedback: Multiply then add: 2 × 3 + 4 = 10. The toy scalar example illustrates the operation; real Tensor Cores process supported matrix tiles and precisions.
questions.retryFeedback: Evaluate the product first and then include the accumulated term. The operation combines multiplication with addition.

questions.question: What operation does the course use to illustrate a Tensor Core?
questions.feedback: Tensor Cores accelerate supported matrix multiply-accumulate operations.
questions.retryFeedback: The illustrative operation multiplies matrices and accumulates another matrix. It is not just an elementwise comparison or a storage operation.

questions.question: Are Tensor Cores separate full computers?
options: No, specialized circuits within certain NVIDIA GPUs
questions.feedback: They are specialized execution hardware inside the GPU.
questions.retryFeedback: Specialized arithmetic hardware sits within a larger processor. It depends on the surrounding execution and memory system.

questions.question: For scalar illustration A = 3, B = 4, C = 2, what is D?
questions.feedback: Multiply 3×4 and add 2.
questions.retryFeedback: Use the stated multiply-accumulate operation with the scalar illustration. Do not multiply the accumulator into the product.

questions.question: Do all Tensor Core generations support exactly the same numerical formats?
questions.feedback: Supported formats and operations depend on the hardware generation.
questions.retryFeedback: Hardware capabilities change by generation. Check the specific device's supported arithmetic rather than assuming a universal format list.

questions.question: Why do supported matrix shapes and data layouts matter?
options: They affect whether specialized operations can be used efficiently
They change the laws of arithmetic
questions.feedback: Hardware instructions operate on specific supported arrangements.
questions.retryFeedback: Specialized instructions have compatibility requirements. An application's data must be arranged and typed appropriately to use them effectively.

questions.question: Does the presence of Tensor Cores accelerate every part of an application equally?
questions.feedback: Nonmatrix work and data movement may not benefit directly.
questions.retryFeedback: Only suitable operations can use the specialized units. Other work and bottlenecks remain part of end-to-end runtime.

questions.question: What does the C term contribute to D = AB + C?
options: An accumulated matrix added to the product
questions.feedback: The operation combines a matrix product with an existing accumulation.
questions.retryFeedback: The product AB supplies one contribution. The C input contributes existing values to be accumulated with that product.

questions.question: Why validate numerical behavior when selecting lower-precision Tensor Core operations?
options: Supported arithmetic can change rounding and accuracy
questions.feedback: Acceleration and numerical quality must both meet the task's needs.
questions.retryFeedback: Different formats and accumulation rules can change representable values and rounding. Speed and numerical behavior must both be considered.

questions.question: What should determine whether Tensor Cores help a model workload?
options: Its supported operations and measured bottlenecks
The word tensor in a filename
questions.feedback: A matching workload and implementation are needed to benefit.
questions.retryFeedback: Having specialized hardware is insufficient if the workload cannot use it or spends most of its time elsewhere. Measure the relevant computation.

concepts.title: CUDA
concepts.definition: CUDA is NVIDIA’s platform for programming its GPUs. A kernel is a function run by many logical workers called threads. Threads have indices and are organized into blocks.
concepts.formula: i = block index × B + thread index
concepts.formulaNote: For a one-dimensional launch, B is the number of threads per block. Indices start at 0.
concepts.example: With B = 4, block 1 and thread 2 give i = 1×4+2 = 6. That thread can compute y₆ = 2x₆. Eight such blocks launch 8×4 = 32 threads.
concepts.metaphor: CUDA is the instruction system that assigns numbered tasks to a parallel workshop.
concepts.question: A CUDA launch has 8 blocks of 128 threads. How many threads launch?
concepts.feedback: Multiply blocks by threads per block. Threads are logical workers scheduled on hardware, not a promise that all execute simultaneously. CUDA is software, not a chip.

questions.question: A CUDA launch has 8 blocks of 128 threads. How many threads launch?
questions.feedback: Multiply blocks by threads per block. Threads are logical workers scheduled on hardware, not a promise that all execute simultaneously. CUDA is software, not a chip.
questions.retryFeedback: Each block contains the stated number of threads. Count the logical threads across all launched blocks.

questions.question: What is a CUDA kernel?
options: A function launched across GPU threads
questions.feedback: A kernel defines work performed by logical GPU threads.
questions.retryFeedback: A kernel describes work for GPU execution across a configured launch. It is not the entire device or just its memory.

questions.question: With block index 2, 128 threads per block, and thread index 5, what is global index i?
questions.feedback: Using zero-based indices, i = 2×128 + 5.
questions.retryFeedback: The block index contributes the number of threads in earlier blocks. Add the thread's local index to that block offset.

questions.question: How many logical threads are launched by 4 blocks of 64 threads?
questions.feedback: Multiply blocks by threads per block.
questions.retryFeedback: Multiply blocks by threads per block. The launch count does not itself state how many run at the same instant.

questions.question: Does a launch of 1,000 threads guarantee 1,000 threads execute simultaneously?
questions.feedback: Logical threads are scheduled onto finite hardware resources.
questions.retryFeedback: Launch geometry describes logical work. Available hardware resources determine how that work is scheduled over time.

questions.question: Why check i < N in an elementwise kernel with a rounded-up launch size?
options: It changes N to a probability
Some launched threads can lie beyond the data bounds
questions.feedback: Bounds checks prevent out-of-range operations by extra threads.
questions.retryFeedback: Rounding the launch upward can create valid thread indices with no corresponding data element. Guard the data access using its actual length.

questions.question: Is CUDA hardware or a programming platform?
questions.feedback: CUDA provides software tools and interfaces for NVIDIA GPU programming.
questions.retryFeedback: Distinguish the programming environment and software interfaces from the physical processor that executes the work.

questions.question: What is a block in a CUDA launch?
questions.feedback: The launch organizes threads into blocks.
questions.retryFeedback: CUDA organizes threads into groups within a launch. A group is not necessarily one data element or one complete GPU.

questions.question: A CUDA launch may return to the CPU while its GPU calculation is still queued or running. Why wait for completion when measuring the calculation’s full runtime?
options: Every queued calculation takes zero time
Otherwise the measurement may include only submission time
questions.feedback: Submitting work is not the same as finishing it. A timer stopped immediately after submission can miss the GPU’s execution time.
questions.retryFeedback: Separate sending an instruction from completing the requested work. The endpoint of the measurement must match the duration you want to measure.

questions.question: Two threads both read shared count = 0, each adds 1 locally, then each writes 1 back without coordination. What final count can this produce?
questions.feedback: Both writes contain 1, so the final value is 1 instead of the intended 2. Such conflicting uncoordinated accesses are a race condition.
questions.retryFeedback: Track what each thread actually reads and writes in the stated ordering. A local increment does not automatically combine with another thread’s write.

concepts.title: Memory capacity
concepts.definition: Memory capacity is the amount of information a device can hold. Model execution needs space for weights, intermediate values, and working buffers. Training also stores computed gradients and may keep extra values for parameter updates, called optimizer state. Activations are intermediate layer outputs that also occupy memory.
concepts.formula: weight bytes = parameter count × bits per parameter / 8
concepts.example: 1 billion parameters at 16 bits use 2 billion bytes, or 2 GB, for weights alone.
concepts.metaphor: A kitchen counter limits how many ingredients and partly prepared dishes fit at once.
concepts.question: Can a 2 GB device necessarily train a 1-billion-parameter model at 16 bits?
options: Yes, if the model has a short name
No, training also needs gradients, activations, and optimizer state
No, each bit always takes one byte
Yes, weights are the only memory cost
concepts.feedback: Two GB is only the weight storage estimate in decimal units. Training and inference have additional memory costs; autoregressive inference also caches attention keys and values.

questions.question: Can a 2 GB device necessarily train a 1-billion-parameter model at 16 bits?
options: Yes, if the model has a short name
No, training also needs gradients, activations, and optimizer state
No, each bit always takes one byte
Yes, weights are the only memory cost
questions.feedback: Two GB is only the weight storage estimate in decimal units. Training and inference have additional memory costs; autoregressive inference also caches attention keys and values.
questions.retryFeedback: The raw weight estimate covers only one stored component. Training also retains intermediate quantities and information needed for updates.

questions.question: How many bytes store 1,000 parameters at 32 bits each, excluding overhead?
questions.feedback: Each parameter uses four bytes.
questions.retryFeedback: Convert bits per parameter to bytes first, then multiply by the parameter count. The estimate excludes other memory use.

questions.question: Does a weights-only storage estimate include all inference memory?
questions.feedback: Activations, working buffers, and caches can also require space.
questions.retryFeedback: Executing a model requires more than its coefficients. Inputs, intermediate results, caches, and working buffers may also occupy memory.

questions.question: Bandwidth means data transferred per second. How does memory capacity differ from bandwidth?
options: Capacity is amount stored; bandwidth is transfer rate
questions.feedback: Storage size and movement speed are separate limits.
questions.retryFeedback: Compare a quantity of stored information with a quantity moved in a unit of time. They constrain different parts of execution.

questions.question: How much weight storage do 2 billion parameters at 2 bytes each need in decimal units?
questions.feedback: Multiply parameter count by bytes per parameter.
questions.retryFeedback: Multiply parameter count by bytes per parameter. Then express the total using the stated decimal gigabyte convention.

questions.question: Why can training need more memory than storing weights alone?
options: Every weight becomes a source document
Gradients, optimizer state, and activations also use memory
questions.feedback: The training process retains additional data.
questions.retryFeedback: Updating a model requires information about derivatives and the optimizer, while differentiating layers can require retained intermediate outputs.

questions.question: Does unused storage on another GPU automatically enlarge a single allocation's capacity?
options: Only when both GPUs are idle
questions.feedback: Using multiple devices' memory requires an appropriate distributed design.
questions.retryFeedback: Separate physical memories do not automatically behave as one allocation. Using them together requires a compatible distribution strategy.

questions.question: What may increasing batch size do to activation memory?
questions.feedback: More examples often mean more intermediate values stored simultaneously.
questions.retryFeedback: More examples processed together generally require more simultaneous intermediate outputs. Those outputs contribute to activation storage.

questions.question: Why can a model that barely fits its weights still fail to run?
options: Runtime memory overhead may exceed remaining capacity
questions.feedback: Execution needs headroom beyond the weight payload.
questions.retryFeedback: Enough space for coefficients alone leaves no guarantee of room for execution. Consider the additional working quantities required by the workload.

questions.question: What usually happens to raw weight bytes when precision drops from 32 to 16 bits?
questions.feedback: The number of bits per stored parameter is halved.
questions.retryFeedback: Hold parameter count fixed and compare bits per stored value. Raw storage scales with that per-value width.

concepts.title: Context windows and KV caching
concepts.definition: A context window limits the token sequence a model can process in a request. During autoregressive decoding, a key-value cache stores prior attention keys and values so they can be reused for new tokens.
concepts.formula: KV bytes = 2 × layers × tokens × KV heads × head dimension × bytes/value
concepts.formulaNote: A simple full-attention cache estimate. The factor 2 accounts for stored keys and values; a head’s dimension is its number of coordinates.
concepts.example: For 2 layers, 10 tokens, 1 KV head, dimension 4, and 2 bytes/value, the cache uses 2×2×10×1×4×2 = 320 bytes, excluding overhead and other memory.
concepts.metaphor: Keep notes from earlier pages so you can consult them without rewriting them every time you turn a page.
concepts.question: Using KV bytes = 2 × layers × tokens × KV heads × head dimension × bytes/value, what is the cache size for 3 layers, 12 tokens, 2 KV heads, dimension 4, and 2 bytes/value, excluding overhead?
concepts.feedback: Substitute every factor: 2×3×12×2×4×2 = 1152 bytes. The leading 2 accounts for both keys and values.

sources.label: Documentation

questions.question: Using KV bytes = 2 × layers × tokens × KV heads × head dimension × bytes/value, what is the cache size for 3 layers, 12 tokens, 2 KV heads, dimension 4, and 2 bytes/value, excluding overhead?
questions.feedback: Substitute every factor: 2×3×12×2×4×2 = 1152 bytes. The leading 2 accounts for both keys and values.
questions.retryFeedback: Keep both the keys-and-values factor and the per-value storage factor. They represent different parts of the storage calculation.

questions.question: What does a context-window limit constrain?
options: The amount of knowledge guaranteed in an answer
The number of training examples ever seen
The token sequence a model can process under its configured setup
The number of users in an account
questions.feedback: A context limit concerns the request's usable token sequence, not unlimited reliable recall.
questions.retryFeedback: The limit concerns the sequence supplied and generated under a configured model setup. It is not the number of learned parameters.

questions.question: Why cache keys and values during autoregressive decoding?
options: To retrain the model after every token
To reuse earlier attention computations for newly generated tokens
To avoid computing any attention for new tokens
To make the prompt infinitely long
questions.feedback: Earlier keys and values remain useful, while each new token still requires computation.
questions.retryFeedback: Earlier tokens' attention representations would otherwise be recomputed during later decoding steps. A cache retains reusable intermediate results.

questions.question: Under the stated full-attention formula, what happens to KV memory if token count doubles?
questions.feedback: The cache-storage estimate is linear in retained token count when other factors are fixed.
questions.retryFeedback: In the given formula, token count is a single multiplicative factor. Hold all other storage assumptions fixed.

questions.question: What does the factor 2 in the simple KV-memory formula count?
questions.feedback: Both kinds of attention vectors are stored.
questions.retryFeedback: Each cached token contributes two kinds of attention representation. Distinguish those from the query computed for the new token.

questions.question: If a 320-byte cache uses 2 bytes per value, what would it use at 1 byte per value under otherwise identical idealized storage?
questions.feedback: Halving bytes per value halves the estimate, excluding quantization metadata and other overhead.
questions.retryFeedback: The stored value count is unchanged; only bytes per value changes. Scale the original size by that byte-width ratio.

questions.question: Does a longer context window guarantee that a model uses every detail correctly?
questions.feedback: Capacity to accept tokens differs from reliable retrieval, reasoning, and use of the content.
questions.retryFeedback: Accepting a long sequence does not prove reliable reasoning over all its details. Capacity and effective use need separate evaluation.

questions.question: For a shared 4,096-token prompt-plus-generation budget, a 3,000-token prompt leaves at most how many tokens for generation?
questions.feedback: Subtract the prompt length from the stated shared budget; actual products may impose additional limits.
questions.retryFeedback: The prompt already occupies part of the shared token allowance. Subtract its usage from the total budget.

questions.question: Can KV caching remove the memory needed to store model weights?
questions.feedback: Weights and the request's cache are different memory requirements.
questions.retryFeedback: Cached activations and model parameters serve different roles. Retaining earlier attention results does not replace the learned coefficients.

questions.question: Suppose an attention cache keeps keys and values for only the last W tokens, discarding older ones. Why can it use less memory than caching the full sequence?
options: Its retained-token count stops growing after W
It doubles the stored history at each step
It removes all keys and values
It uses exactly one byte for every sequence
questions.feedback: Once the sequence exceeds W tokens, this cache retains only the stated recent window. The full-attention formula counts every retained token.
questions.retryFeedback: Look at the token-count factor in the cache-size formula. Count retained tokens rather than every token ever processed.

concepts.title: Memory bandwidth
concepts.definition: Memory bandwidth is the amount of data transferred per unit time. It can limit speed even when computation units are fast. An operation limited mainly by moving data is called memory-bound.
concepts.formula: transfer time ≥ bytes moved / peak bytes per second
concepts.example: Moving 10 GB through a 100 GB/second channel takes at least 0.1 seconds under ideal conditions.
concepts.metaphor: A giant pantry does not help a cook if ingredients arrive through a narrow serving hatch.
concepts.question: At an ideal 300 GB/second, how long does moving 18 GB take?
concepts.feedback: Transfer time is data divided by rate: 18/300 = 0.06 seconds under the stated ideal conditions.

questions.question: At an ideal 300 GB/second, how long does moving 18 GB take?
questions.feedback: Transfer time is data divided by rate: 18/300 = 0.06 seconds under the stated ideal conditions.
questions.retryFeedback: Divide the amount transferred by the amount transferable each second. Check that the data units cancel to leave time.

questions.question: At an ideal 80 GB/s, what is the lower-bound time to move 24 GB?
questions.feedback: The ideal lower bound is 24/80 = 0.3 seconds. Other costs or lower effective bandwidth could increase actual time.
questions.retryFeedback: Use bytes moved divided by bytes per second. The ideal calculation gives a lower bound, not a promise about every actual transfer.

questions.question: Can effective transfer speed be lower than advertised peak bandwidth?
questions.feedback: Access patterns and system overhead affect achieved bandwidth.
questions.retryFeedback: Peak specifications describe favorable conditions. Access patterns, contention, and overhead can lower the achieved rate.

questions.question: What does a memory-bound computation spend much of its time waiting for?
questions.feedback: Arithmetic resources can be idle while needed data arrive.
questions.retryFeedback: Identify the resource supplying operands and storing results. The arithmetic units may be ready before that resource supplies the data.

questions.question: If bytes moved double at the same effective bandwidth, what happens to transfer time?
questions.feedback: Transfer time scales linearly with moved data in the simple model.
questions.retryFeedback: At fixed effective rate, transfer time scales with total data volume. Only the numerator of the time formula changes.

questions.question: Why can reusing cached data help performance?
options: It can reduce traffic to slower memory
questions.feedback: Reuse avoids repeated expensive transfers.
questions.retryFeedback: A nearby cached copy can serve repeated accesses without returning to a slower memory level every time.

questions.question: Does high memory capacity imply high bandwidth?
options: Only for the same byte count
questions.feedback: A device's size and transfer rate are distinct specifications.
questions.retryFeedback: Storage amount and transfer rate are independent specifications. A larger container need not deliver its contents faster.

questions.question: At 60 GB/s effective bandwidth, how long does a 21 GB transfer take in the simple model?
questions.feedback: Using the effective transfer rate gives 21/60 = 0.35 seconds.
questions.retryFeedback: Keep the data amount in the numerator and the effective transfer rate in the denominator. Match their data units before dividing.

questions.question: Why count repeated transfers when estimating runtime?
options: Memory units change after the first transfer
The same data may be moved more than once
Only unique file size ever matters
questions.feedback: Total traffic can exceed the size of the stored dataset.
questions.retryFeedback: The cost depends on traffic, not just the size of the distinct dataset. Repeated movement contributes again each time.

questions.question: Would doubling peak arithmetic throughput necessarily speed up a bandwidth-bound operation?
questions.feedback: The limiting data supply may remain unchanged.
questions.retryFeedback: Increasing a resource that is not the limiting one may leave runtime nearly unchanged. Identify whether the operation is waiting on arithmetic or data.

concepts.title: H100
concepts.definition: The NVIDIA H100 is a Hopper-generation data-center GPU. Its variants differ; the H100 SXM specification includes 80 GB of HBM3 memory.
concepts.formulaNote: A weights-only capacity estimate using decimal units. Execution also needs memory for other data.
concepts.example: A 10-billion-parameter model uses about 20 GB at 16 bits for weights, leaving nominal space for other needs.
concepts.metaphor: An H100 is a particular workshop machine, with a specified counter size and arithmetic tools.
concepts.question: Does 80 GB at 2 bytes/value prove a 40-billion-parameter model will run?
concepts.feedback: The estimate concerns weights alone. H100 is one specific GPU family, not a generic synonym for GPU or a claim about the newest hardware. Capacities vary by variant.

questions.question: Does 80 GB at 2 bytes/value prove a 40-billion-parameter model will run?
questions.feedback: The estimate concerns weights alone. H100 is one specific GPU family, not a generic synonym for GPU or a claim about the newest hardware. Capacities vary by variant.
questions.retryFeedback: The division estimates raw weight storage only. An executing model also needs room for working data, activations, and other state.

questions.question: What does H100 name?
questions.feedback: H100 identifies a specific hardware family.
questions.retryFeedback: Identify whether the name refers to a hardware product, a software interface, or a model architecture. Those are different categories.

questions.question: Which architecture generation is associated with H100?
questions.feedback: H100 belongs to NVIDIA's Hopper generation.
questions.retryFeedback: This asks for the processor architecture associated with the named device family. Distinguish that from an older GPU generation or a software platform.

questions.question: Why specify the H100 variant when discussing memory?
options: All variants are identical by definition
questions.feedback: A family name alone is not a complete configuration.
questions.retryFeedback: A product family can include different form factors and configurations. Use the specification for the exact device being discussed.

questions.question: Using the course's 80 GB H100 SXM example, how many 4-byte values fit in a weights-only decimal estimate?
questions.feedback: Divide 80 billion bytes by four bytes per value.
questions.retryFeedback: Divide the stated decimal byte capacity by bytes per value. Keep this as an ideal weight-only count rather than a full runtime estimate.

questions.question: Does the weights-only estimate include space for all runtime buffers?
questions.feedback: Usable model capacity also depends on execution overhead.
questions.retryFeedback: A weights-only calculation counts coefficients. Temporary storage and other execution data must be budgeted separately.

questions.question: In a hypothetical H100 run, transferring 75 GB at an effective 500 GB/s takes at least how long, ignoring other costs?
questions.feedback: The transfer estimate is 75/500 = 0.15 seconds. This hypothetical rate is supplied for the calculation, not a device specification.
questions.retryFeedback: Use the given effective bandwidth to convert a data amount into time. Divide amount by rate and retain the seconds unit.

questions.question: What should be checked before comparing H100 performance claims?
options: Variant, precision, workload, and measurement setup
questions.feedback: Different configurations and operations can produce different performance figures.
questions.retryFeedback: Performance numbers depend on the operation, arithmetic format, device configuration, and timing procedure. Compare like with like.

questions.question: Is H100 a synonym for CUDA?
questions.feedback: H100 is hardware; CUDA is a programming platform.
questions.retryFeedback: One name identifies a GPU family, while the other identifies a programming platform used across supported devices.

questions.question: Why avoid treating one H100 capacity estimate as a complete deployment plan?
options: The GPU automatically distributes every model
Memory overhead and actual workload requirements still matter
questions.feedback: Deployment sizing needs more than a weights-only calculation.
questions.retryFeedback: Capacity is only one constraint. Execution needs additional memory and suitable performance under the real workload, not just a weight-count calculation.

concepts.title: Compute cluster
concepts.definition: A compute cluster is a set of networked computers working together. Distributed training may divide data, model parameters, or both across devices. Data parallelism copies the model onto workers handling different batches and combines their gradients for a shared update. Model parallelism splits the model’s parameters or computation across devices.
concepts.formulaNote: A simplified model with n equally capable workers. Communication adds further time.
concepts.example: An 80-second job has 20 seconds of serial work and 60 divisible seconds. Four workers need at least 20 + 60/4 = 35 seconds in this model.
concepts.metaphor: Eight kitchens can cook together, but they still need roads to exchange ingredients and results.
concepts.question: Why might eight GPUs deliver less than eightfold speedup?
options: Each GPU must permanently store all data
More GPUs always slow every task
Communication, synchronization, and serial work consume time
concepts.feedback: Data parallelism replicates a model and combines gradients; model parallelism splits model computation. Network links and synchronization can become the bottleneck, and memory does not automatically become one shared pool.

questions.question: Why might eight GPUs deliver less than eightfold speedup?
options: Each GPU must permanently store all data
More GPUs always slow every task
Communication, synchronization, and serial work consume time
questions.feedback: Data parallelism replicates a model and combines gradients; model parallelism splits model computation. Network links and synchronization can become the bottleneck, and memory does not automatically become one shared pool.
questions.retryFeedback: Only independent work can divide ideally across devices. Coordination, data movement, and nonparallel work still occupy time.

questions.question: What is a compute cluster?
questions.feedback: A cluster coordinates computation across machines.
questions.retryFeedback: The defining feature is cooperation among separate computing machines through connections. It is not simply a single processor with several cores.

questions.question: What does data parallelism usually replicate?
questions.feedback: Workers process different data and combine training information.
questions.retryFeedback: Data parallelism distributes different examples to workers performing the same model computation. Consider what must be available on each worker.

questions.question: What does model parallelism split?
options: Model computation or parameters across devices
questions.feedback: Different devices execute different parts of the model.
questions.retryFeedback: Model parallelism distributes parts of the model itself. Contrast that with copying a complete model for each subset of data.

questions.question: Why can adding workers give diminishing returns?
questions.feedback: Coordination and sequential portions limit scaling.
questions.retryFeedback: As divisible computation shrinks, fixed work and coordination become a larger share of runtime. More workers do not shrink every term.

questions.question: For time = 2 + 8/n seconds, what is time with n = 4, excluding communication?
questions.feedback: The parallel work takes 8/4 = 2 seconds, plus 2 serial seconds.
questions.retryFeedback: Substitute the worker count only into the parallel term. The fixed-time contribution is not divided among workers.

questions.question: For T(n) = 2 + 8/n seconds, what is the limiting time as the number of workers n becomes very large?
questions.feedback: The parallel term 8/n approaches zero, but the serial 2-second term remains. The limiting time is 2 seconds.
questions.retryFeedback: Separate the part divided by the worker count from the fixed part. Increasing workers affects only the divided term in this model.

questions.question: Why combine gradients in ordinary data-parallel training?
options: To coordinate a shared model update
questions.feedback: Workers contribute information from their different batches.
questions.retryFeedback: Workers estimate gradients from different data. Combining those estimates keeps their parameter updates coordinated for the shared model.

questions.question: Does cluster memory automatically act like one unlimited local memory pool?
questions.feedback: Distributed storage and communication require explicit software support.
questions.retryFeedback: Memory on different machines must be managed and accessed through a distribution strategy. It is not automatically one local allocation space.

questions.question: What can become a bottleneck in distributed training?
questions.feedback: Moving and coordinating model information can limit throughput.
questions.retryFeedback: Workers exchange information and may need to wait for one another. Those costs can dominate even when local arithmetic is fast.

concepts.title: TSMC and chip fabrication
concepts.definition: TSMC is a semiconductor foundry: it manufactures chips designed by customers. Circuits are formed on a silicon wafer, then separated into individual chips called dies.
concepts.example: In a hypothetical batch of 100 dies, 80 passing inspection gives 80% yield. This is a teaching example, not TSMC production data.
concepts.metaphor: A foundry is the factory that fabricates another company's machine design.
concepts.question: Which role best describes TSMC's foundry business?
options: Creating every neural network's training labels
concepts.feedback: Chip design, fabrication, packaging, memory production, and software are distinct parts of the computing supply chain. Yield affects usable output and cost.

sources.title: About TSMC, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company
sources.label: Reading

questions.question: Which role best describes TSMC's foundry business?
options: Creating every neural network's training labels
questions.feedback: Chip design, fabrication, packaging, memory production, and software are distinct parts of the computing supply chain. Yield affects usable output and cost.
questions.retryFeedback: Distinguish specifying a circuit's design from physically producing it. A foundry provides manufacturing for designs supplied by customers.

questions.question: What is a semiconductor foundry's central role?
questions.feedback: A foundry fabricates semiconductor devices.
questions.retryFeedback: The foundry role concerns the physical production process. Chip architecture, end-user software, and data-center operation are different activities.

questions.question: What is a wafer?
options: A substrate on which many chip dies are fabricated
questions.feedback: Manufacturing forms many circuits before individual dies are separated.
questions.retryFeedback: Many repeated circuit patterns are fabricated on a larger substrate before separation. Identify that shared starting surface.

questions.question: What is a die?
options: An individual chip separated from a wafer
questions.feedback: A wafer can yield many individual dies.
questions.retryFeedback: The fabricated wafer contains many individual circuit units. After separation, each unit still needs suitable packaging and integration.

questions.question: In a hypothetical batch, 210 of 250 fabricated dies pass inspection. What is the yield?
questions.feedback: Yield is usable divided by manufactured: 210/250 = 0.84, or 84%.
questions.retryFeedback: Use all manufactured dies as the denominator and the usable subset as the numerator. Convert the resulting fraction to a percentage.

questions.question: Why does yield matter economically?
options: It affects usable output per manufacturing effort
questions.feedback: Lower usable output can increase cost per functioning die.
questions.retryFeedback: Manufacturing effort also produces units that cannot be used. The fraction that works affects the cost of each usable unit.

questions.question: Are chip design and chip fabrication the same activity?
questions.feedback: Design specifies circuits; fabrication physically produces them.
questions.retryFeedback: A design specifies circuitry and behavior; fabrication realizes physical devices. They can be performed by different organizations.

questions.question: Does fabrication alone produce a complete usable AI system?
questions.feedback: Packaging, memory, boards, software, and other components are also needed.
questions.retryFeedback: A fabricated chip still needs packaging, systems, software, data, and a useful application. One manufacturing stage does not supply all of them.

questions.question: After fabrication, a die is put into a package with electrical connections and physical protection. What does this packaging step contribute?
options: Connections and protection for integrating a die into a system
questions.feedback: Packaging is a distinct step in making chips usable in devices.
questions.retryFeedback: Distinguish forming the circuits on a wafer from making a separated die connectable and usable inside a device.

questions.question: If 200 dies are fabricated at 75% yield, how many are usable?
questions.feedback: Multiply 200 by 0.75.
questions.retryFeedback: Apply the usable fraction to the total die count. Express the percentage as a fraction before multiplying.

concepts.title: Borehole logs and assays
concepts.definition: Borehole logs describe rock or record sensor readings along a drilled hole. Assays measure the composition of collected samples. Together they connect geological patterns to measured mineral content. A detection limit describes a method’s ability to distinguish a small amount from background. A below-limit report does not prove the element is absent.
concepts.formula: sample record = (borehole ID, from depth, to depth, assay, units)
concepts.example: Sample A from borehole BH01 spans 100–102 m and assays 0.8% copper by mass. Its sampled interval is 102 − 100 = 2 m. A sensor log is a different measurement over depth.
concepts.metaphor: A borehole is a vertical notebook: logs describe the pages, while assays analyze selected pieces of them.
concepts.question: An analyzed sample has mass 1,000 grams and assays 0.6% copper by mass. How much copper does that assay imply in this sample?
concepts.feedback: A mass percentage of 0.6% is the fraction 0.006. Multiplying 1,000 grams by 0.006 gives 6 grams of copper.

questions.question: An analyzed sample has mass 1,000 grams and assays 0.6% copper by mass. How much copper does that assay imply in this sample?
questions.feedback: A mass percentage of 0.6% is the fraction 0.006. Multiplying 1,000 grams by 0.006 gives 6 grams of copper.
questions.retryFeedback: Convert the mass percentage to a fraction before multiplying by sample mass. Keep the resulting mass in the supplied unit.

questions.question: What identifies where a drill sample came from?
options: Borehole ID and sampled depth interval
questions.feedback: A sample needs a location along a particular borehole as well as its measured properties.
questions.retryFeedback: A sample needs both a borehole reference and a location within it. A depth number alone can occur in many different holes.

questions.question: How long is the sampled interval from 40 m to 42.5 m along a borehole?
questions.feedback: Subtract the start depth from the end depth: 42.5 − 40 = 2.5 m.
questions.retryFeedback: Interval length is the end depth minus the start depth in the same along-hole coordinate system.

questions.question: A borehole sensor measures electrical resistance, not composition. Does a high reading by itself establish copper grade?
options: No, it is a different measured property
Only if the reading has many digits
questions.feedback: No. The sensor measures a different property. It may help a validated prediction model, but its reading is not itself a copper assay.
questions.retryFeedback: Identify what the instrument actually measures. A useful relationship between two quantities does not make their measurements interchangeable.

questions.question: Why keep assay units alongside the numerical result?
options: Percent and grams per tonne describe different scales
questions.feedback: The constituent, concentration basis, and units are necessary to interpret a result.
questions.retryFeedback: A concentration number must be interpreted using its scale. The same written value means different mass fractions under different units.

questions.question: Sample M17 from BH09 at 65–66 m assays 1.4% copper. Sample M18 from BH09 at 66–67 m assays 2.1%. Which measured assay belongs to 65–66 m?
options: No copper because the samples have different IDs
questions.feedback: The requested interval belongs to M17 and its measured assay is 1.4%. The adjacent sample or a new average is not that sample's reported assay.
questions.retryFeedback: Match the requested borehole interval to its own sample record. Preserve the connection between a measured result and the material actually analyzed.

questions.question: Can a sample assay be assigned to every unsampled depth without further evidence?
options: Only if the borehole is deep
Only if its value is positive
questions.feedback: A sampled interval does not establish the composition of all the surrounding rock.
questions.retryFeedback: A measurement applies to sampled material with a defined location and extent. Extending it to unsampled intervals is an estimation step.

questions.question: Why distinguish a missing assay from a measured zero?
options: No result is different from an observed value
It makes all samples equally representative
questions.feedback: Retain observation status and any detection-limit qualification rather than silently inventing a measurement.
questions.retryFeedback: A missing result supplies no measured concentration. An observed zero or a detection-limited result has a different evidential meaning.

questions.question: Why inspect depth spacing before analyzing a sensor log?
options: Gaps and unequal spacing affect how samples should be processed
questions.feedback: The preprocessing must reflect the actual sampling positions.
questions.retryFeedback: Sequence indices do not always represent uniform physical spacing. Processing methods may depend on actual distances and gaps.

questions.question: A lab reports copper as below its detection limit: the method did not distinguish it reliably from background at that level. What does this establish?
options: The concentration equals the limit exactly
The result is below the method’s reliable detection capability
questions.feedback: Keep the below-limit qualification. It describes the method’s detection capability and is not an exact zero concentration.
questions.retryFeedback: Separate what a measurement procedure can distinguish from what material is actually absent. Preserve the qualification instead of inventing an exact value.

concepts.title: Assay quality control
concepts.definition:
Assay quality control uses reference materials, blanks, and repeated samples to assess measurement quality. These help distinguish systematic bias, contamination, and poor repeatability.

A reference material has a known composition for comparison. A blank should contain negligible target material and helps reveal contamination or background. Duplicate analyses repeat a measurement to assess repeatability.
concepts.example: A certified reference value is 1.00% copper and a lab reports 1.10%. Relative bias is 100×(1.10−1.00)/1.00 = +10%. Whether this passes depends on the specified acceptance limits and uncertainty.
concepts.metaphor: Check a scale with a known weight, check that an empty pan reads empty, then weigh the same item again.
concepts.question: A reference material has copper value 2.00% and the lab reports 2.30%. What is the relative bias?
concepts.feedback: Relative bias is 100×(2.30−2.00)/2.00 = +15%. The percentage-point difference in grades is not the relative bias.

sources.title: Quality Assurance and Quality Control, USGS
sources.label: USGS

questions.question: A reference material has copper value 2.00% and the lab reports 2.30%. What is the relative bias?
questions.feedback: Relative bias is 100×(2.30−2.00)/2.00 = +15%. The percentage-point difference in grades is not the relative bias.
questions.retryFeedback: Subtract reference from measurement, divide that difference by the reference, and then convert to percent. Preserve the sign of the difference.

questions.question: What is the main role of a blank sample?
options: Establish the grade of the entire deposit
questions.feedback: A blank is expected to contain little or none of the target analyte under its specified preparation.
questions.retryFeedback: A blank is intended to contain no relevant analyte. An unexpected signal can reveal contributions from contamination or the procedure.

questions.question: What does a certified reference material help assess?
options: Agreement with a known reference composition
questions.feedback: Its certified values and uncertainty provide a comparison for measurement performance.
questions.retryFeedback: A known reference composition allows comparison with an expected value. Repeated unknown samples test a different aspect of measurement quality.

questions.question: What do duplicate analyses primarily help assess?
options: Repeatability or precision at the duplicated stage
questions.feedback: The duplicate design determines whether it tests analytical, preparation, or sampling variability.
questions.retryFeedback: Duplicates compare repeated results at a specified processing stage. Agreement between them does not by itself establish agreement with the true value.

questions.question: Two results agree closely but are both well above a reference value. What does this suggest?
options: Good repeatability can coexist with systematic bias
questions.feedback: Consistent measurements can be consistently wrong relative to a valid reference.
questions.retryFeedback: Closeness between repeated measurements concerns precision. A shared displacement from a reference concerns a different property.

questions.question: For reference 2.0 and measured value 1.8, what is relative bias?
questions.retryFeedback: Subtract the reference from the measured value, divide by the reference, and convert the signed ratio to a percentage.

questions.question: What should happen when a QC result exceeds a predefined acceptance limit?
options: Change the limit after seeing the result without justification
Accept every assay because the file opened
Investigate the affected batch and document the disposition
questions.feedback: A failed control needs a traceable response, which may include reanalysis under the quality plan.
questions.retryFeedback: A predefined limit identifies a result requiring attention. The affected material needs a documented investigation rather than silent acceptance or arbitrary adjustment.

questions.question: Why place controls throughout analytical batches?
options: To make the sample count look larger
To reveal changes or contamination during processing
questions.feedback: Controls distributed over a run can detect problems that a single initial check misses.
questions.retryFeedback: Controls distributed through a batch can reveal effects that begin partway through processing. One control at the start may miss later changes.

questions.question: Duplicate values are 9 and 11. What is their relative percent difference, 100×abs(a−b)/((a+b)/2)?
questions.feedback: The absolute difference is 2 and the mean is 10, giving 20%.
questions.retryFeedback: The denominator is the average of the two results. Divide the absolute difference by that average before multiplying by a hundred.

questions.question: Does a below-detection-limit assay establish an exactly zero concentration?
questions.feedback: The result is qualified by the method's detection capability; preserve that qualification in the data.
questions.retryFeedback: A method can fail to distinguish a small signal from background without proving that no element is present. Preserve that distinction in the record.

concepts.title: Provenance and uncertainty
concepts.definition: Provenance records a result's origin and transformations. Uncertainty describes what is not known about its value, using a stated method or bound.
concepts.formulaNote: This interval follows if the absolute measurement error is at most δ.
concepts.example: Borehole A, 100 m depth, sensor S2: 30 °C. With a justified error bound ±0.2 °C, the interval is [29.8, 30.2] °C. Keep the source and calibration version.
concepts.metaphor: A measurement needs both a return address and a ruler showing its fuzziness.
concepts.question: What does a model score of 0.9 establish on its own?
options: A reported score whose reliability must be assessed
A guaranteed 90% chance of scientific truth
concepts.feedback: Keep source borehole, depth, units, masks, transformation versions, and uncertainty meaning. A deterministic error bound is not the same object as a statistical confidence interval or an uncalibrated score.

questions.question: What does a model score of 0.9 establish on its own?
options: A reported score whose reliability must be assessed
A guaranteed 90% chance of scientific truth
questions.feedback: Keep source borehole, depth, units, masks, transformation versions, and uncertainty meaning. A deterministic error bound is not the same object as a statistical confidence interval or an uncalibrated score.
questions.retryFeedback: A reported numerical score has a definition and calibration context. Its appearance alone does not establish reliability or an uncertainty interval.

questions.question: What does provenance describe?
options: Where a result came from and how it was transformed
Only how confident the prose sounds
questions.feedback: Origin and processing history make a result traceable.
questions.retryFeedback: Tracing a result involves its original data and the operations applied afterward. A final value alone omits that history.

questions.question: For reading 10 with an absolute error bound 2, what interval is implied?
questions.feedback: Subtract and add the bound to the reading.
questions.retryFeedback: An absolute bound allows deviations in both directions around the reading. Subtract and add the bound to form the endpoints.

questions.question: A reading is 10 and a justified absolute-error bound is 0.5. Which true value is excluded by that bound?
questions.feedback: The bound gives the interval [9.5, 10.5], including its endpoints. A true value of 10.8 would differ by 0.8 and violate the stated bound.
questions.retryFeedback: Subtract and add the error bound to form the allowed interval. Compare each candidate with both endpoints.

questions.question: Why keep preprocessing versions with outputs?
options: Transformations can change the resulting values
A version proves every result correct
questions.feedback: Reproduction needs the transformation as well as the original input.
questions.retryFeedback: Changing a transformation can alter values even when raw measurements stay fixed. Reproduction needs the transformation's identity.

questions.question: Which report best preserves provenance?
questions.feedback: The first links value, units, source interval, and computation context.
questions.retryFeedback: A traceable report identifies the value's source, scope, units, and procedure. Extra decimal places do not substitute for that context.

questions.question: Does a model's uncalibrated confidence score automatically quantify measurement uncertainty?
options: Only if between zero and one
questions.feedback: A score needs a defined, validated interpretation.
questions.retryFeedback: Model confidence and measurement uncertainty are distinct quantities. One cannot replace the other without an explicit justified relationship.

questions.question: Why distinguish a measured value from an estimated replacement filled in for a missing measurement?
options: Their evidential status and uncertainty differ
questions.feedback: An estimated replacement is not an original observation. Recording how it was produced preserves its source and uncertainty.
questions.retryFeedback: Two equal-looking numbers can come from different processes. Consider what evidence supports each value and how a later user could trace it.

questions.question: What uncertainty should a report explain?
options: What the stated interval or score actually means
Only the number of decimal places
questions.feedback: Users need the method, assumptions, and scope of an uncertainty statement.
questions.retryFeedback: Uncertainty notation can describe different kinds of variation or coverage. A report must explain the claim attached to its number.

questions.question: Can a precise-looking decimal still be highly uncertain?
questions.feedback: Displayed precision and knowledge about the true value are different properties.
questions.retryFeedback: Displayed precision describes formatting. Evidence and measurement quality determine how much uncertainty remains behind those digits.

concepts.title: Geoscience data integration
concepts.definition: Geoscience data integration connects drillhole locations, depth surveys, geological logs, assays, and other observations using consistent identifiers, coordinates, intervals, and units. A coordinate reference system defines how map coordinates correspond to locations.
concepts.formula: borehole ID + sample interval → matched observations + source metadata
concepts.example: BH01 has an assay for 100–102 m. Match it to geological records from BH01 covering that interval, check units, and retain both sources. A row at 100 m in BH02 refers to different rock.
concepts.metaphor: Assemble a map from transparent layers, checking that their landmarks line up.
concepts.question: Which key is needed to connect an assay interval to the correct borehole log?
options: Borehole identity and compatible depth intervals
concepts.feedback: Validate identity, interval overlap, units, and coordinate conventions. Depths along a deviated hole are not automatically vertical elevations. Preserve unmatched records and explain any aggregation.

sources.title: Mineral Resource Assessments, U.S. Geological Survey
sources.label: USGS

questions.question: Which key is needed to connect an assay interval to the correct borehole log?
options: Borehole identity and compatible depth intervals
questions.feedback: Validate identity, interval overlap, units, and coordinate conventions. Depths along a deviated hole are not automatically vertical elevations. Preserve unmatched records and explain any aggregation.
questions.retryFeedback: Match the physical sampling context, including the hole and interval. Coinciding row positions do not establish that correspondence.

questions.question: Why is joining drillhole records by row number unreliable?
options: Different files can order and sample records differently
questions.feedback: Use stable identities and compatible spatial or interval information.
questions.retryFeedback: Rows reflect file organization, which can differ across sources. A reliable join uses identifiers and compatible sampling coordinates.

questions.question: What should be checked before overlaying two geological maps?
options: Coordinate reference systems and spatial alignment
questions.feedback: Coordinates must have compatible meaning before positions can be compared.
questions.retryFeedback: The same numerical coordinates can locate different places under different reference systems. Check the spatial conventions before combining maps.

questions.question: An assay spans 10–12 m, but a log has readings every 0.1 m. What must integration define?
options: That the first reading always represents the interval
How log readings are summarized over that assay interval
That every reading is a separate assay
That both datasets have identical resolution
questions.feedback: The aggregation should respect the measurement support and record its method.
questions.retryFeedback: A point reading and an interval assay have different support. Define how measurements over the interval are aggregated or matched.

questions.question: What should happen to an assay with no matching borehole ID?
options: Flag it for investigation and retain its source
Attach it to the nearest row silently
Replace its ID with a random valid one
questions.feedback: An unresolved identity must not become an apparently valid match.
questions.retryFeedback: An unmatched identity means the association is unresolved. Preserve the record and its origin while investigating the mismatch.

questions.question: If a concentration is 10,000 grams per tonne, what is it in mass percent?
questions.feedback: A tonne contains 1,000,000 grams; 10,000 divided by 1,000,000 is 0.01, or 1%.
questions.retryFeedback: Convert a tonne into grams to form a dimensionless mass fraction, then multiply that fraction by a hundred for percent.

questions.question: Why retain source record IDs after joining data?
options: To guarantee the model is unbiased
To trace values back to their original records
questions.feedback: A joined dataset should preserve the origin of each contribution.
questions.retryFeedback: Integration creates new combined records. Original identifiers let someone verify where each included value came from afterward.

questions.question: Why can duplicate join keys unexpectedly increase row counts?
options: Every join always keeps the original count
One record can match several rows in the other table
questions.feedback: Check the intended one-to-one or one-to-many relationship before treating joined rows as observations.
questions.retryFeedback: A join can create one output for each matching pair. Multiple matches on a key can therefore expand the result.

questions.question: Does a successful data join prove the inputs are suitable for model training?
options: Only when there are no nulls
questions.feedback: Coverage, quality, permissions, and the prediction task still matter.
questions.retryFeedback: Syntactic compatibility does not establish correct units, labels, timing, or sampling. Suitability for a learning task needs those checks too.

questions.question: A borehole slopes away from vertical. Is distance measured along the hole automatically the same as vertical depth?
questions.feedback: Borehole trajectory is needed to relate distance along the hole to its three-dimensional position.
questions.retryFeedback: Along-hole distance follows the drilled path. Its vertical component also depends on the borehole's inclination and trajectory.

concepts.title: Windowing and missing data
concepts.definition: Windowing divides an ordered signal into local segments. A mask records which entries are observed so absent values are not mistaken for measurements.
concepts.example: Sequence (2, 4, missing, 6) gives length-3 windows (2, 4, missing) and (4, missing, 6). The second has mask (1, 0, 1): its middle value is absent.
concepts.metaphor: Cut a long film into scenes, while marking damaged frames rather than pretending they show darkness.
concepts.question: Why keep a missing-value mask after filling blanks with zero?
options: To turn every curve into a class label
To distinguish absence from a real zero
concepts.feedback: Masks carry observation status. Split boreholes before windowing; preserve curve units, sampling intervals, and preprocessing. Reconstruction losses should handle missing entries explicitly.

questions.question: Why keep a missing-value mask after filling blanks with zero?
options: To turn every curve into a class label
To distinguish absence from a real zero
questions.feedback: Masks carry observation status. Split boreholes before windowing; preserve curve units, sampling intervals, and preprocessing. Reconstruction losses should handle missing entries explicitly.
questions.retryFeedback: Filling a blank supplies a numerical placeholder. A separate indicator preserves whether that value was observed or inserted.

questions.question: For sequence (1, 2, 3, 4) and length-3 stride-1 windows, what are the windows?
questions.feedback: Move the length-three window one position at a time while it fits.
questions.retryFeedback: Slide the window one position at a time, keeping only placements where its full length fits inside the sequence.

questions.question: What does an observation mask record?
questions.feedback: Masks distinguish observed data from absent values.
questions.retryFeedback: The mask describes availability at each position. It is different from the values themselves or their estimated replacements.

questions.question: Why not treat every missing value as a genuine zero?
options: Zero can be a valid measurement
Missing data always equal the mean
questions.feedback: A placeholder and a measured zero have different meanings.
questions.retryFeedback: Replacing absence with a valid measurement value can make two different situations indistinguishable unless missingness is retained separately.

questions.question: When should boreholes be split for new-borehole evaluation?
questions.feedback: Grouping first prevents related windows from crossing the evaluation boundary.
questions.retryFeedback: Define held-out groups before creating overlapping examples. Otherwise windows derived from one physical source can cross the boundary.

questions.question: For length 8, window length 3, stride 1, and no padding, how many windows fit?
questions.feedback: The count is 8−3+1.
questions.retryFeedback: Count valid starting positions from the first index through the last index where the full window fits.

questions.question: How should a masked reconstruction loss handle absent targets?
options: Exclude or explicitly handle them under the defined policy
Treat their placeholder as ground truth automatically
Assign every one a perfect score
questions.feedback: An absent measurement is not a known reconstruction target.
questions.retryFeedback: An absent target is not a measured reconstruction reference. The loss must follow an explicit rule for excluding or handling it.

questions.question: What is the effect of increasing stride at fixed window length?
options: Less overlap and usually fewer windows
questions.feedback: The start position advances farther between windows.
questions.retryFeedback: Larger steps between window starts reduce how often nearby observations are reused. Compare the positions still visited.

questions.question: Why preserve depth information with each window?
options: To turn metres into token IDs
To reconnect outputs to the original interval
questions.feedback: A window's meaning depends on where it came from.
questions.retryFeedback: A window's array position does not fully locate it in the original borehole. Keep the metadata needed to recover that location.

questions.question: What must a loss routine handle when a window has no observed target entries?
options: A full set of invented targets
An empty-mask case without dividing by zero
questions.feedback: A masked mean needs an explicit policy when its denominator is zero.
questions.retryFeedback: A mean over observed targets uses their count as a denominator. An empty observed set requires a defined special case.

concepts.title: Ore grade estimation
concepts.definition: Ore grade is the concentration of a valuable constituent in rock. Grade estimation uses sample assays and geological information to infer values for unsampled material; an AI prediction still needs validation.
concepts.example: In a toy estimate, 1,000 tonnes of rock at 0.8% copper contain 1,000 × 0.8 / 100 = 8 tonnes of copper before recovery losses.
concepts.metaphor: Grade is the concentration of an ingredient in a mixture; knowing the mixture mass lets you estimate the ingredient mass.
concepts.question: How much copper is contained in 2,500 tonnes of rock at 1.2% copper by mass, before recovery losses?
concepts.feedback: Contained copper is 2,500×1.2/100 = 30 tonnes. Recovery would be applied separately if requested.

sources.title: Mineral resource classification: Mineral resource estimation, Wikipedia
sources.label: Wikipedia

sources.title: MapMark4: Probability calculations for mineral resource assessment, USGS
sources.label: USGS

sources.title: Direct mineral content prediction from drill core images via transfer learning, 2024
sources.label: Paper

questions.question: How much copper is contained in 2,500 tonnes of rock at 1.2% copper by mass, before recovery losses?
questions.feedback: Contained copper is 2,500×1.2/100 = 30 tonnes. Recovery would be applied separately if requested.
questions.retryFeedback: Convert grade from percent to a fraction and multiply by rock mass. This question concerns contained metal before processing losses.

questions.question: What does copper grade expressed as a mass percentage measure?
options: Copper mass divided by rock mass, multiplied by 100
Borehole depth divided by sample count
questions.feedback: Grade describes concentration; tonnage describes the amount of material.
questions.retryFeedback: Grade compares the mass of the constituent with the mass of the material containing it. Distinguish this concentration from total metal mass.

questions.question: At the same grade, what happens to contained copper when rock mass doubles?
questions.feedback: Contained metal is proportional to mass when grade stays fixed.
questions.retryFeedback: Contained metal is rock mass multiplied by the grade fraction. Hold that fraction fixed while changing the mass.

questions.question: If rock contains 8 tonnes of copper and processing recovers 75%, how much copper is recovered?
questions.feedback: Recovery applies to contained metal: 8 × 0.75 = 6 tonnes.
questions.retryFeedback: Recovery is the fraction of contained metal captured through processing. Apply it to the metal amount, not the rock mass.

questions.question: Equal masses of rock grade 1% and 3% copper. What is their combined grade?
questions.feedback: Equal masses give equal weights: (1 + 3) / 2 = 2%.
questions.retryFeedback: Combine contained metal and total rock mass. Equal rock masses give the two grades equal weight.

questions.question: A mixture has 100 tonnes at 1% copper and 300 tonnes at 3%. What is its grade?
questions.feedback: Contained copper is 1 + 9 = 10 tonnes in 400 tonnes of rock: 10 / 400 × 100 = 2.5%.
questions.retryFeedback: Weight each grade by its rock mass. A simple average of percentages is only appropriate for equal masses.

questions.question: What usually supplies measured copper-grade targets for supervised learning?
options: Laboratory assays linked to sampled material
questions.feedback: Assays provide measured labels; their quality and correspondence to input intervals still need checking.
questions.retryFeedback: A supervised grade model needs reference measurements tied to the sampled material. A sensor proxy or predicted label is not the same evidence.

questions.question: Why evaluate a grade model on spatially separated held-out data?
options: Nearby samples can be similar and make random-split scores too optimistic
A random split is never mathematically possible
questions.feedback: Choose separation that reflects the intended deployment, such as prediction in a new area.
questions.retryFeedback: Nearby observations can share spatial structure. Holding out separated locations tests a harder and more relevant form of generalization.

questions.question: Does low training error establish reliable grade estimates for a new deposit?
options: Only when all grades are positive
questions.feedback: New geology or measurement conditions may differ from training, so appropriate validation is required.
questions.retryFeedback: Fit to training samples does not establish behavior in a deposit with different geology, sampling, or measurement conditions.

questions.question: What should accompany a predicted grade for an unsampled block?
options: A claim that it is a direct assay
Its estimation method, supporting data, and uncertainty context
questions.feedback: An estimate needs traceable evidence and a clear account of its limits.
questions.retryFeedback: An unsampled block's grade is an estimate rather than a direct assay. Its interpretation needs the evidence and assumptions supporting that estimate.

concepts.title: Variograms and kriging
concepts.definition:
A semivariogram shows how differences between observations change with their separation. For sample pairs at a similar distance, average half the squared differences; this is their estimated semivariance.

Kriging uses this spatial pattern to weight observations when estimating an unsampled location. Ordinary kriging assumes an unknown constant mean within the modeled neighborhood; its weights sum to 1.
concepts.formula:
γ̂(h) = Σpairs [z(sᵢ)−z(sⱼ)]² / (2N(h))
ẑ(s₀) = Σᵢ wᵢz(sᵢ),   Σᵢwᵢ = 1
concepts.formulaNote: For separation h, average squared differences over N(h) sample pairs and divide by 2. Ordinary kriging then estimates a value at s₀ by weighting observed values z(sᵢ).
concepts.example: At one distance bin, two pairs have value differences 2 and 4. Estimated semivariance is (2²+4²)/(2×2) = 5. Kriging weights would then require a fitted model and sample geometry.
concepts.metaphor: Nearby clues can inform a missing location, but their usefulness depends on both distance and the pattern of similarity.
concepts.question: Three pairs in a distance bin have value differences −1, 3, and 4. What is their estimated semivariance?
concepts.feedback: Square all three differences and divide by twice the pair count: (1+9+16)/(2×3) = 26/6 = 13/3.

questions.question: Three pairs in a distance bin have value differences −1, 3, and 4. What is their estimated semivariance?
questions.feedback: Square all three differences and divide by twice the pair count: (1+9+16)/(2×3) = 26/6 = 13/3.
questions.retryFeedback: Negative differences are squared too. After summing the squares, divide by both the number of pairs and the factor of two in the estimator.

questions.question: What does a semivariogram plot relate?
options: Separation distance or direction to average half-squared differences
Model parameter count to token count
questions.feedback: Pairs are grouped by spatial separation to estimate how similarity changes across space.
questions.retryFeedback: The paired differences are grouped by spatial separation. The semivariogram describes how dissimilarity changes with that separation.

questions.question: If all paired observations in a distance bin are equal within each pair, what is empirical semivariance in that bin?
questions.feedback: Every paired difference is zero, so all squared contributions vanish.
questions.retryFeedback: Equal values within every pair make each pair difference vanish. Apply that to the squared-difference average.

questions.question: One pair has values 2 and 6. What is its semivariance contribution when it is the only pair in the bin?
questions.feedback: Square the difference 4 and divide by 2: 16/2=8.
questions.retryFeedback: Subtract the paired observations, square that difference, and then apply the one-half factor for semivariance.

questions.question: For a fixed set of observation pairs, every value difference doubles. What happens to the estimated semivariance?
options: It becomes four times as large
questions.feedback: Semivariance averages squared pair differences with the same denominator. Doubling each difference multiplies every squared term by four.
questions.retryFeedback: Follow the change through the square in the numerator. The number of pairs and the factor of two in the denominator remain fixed.

questions.question: At the same separation distance, east–west sample pairs differ little, while north–south pairs differ much more. What extra information should a spatial-dependence model consider?
options: Only the number of decimal places
questions.feedback: The observed differences depend on direction as well as distance. A model may need to represent that directional structure.
questions.retryFeedback: Distance is held fixed in the comparison. Identify which spatial property changes between the two sets of pairs.

questions.question: For ordinary kriging, what must the weights sum to?
questions.feedback: The unit-sum condition preserves an unknown constant mean under the model.
questions.retryFeedback: Ordinary kriging uses a constraint so an unknown constant mean is reproduced without bias. Apply the estimator to a constant field.

questions.question: Given kriging weights 0.4 and 0.6 and corresponding observations 3 and 8, what is the estimate?
questions.feedback: The weighted estimate is 0.4×3+0.6×8 = 1.2+4.8 = 6.
questions.retryFeedback: Pair each observation with its own weight and add the products. Normalized weights need not make this an equally weighted average.

questions.question: Fixed ordinary-kriging weights have a total of 1. If every sample value increases by 2, how much does the weighted estimate increase?
questions.feedback: The change is Σwᵢ×2 = 2Σwᵢ = 2. The sum-to-one condition preserves a common shift of all sample values.
questions.retryFeedback: Separate the original weighted sum from the extra contribution of the same added value at each sample. Use the stated sum of weights.

questions.question: A kriging uncertainty estimate is calculated from a fitted spatial model. Does that number automatically include all errors in the model assumptions and sample measurements?
questions.feedback: It is conditional on the spatial model and setup; model misspecification, uncertain parameters, and sampling biases need separate consideration.
questions.retryFeedback: The reported variance is conditional on the statistical model and assumptions. Geological, measurement, or model uncertainty can extend beyond it.

concepts.title: Spatial cross-validation
concepts.definition: Spatial cross-validation separates training and evaluation by location to assess predictions beyond nearby observations. Blocks, held-out sites, and optional buffers should reflect the intended deployment. Cross-validation repeats the split across different held-out regions. Each split is a fold, with its own training and evaluation data.
concepts.formulaNote: With a buffer of width b, exclude training locations closer than b to the test region.
concepts.example: A held-out block has a 100 m exclusion buffer. A candidate training sample 30 m from its boundary is excluded; one 150 m away satisfies this distance rule.
concepts.metaphor: Practice on one neighborhood, then test across a boundary wide enough to avoid copying from next door.
concepts.question: A held-out test block has an 80 m exclusion buffer. Which candidate training point satisfies distance ≥ 80 m from the test region?
concepts.feedback: Only the point 90 m away reaches or exceeds the stated 80 m boundary. The other distances lie inside the exclusion buffer.

sources.title: Cross-validation Strategies for Data with Spatial Structure, Roberts et al.
sources.label: Paper

questions.question: A held-out test block has an 80 m exclusion buffer. Which candidate training point satisfies distance ≥ 80 m from the test region?
questions.feedback: Only the point 90 m away reaches or exceeds the stated 80 m boundary. The other distances lie inside the exclusion buffer.
questions.retryFeedback: Apply the stated inequality to each candidate distance. The buffer is a minimum allowed separation, not a preferred maximum distance.

questions.question: Why can a random row split overstate performance on new geological areas?
options: Nearby training and test samples may share strong spatial information
questions.feedback: The split may measure interpolation near observed material when deployment requires generalization farther away.
questions.retryFeedback: A row-level split can place highly related neighbors on opposite sides. That does not simulate prediction in a genuinely unfamiliar region.

questions.question: What should determine the spatial split design?
options: The intended prediction setting and dependence in the data
