questions.feedback: A new borehole, a nearby block, and a new deposit are different generalization tasks.
questions.retryFeedback: The split should reflect where predictions will be made and how information is shared across space. One fixed recipe is not appropriate everywhere.

questions.question: Why keep all windows from a held-out borehole together?
options: Overlapping or related windows can leak information across folds
questions.feedback: Split related units before creating examples that share source measurements.
questions.retryFeedback: Windows can reuse raw measurements and share geological context. Keeping only their row IDs separate does not remove that dependence.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an exclusion buffer around a test block?
options: Guarantee identical geology in every fold
Reduce very close training-test contact under the chosen evaluation design
Add synthetic assays to the test set
Ensure the training set is always larger
questions.feedback: A buffer can make the spatial separation better resemble a harder deployment setting.
questions.retryFeedback: A buffer removes nearby training support around the test region. It changes the spatial information available during evaluation.

questions.question: If a 100 m buffer is required, is a training sample exactly 100 m from the test region allowed under a distance-at-least rule?
options: Only if its grade is high
Only if it is in the test set
questions.feedback: The stated inequality includes equality: distance ≥100 m.
questions.retryFeedback: “At least” includes equality at the threshold. Distinguish that rule from a strictly-greater-than requirement.

questions.question: When should parameters for normalization or for filling missing values (imputation) be fitted in spatial cross-validation?
options: On the full dataset before splitting
On each test block's target labels
Only after combining predictions with test answers
questions.feedback: Preprocessing can leak information too, so it belongs inside the fold-specific training workflow.
questions.retryFeedback: Preprocessing parameters are learned from observations. Fit them again using only the training portion of each fold.

questions.question: Does leave-one-borehole-out evaluation necessarily prove performance on a distant new deposit?
options: Only if there are ten holes
questions.feedback: Nearby held-out holes may not reproduce the geological and measurement shifts of a distant deposit.
questions.retryFeedback: Holding out one hole tests that design's separation and coverage. A distant deposit can introduce a larger change in conditions.

questions.question: What can happen if spatial separation leaves very little training data?
options: The test may be harder and estimates less stable
questions.feedback: Report data coverage and uncertainty, and choose a split that answers a useful deployment question.
questions.retryFeedback: Greater separation can reduce training coverage and sample size. The resulting score and its uncertainty depend on those changes.

questions.question: Why report performance across several spatial folds rather than only the best one?
options: Different regions can have different difficulty
The best fold proves universal accuracy
Fold selection may use the desired conclusion
questions.feedback: Across-region variation is relevant evidence about how performance transfers.
questions.retryFeedback: Selecting only the easiest region gives an incomplete account. Across-fold results reveal variation in performance across locations.

concepts.title: Mineral processing and recovery
concepts.definition: Mineral processing separates valuable material into a concentrate and leaves a tailings stream. Metal recovery measures how much of the feed's contained metal reaches the concentrate; concentrate grade measures its concentration.
concepts.formula: Recovery = (concentrate mass × concentrate grade)/(feed mass × feed grade)
concepts.formulaNote: Express both grades as mass fractions and use the same mass units in numerator and denominator.
concepts.example: For a steady, balanced example, 100 t of feed at 2% copper contains 2 t copper. A 10 t concentrate at 16% contains 1.6 t, giving recovery 1.6/2 = 80%. The 90 t tailings contain the remaining 0.4 t copper.
concepts.metaphor: Sort useful grains from a mixture: the selected pile's purity differs from the fraction of useful grains you managed to collect.
concepts.question: Feed contains 5 tonnes of copper and the concentrate contains 3.5 tonnes. What is copper recovery?
concepts.feedback: Recovery is captured copper divided by feed copper: 3.5/5 = 0.7 = 70%.

sources.title: Mass Balancing of Concentrator Data, Metso
sources.label: Reading

questions.question: Feed contains 5 tonnes of copper and the concentrate contains 3.5 tonnes. What is copper recovery?
questions.feedback: Recovery is captured copper divided by feed copper: 3.5/5 = 0.7 = 70%.
questions.retryFeedback: Compare contained metal masses on the same basis. The denominator is metal entering in the feed, not the concentrate's total mass.

questions.question: How does concentrate grade differ from metal recovery?
options: Both always have the same numerical value
Grade is concentration in the concentrate; recovery is the fraction of feed metal captured
questions.feedback: The denominators differ: concentrate mass for grade, feed contained metal for recovery.
questions.retryFeedback: The two ratios use different denominators: product material for concentration and incoming metal for capture efficiency.

questions.question: A 5-tonne concentrate has copper grade 20% by mass. How much copper does it contain?
questions.feedback: Multiply 5 by 0.20.
questions.retryFeedback: Convert concentrate grade to a mass fraction and multiply by concentrate mass. Keep metal mass distinct from total concentrate mass.

questions.question: In a steady two-output dry-mass balance, feed is 250 tonnes and concentrate is 40 tonnes. What is tailings mass?
questions.feedback: Conservation gives feed = concentrate + tailings. Thus tailings = 250−40 = 210 tonnes.
questions.retryFeedback: Both output streams must add to the supplied feed mass under the closed balance. Subtract the known output to find the other.

questions.question: Feed contains 7.5 tonnes of copper and concentrate captures 6.3 tonnes. How much copper remains in tailings under a closed balance?
questions.feedback: Under the stated balance, remaining copper is 7.5−6.3 = 1.2 tonnes. This is metal mass, not total tailings mass.
questions.retryFeedback: Track the same material through both streams. Subtract captured copper from feed copper, keeping metal mass distinct from bulk stream mass.

questions.question: Does a higher concentrate grade necessarily mean higher metal recovery?
questions.feedback: A tighter separation may produce a purer concentrate while sending more valuable metal to tailings.
questions.retryFeedback: A product can become richer by rejecting more material while losing some valuable metal. Concentration and capture can trade off.

questions.question: A wet mass includes water; a dry mass excludes it. Grades are stated on a specified mass basis. Why use compatible mass and grade bases for feed and concentrate?
options: All wet masses equal dry masses
Moisture determines the atomic mass of copper
Water content can distort the mass and metal balance
Grades are independent of their stated basis
questions.feedback: Multiplying a dry-basis grade by an uncorrected wet mass includes water as though it carried that grade. Convert the measurements to compatible bases before balancing metal.
questions.retryFeedback: Check what material is counted in the denominator of each grade and in the mass it multiplies. Extra water changes mass without adding metal.

questions.question: If contained feed metal is 10 tonnes and recovery is 70%, what metal mass reaches concentrate?
questions.feedback: Multiply contained metal by the recovered fraction: 10×0.70=7 tonnes.
questions.retryFeedback: Apply the recovery fraction to contained feed metal. The result concerns metal reaching the product, not total product mass.

questions.question: What does a calculated recovery above 100% suggest in a closed, steady metal balance?
options: Creation of additional metal by separation
A problem with measurements, bases, time alignment, or balance assumptions
A normal requirement of high concentrate grade
questions.feedback: Account for inventory and other streams when applicable, and check the data before accepting an impossible closed-balance result.
questions.retryFeedback: A closed steady balance cannot create extra metal. An apparent excess calls for checking measurements and the balance's assumptions.

questions.question: Why can AI predictions of processing recovery need validation when ore properties change?
options: Feed properties cannot be model inputs
A high training score proves future performance
The feed's mineralogy and behavior may differ from training conditions
Recovery is always a universal constant
questions.feedback: Recovery depends on process and material conditions, so evaluate the intended operating range.
questions.retryFeedback: The relationship between inputs and processing outcomes depends on material properties. New mineralogy can change that relationship from training.

concepts.title: Representation alignment
concepts.definition: Representation alignment connects domain vectors or tokens to language tasks. Paired examples can train a model to use those representations when predicting an answer.
concepts.formula: minimize −Σᵢ ln P_θ(answerᵢ ∣ qᵢ, codesᵢ, metadataᵢ)
concepts.formulaNote: An example supervised objective: increase the probability of each known answer given its question, codes, and metadata.
concepts.example: For a code paired with answer “rising,” predicting probability 0.2 gives loss −ln(0.2) ≈ 1.61. At 0.8, loss ≈ 0.22. Paired data teach the connection.
concepts.metaphor: Inventing an alphabet is easy; teaching readers what its symbols refer to takes examples and practice.
concepts.question: What must follow assigning new IDs to log patterns?
options: Assume the LLM understands them immediately
Interpret larger IDs as deeper rocks
Establish and evaluate their connection to language and tasks
concepts.feedback: Options include learned embeddings or adapters, paired language training, or a defined tool interface. New vocabulary tokens require model/tokenizer support; printed ID strings alone are not a learned scientific language.

questions.question: What must follow assigning new IDs to log patterns?
options: Assume the LLM understands them immediately
Interpret larger IDs as deeper rocks
Establish and evaluate their connection to language and tasks
questions.feedback: Options include learned embeddings or adapters, paired language training, or a defined tool interface. New vocabulary tokens require model/tokenizer support; printed ID strings alone are not a learned scientific language.
questions.retryFeedback: Creating identifiers establishes a coding convention. Using them meaningfully in language requires a supported relationship to evidence and tasks.

questions.question: What does representation alignment connect in this course?
options: Only training and test row numbers
questions.feedback: The interface must relate domain information to what the language task needs.
questions.retryFeedback: Separate representation construction from establishing how a language-facing system interprets and uses those representations.

questions.question: Why are paired domain examples and answers useful?
options: They provide evidence for learning the relationship
They make every ID meaningful without training
questions.feedback: Training pairs can teach how representations support answers.
questions.retryFeedback: Paired observations supply examples of how domain information relates to the desired language output. An ID list alone lacks that relation.

questions.question: Does assigning an integer ID to a code teach an LLM its scientific meaning?
options: Only if the ID is short
questions.feedback: Naming a code is different from learning or defining its semantics.
questions.retryFeedback: The numerical identity is arbitrary. Its intended scientific interpretation must enter through training, metadata, or a defined interface.

questions.question: An adapter here is a learned mapping from domain vectors into representations a language model can accept. What role can it play in alignment?
options: Map domain representations into a usable model interface
questions.feedback: An adapter is one possible learned connection between spaces or components.
questions.retryFeedback: Follow what the mapping connects. Making representations usable by another component is distinct from proving the truth of every resulting answer.

questions.question: Why include units and depth metadata alongside codes?
options: The codes alone may not preserve the needed context
questions.feedback: A representation must support interpreting the underlying observations.
questions.retryFeedback: A compact code may omit where a signal was measured or the units used. Those details can be essential for interpretation.

questions.question: What is a tool interface an alternative way to provide?
options: Defined operations over domain data or representations
questions.feedback: Tools can expose explicit semantics without relying solely on learned token meanings.
questions.retryFeedback: A model can request operations through a contract without directly interpreting every internal coordinate. The operation's meaning must be defined.

questions.question: How should alignment quality be evaluated?
options: On held-out language tasks grounded in domain evidence
questions.feedback: The desired connection is demonstrated by correct use on relevant new cases.
questions.retryFeedback: Alignment should be assessed on the tasks it is meant to support, using examples and evidence excluded from fitting.

questions.question: Could an aligned model still give an unsupported answer?
questions.feedback: Training does not remove the need for grounding and validation.
questions.retryFeedback: Learning a useful representation connection does not guarantee every generated statement follows from available evidence. Check the answer itself.

questions.question: What extra work accompanies adding new vocabulary tokens?
options: Tokenizer/model support and meaningful training or interfaces
questions.feedback: New discrete symbols need a supported, useful role in the full system.
questions.retryFeedback: New symbols must be handled consistently by encoding and model interfaces. Useful interpretation also requires a learning signal or defined semantics.

concepts.title: Benchmark and ablation
concepts.definition: A benchmark defines fixed evaluation tasks and metrics. An ablation changes one component to test what it contributes under a controlled comparison.
concepts.formula: accuracy = correct / total;   change = scorefull − scorewithout
concepts.example: On the same 50 held-out questions, the full system gets 40 right (80%). Disabling its learned-token input gives 35 (70%). The observed drop is 10 percentage points.
concepts.metaphor: Race on the same course, then remove one engine part to see whether it actually helped.
concepts.question: What would best test whether learned tokens add value?
options: Compare different tasks with different answer rules
Tune on the final test until the score rises
Compare matched systems with and without tokens on held-out boreholes
concepts.feedback: Hold the task, dataset and evaluation rules fixed. The example is an inference-time ablation of token input, not proof that tokens caused the whole gain. Such removal can introduce distribution shift; matched retraining and repeated runs answer complementary questions. Compare against raw-data tools and conventional representations, and evaluate reconstruction, scientific accuracy and cost.

questions.question: What would best test whether learned tokens add value?
options: Compare different tasks with different answer rules
Tune on the final test until the score rises
Compare matched systems with and without tokens on held-out boreholes
questions.feedback: Hold the task, dataset and evaluation rules fixed. The example is an inference-time ablation of token input, not proof that tokens caused the whole gain. Such removal can introduce distribution shift; matched retraining and repeated runs answer complementary questions. Compare against raw-data tools and conventional representations, and evaluate reconstruction, scientific accuracy and cost.
questions.retryFeedback: Isolate the proposed component's effect by making the comparison otherwise similar. Use evidence excluded from training to judge the difference.

questions.question: What should a benchmark fix?
options: Tasks, data splits, metrics, and evaluation rules
questions.feedback: Fixed evaluation conditions support meaningful comparisons.
questions.retryFeedback: A fair comparison needs common task definitions and measurement procedures. Different splits or metrics can change what a score means.

questions.question: What is an ablation?
options: Adding many changes and attributing the result to one
A controlled change to test a component's contribution
questions.feedback: An ablation isolates a specific component or choice as far as the setup permits.
questions.retryFeedback: Change a component while controlling other relevant factors. An unrelated second system may differ for several reasons at once.

questions.question: If 18 of 20 answers are correct, what is accuracy?
questions.feedback: Divide 18 by 20.
questions.retryFeedback: Divide the number of correct answers by the total evaluated, then express the fraction as a percentage.

questions.question: On the same benchmark, a full system scores 0.86 and an ablated system scores 0.74. What is the absolute score difference in decimal form?
questions.feedback: The difference is 0.86−0.74 = 0.12, equivalent to 12 percentage points if these scores are accuracies.
questions.retryFeedback: Subtract the ablated score from the full-system score. The question requests an absolute difference, not a relative percentage change.

questions.question: Why can removing an input only at inference complicate an ablation?
options: It proves the input has no value
questions.feedback: The model may encounter inputs unlike those used in training.
questions.retryFeedback: The model was trained with a particular input distribution. Removing information only at test time can introduce an additional mismatch.

questions.question: Why compare against a raw-data computation tool?
options: A simpler approach may already solve the task
questions.feedback: A relevant baseline tests whether the proposed representation adds value.
questions.retryFeedback: A complex representation should add value beyond readily available alternatives. A direct computation may answer some questions without that extra machinery.

questions.question: Should reconstruction quality and question-answering accuracy be reported separately?
questions.feedback: They measure different properties and can diverge.
questions.retryFeedback: These metrics test different objectives. A system can reproduce signals accurately without answering evidence-based questions well, or vice versa.

questions.question: Why use repeated runs or uncertainty estimates when appropriate?
options: Scores can vary with sampling and training randomness
They permit tuning on every test result
questions.feedback: A single difference may be noisy rather than a stable improvement.
questions.retryFeedback: Both sampled data and fitting randomness can affect the observed result. One run may not reveal how stable the comparison is.

questions.question: Does higher accuracy automatically mean a better deployable system?
options: Only with a large test set
questions.feedback: Cost, latency, reliability, and user needs also affect usefulness.
questions.retryFeedback: Deployment also depends on costs, reliability, integration, and consequences of mistakes. One predictive score does not capture all of those needs.

concepts.title: Open source and reproducibility
concepts.definition: Open-source licensing permits use, study, modification, and redistribution under stated terms. Reproducibility requires enough materials to repeat and evaluate a result.
concepts.formula: data + code + settings + environment → reproducible result
concepts.formulaNote: A reminder of the materials needed to repeat a computation.
concepts.example: Publish allowed data (2, 4, 6), code mean(x), and the environment. Another person obtains (2+4+6)/3 = 4. Publishing only “result = 4” cannot reproduce the calculation.
concepts.metaphor: Share the recipe, ingredients, oven settings, and tasting rules so others can check the cake.
concepts.question: Is publishing only trained weights sufficient for a reproducible open-source experiment?
options: Yes, all missing details are inside the weights
Only if the weights are large
No, licensing and the experimental materials also matter
concepts.feedback: Publish appropriate licenses, code, dependencies, configurations, splits, and permitted data or retrieval instructions. Numerical reproducibility may require tolerances because hardware and software can change rounding.

sources.title: The Open Source Definition, Open Source Initiative
sources.label: Reading

questions.question: Is publishing only trained weights sufficient for a reproducible open-source experiment?
options: Yes, all missing details are inside the weights
Only if the weights are large
No, licensing and the experimental materials also matter
questions.feedback: Publish appropriate licenses, code, dependencies, configurations, splits, and permitted data or retrieval instructions. Numerical reproducibility may require tolerances because hardware and software can change rounding.
questions.retryFeedback: Weights are one experimental ingredient. Repeating and legitimately reusing an experiment also depends on its materials, procedure, and permissions.

questions.question: What does open-source licensing provide under its terms?
options: Rights to use, study, modify, and redistribute
Automatic access to every training dataset
questions.feedback: Permissions come from the applicable license.
questions.retryFeedback: An open-source license defines permitted activities and conditions. Public visibility alone does not establish those rights.

questions.question: Does publishing code alone guarantee reproducibility?
questions.feedback: Data, settings, dependencies, and evaluation details may also be needed.
questions.retryFeedback: Code still depends on data, settings, software versions, and execution details. Its availability does not specify the entire experiment.

questions.question: Why record train-validation-test splits?
options: Different splits can produce different results
questions.feedback: The evaluation setup is part of the experiment.
questions.retryFeedback: The exact examples used for fitting and assessment affect reported scores. A new random split is not the same experimental condition.

questions.question: What should be shared when raw data cannot legally be redistributed?
options: Permitted retrieval instructions and sufficient metadata
questions.feedback: Reproducibility materials must respect data rights.
questions.retryFeedback: Sharing must respect the applicable permissions. Reproduction can still be supported by describing lawful access and the required data precisely.

questions.question: Why record the versions of software libraries used by an experiment?
questions.feedback: An environment record helps recreate the computation.
questions.retryFeedback: Dependencies participate in the computation. Different releases can change results or prevent the experiment from running as described.

questions.question: Does open source mean the software has no license obligations?
questions.feedback: The license's conditions still apply.
questions.retryFeedback: A license grants rights under stated terms. “Open” does not remove the need to read and satisfy those terms.

questions.question: Why use numerical tolerances when comparing reproduced results?
options: Hardware and rounding can cause small differences
questions.feedback: A suitable tolerance distinguishes harmless numerical variation from material changes.
questions.retryFeedback: Numerical implementations can differ slightly without changing the substantive result. Comparisons should use a justified tolerance for that context.

questions.question: What does a random seed help reproduce?
options: Random choices under a specified implementation
questions.feedback: Seeds help control randomness but are not a complete reproducibility package.
questions.retryFeedback: Recall how a seed sets a pseudorandom generator’s starting state. Repeating the sequence still depends on using the same implementation.

questions.question: Which bundle best supports repeating a benchmark?
options: Code, data access, configuration, environment, and evaluation rules
Only a screenshot of the score
questions.feedback: A result depends on the full experimental setup.
questions.retryFeedback: Repeating a result requires the complete path from accessible inputs to measured outputs, not merely one trained artifact.

concepts.title: Forward-deployed engineering
concepts.definition: Forward-deployed engineering embeds technical work with users to define a valuable problem, integrate a solution, and measure its performance in real operations.
concepts.formula: time saved per case = previous time − deployed time
concepts.example: If a verified workflow reduces a task from 30 to 10 minutes, 12 tasks save 240 minutes, or 4 hours.
concepts.metaphor: An engineer builds a bridge at the actual river, adjusting to its banks and traffic.
concepts.question: What makes a model demonstration a delivered operational solution?
options: Integration, user acceptance, and measured performance in use
An impressive score on an unrelated dataset
concepts.feedback: For a mineral extraction workflow, work with geologists and processing teams to define acceptance criteria, check data quality, integrate results, and monitor use. The time-saving example is hypothetical.

questions.question: What makes a model demonstration a delivered operational solution?
options: Integration, user acceptance, and measured performance in use
An impressive score on an unrelated dataset
questions.feedback: For a mineral extraction workflow, work with geologists and processing teams to define acceptance criteria, check data quality, integrate results, and monitor use. The time-saving example is hypothetical.
questions.retryFeedback: A demonstration shows a capability under selected conditions. Operational delivery also requires use within the actual workflow and evidence of value there.

questions.question: What is central to forward-deployed engineering here?
options: Working with users on a valuable operational problem
questions.feedback: The work joins problem definition, integration, and measured use.
questions.retryFeedback: Begin with the user's task and constraints. A technically interesting model is useful only if it addresses a relevant operational need.

questions.question: If a task falls from 20 minutes to 12 minutes, what is time saved per case?
questions.feedback: Subtract the deployed time from the previous time.
questions.retryFeedback: Time saved is the old duration minus the new duration. A percentage reduction would require an additional division.

questions.question: Why establish a baseline workflow?
options: To make every model result correct
To measure improvement against actual prior practice
questions.feedback: A baseline gives the comparison needed to assess value.
questions.retryFeedback: An improvement claim needs a reference. Measure how the task was previously accomplished before attributing gains to the new system.

questions.question: Does a polished demonstration prove operational success?
options: Only with a live chat interface
questions.feedback: Production reliability and measurable user benefit require further evidence.
questions.retryFeedback: Presentation quality does not establish sustained usefulness, integration, or reliability under everyday conditions. Those need evidence from use.

questions.question: What should problem discovery clarify?
options: Who needs what decision or task improved
questions.feedback: A useful solution starts from a concrete user need.
questions.retryFeedback: Problem discovery identifies the person, decision, and desired outcome. A chosen algorithm does not by itself define the problem.

questions.question: Why involve domain users during development?
options: They can reveal practical constraints and failure cases
They eliminate the need for tests
questions.feedback: Operational knowledge shapes what will work in context.
questions.retryFeedback: Domain users know exceptions, constraints, and consequences that curated examples may omit. Their feedback can change the solution requirements.

questions.question: What is integration work?
options: Connecting the solution to real data, systems, and workflows
questions.feedback: The solution must fit the environment in which users will operate it.
questions.retryFeedback: A working component must exchange data and fit existing processes. That surrounding connection is part of delivering the solution.

questions.question: Why monitor outcomes after deployment?
options: Actual use may differ from the demo or test setting
questions.feedback: Ongoing evidence reveals reliability and value under real conditions.
questions.retryFeedback: Real users and data can differ from test scenarios and can change over time. Continued observation checks whether intended benefits persist.

questions.question: A geologist must approve extracted assay records before use. What should the deployed workflow include?
options: Automatic approval of every model output
A review step linked to the source records
A confidence score in place of the review
questions.feedback: Integration must support the actual acceptance process and make the evidence available to the reviewer.
questions.retryFeedback: The approval requirement is part of the task, not an inconvenience to skip. The reviewer needs access to the evidence behind extracted values.

concepts.title: Grounded model conversation
concepts.definition: A grounded model conversation links a natural-language question to identified data and a defined computation, then reports the result with assumptions and evidence.
concepts.formula: question → validated inputs → model/tool → result → explained answer
concepts.example: “How much copper is recovered at 80% recovery?” For 1,000 t of rock at 0.8% copper, the tool computes 1,000 × 0.008 × 0.80 = 6.4 t. This assumes the stated grade represents the feed and recovery applies to its contained copper.
concepts.metaphor: Language is the interpreter at the laboratory door; instruments and models do the measured work inside.
concepts.question: What is the strongest scientific answer to a “what if” question?
options: A computed result with the model, inputs, units, and assumptions
A claim that a simulation guarantees reality
concepts.feedback: The answer should expose its source grade, feed mass, recovery assumption, and calculation. A recovery scenario is conditional; a fluent explanation does not establish the performance of a real processing plant.

questions.question: What is the strongest scientific answer to a “what if” question?
options: A computed result with the model, inputs, units, and assumptions
A claim that a simulation guarantees reality
questions.feedback: The answer should expose its source grade, feed mass, recovery assumption, and calculation. A recovery scenario is conditional; a fluent explanation does not establish the performance of a real processing plant.
questions.retryFeedback: A hypothetical conclusion should follow from a stated model and specified inputs. Plausible prose alone does not establish that calculation or its assumptions.

questions.question: What anchors a grounded numerical answer?
options: Identified data and a defined computation
questions.feedback: The answer should be checkable against evidence and method.
questions.retryFeedback: Trace the numerical claim to the measurements used and the operation applied. A confident statement without that trace is not sufficient.

questions.question: What should happen when required input data are missing?
options: Invent plausible values without saying so
Acknowledge the gap or obtain the inputs
questions.feedback: A grounded workflow cannot treat absent evidence as observed data.
questions.retryFeedback: An undefined required input prevents the intended calculation. The response must represent that limitation rather than invent a convenient value.

questions.question: Why validate units before a model calculation?
options: Unit mismatches can invalidate the result
questions.feedback: The computation must receive quantities with the expected meaning.
questions.retryFeedback: A computation interprets numbers according to its expected scales. Correct arithmetic on mismatched units can still produce an invalid result.

questions.question: Does attaching a source link make an unrelated answer grounded?
options: Only if the answer is short
Only if the link is official
questions.feedback: The evidence must support the specific claim and computation.
questions.retryFeedback: Grounding requires a relevant connection between the evidence and the claim. Merely displaying a reference does not create that connection.

questions.question: Which response best separates evidence from inference?
options: 'Everything is certain because the model said so'
'The tool reports X; under assumption Y, this suggests Z'
'The source exists, so all conclusions follow'
questions.feedback: Explicit assumptions show how the conclusion follows and where it is limited.
questions.retryFeedback: Distinguish what was measured or computed from what is concluded under an additional assumption. The wording should make that boundary visible.

questions.question: Why keep the tool result distinct from the language explanation?
options: The model must hide all failures
The explanation should faithfully reflect what was computed
The explanation can change measured values freely
questions.feedback: Language communicates the result; it should not invent additional evidence.
questions.retryFeedback: The calculation has a defined output and scope. A generated explanation must not silently add claims that the output did not establish.

questions.question: Does a correct copper-recovery calculation establish that a plant will achieve that recovery?
questions.feedback: The arithmetic is conditional on the recovery input; actual recovery needs process measurements or a validated predictive model.
questions.retryFeedback: The calculation follows its inputs and assumptions. Actual plant behavior also depends on whether those inputs and assumptions hold in operation.

questions.question: What should a user be able to trace in a grounded answer?
options: The source interval, computation, assumptions, and reported result
questions.feedback: Traceability makes the answer understandable and verifiable.
questions.retryFeedback: Reproducibility requires following the claim back through its evidence and reasoning. A final number alone hides that path.

questions.question: A tool predicts recovered copper assuming 80% recovery. The answer says, "The plant will definitely recover this amount." What must change?
options: Treat a fluent explanation as a plant measurement
Hide the recovery value from the reader
Remove the calculation and keep the guarantee
State that the amount is conditional on the recovery assumption
questions.feedback: The tool computed a scenario, not a measured or guaranteed outcome. A grounded answer reports the amount together with its recovery assumption.
questions.retryFeedback: Compare the certainty in the answer with the evidence supplied to the calculation. An assumed input does not become an observed fact when a tool uses it.
